  • The continual references to "big ships" makes one think of spaceships that are going to leave Earth. They're really just boats.

tropes.name: Regional Redecoration
tropes.html: Hoo-boy, where do we begin? Southern California is torn to shreds by an enormous earthquake, one big enough to rip open a new canyon and causes the fragmented land to sink into the ocean; Yellowstone national park is wiped out when the supervolcano erupts, Las Vegas is split in two by a huge fissure, and Hawaii is buried under miles of lava. However, the crowning moment has to be when the Earth's crust shifts. According to Adrian, it moves about 23 degrees to the southwest, which puts Wisconsin at the center of the new magnetic south pole. Conveniently, it also pushes the Himalayas close to the main characters. And during the crust shift, the African continent somehow rises several thousand feet, which saves it from the floods.

tropes.name: Rekindled Sparks
tropes.html: The film has a divorced chauffeur mending his relationship with his ex-wife and family after a world-ending disaster.

tropes.name: The Remnant
tropes.html: The survivors on the Arks, along with all the animals and cultural treasures they managed to save, are all that remains of human civilization. Everyone and everything else on Earth has perished.

tropes.name: Rousing Speech
tropes.html: Adrian, to get the other world leaders to agree to open the doors and let the last group of refugees in, even though it could harm their ship.

tropes.name: Rule of Cool
tropes.html:
• The depiction of the various calamities, as well as the scene of the various species of animal being air-lifted to the arks.
  • When was the last time you saw a plane dodge a subway train by flying past beneath it?

tropes.name: Rule of Symbolism
tropes.html:
• At the beginning of the movie, after Jackson, Noah, and Lucy sneak into the restricted area of Yellowstone, Noah asks fairly randomly "Haven't you seen the signs?" It takes place just long enough after the signs have been shown that it seems out of place and almost like a warning.
  • The Cristo Redentor crumbles spectacularly. See the Sistine Chapel example below.
  • The Arks. They even carry animals.
  • The Sistine Chapel crumbles and is destroyed. Guess where the ceiling splits? The crack separates Adam's finger from God's finger.
  • Also, just afterwards, the masses praying there are crushed by the dome when it topples from St. Peter's Square.
  • Jackson Curtis' son is named "Noah," and he later rescues Ark 4 from disaster.
  • At the end the human race all goes back to Africa, where it started out in the first place.
  • The White House getting destroyed by the USS John F. Kennedy.

tropes.name: Running Gag
tropes.html:
• Jackson: "I'm on my way toward you/hurtling toward you as we speak!"
  • Jackson's daughter and her obsession with fun hats.
  • Played tragically by all the desperate farewell phone calls cut short by impacting disasters.
  • The various references to Wisconsin throughout the film; first from an old lady at the beginning who regrets moving from there, it becoming the new location of the South Pole at the end of the film, as well as being mentioned in the last sentence of Jackson's novel.
  • There is exactly one prediction done by the scientists that strikes when expected: the mega-tsunami seen by (and that kills) Satnam. All others (including the one of the waters receding) happens faster/earlier than expected.

tropes.name: Russian Guy Suffers Most
tropes.html: All Russian characters who are not children, dogs, or politicians bite the dust sooner or later.

tropes.name: Say My Name
tropes.html: Kate, when she realizes that Noah has snuck off to help Jackson free the hydraulic gears, though it comes out sounding more like a Big "NO!".

tropes.name: Say Your Prayers
tropes.html: The President of Italy remains behind at the Vatican, taking part in a prayer circle led by the Pope, rather than evacuate himself, this costs him and the Pope their lives as the Vatican gets destroyed by an earthquake.

tropes.name: Scenery Gorn
tropes.html:
• Most of the planet. As seen at the top of the page, Emmerich pays particular attention to the destruction of Los Angeles. From all the downtown skyscrapers toppling, massive cracks opening, and chunks of landscape sliding into the sea as seen in the poster above and trailer.
  • A review said the only thing Emmerich did not destroy was the Columbia Pictures logo at the beginning, which was considered a missed opportunity.

tropes.name: Sex Signals Death
tropes.html: Both Sasha and Tamara die because they were having an affair.

tropes.name: Sexy Backless Outfit
tropes.html: Tamara in her first appearance.

tropes.name: Shoot the Shaggy Dog
tropes.html: Gordon tries his best to be a good stepfather to Jackson's children, as well as getting on well with Jackson himself, and he manages to use his minimal flying experience to pilot several drastically different aircraft, and is never anything less than cooperative with the other characters. His reward is death and Jackson's family later reuniting.

tropes.name: Shout-Out
tropes.html:
The film contains various references to the The Bible.
  • During the destruction of the Sistine Chapel inside the Vatican, the cracks forming on the roof directly between God and Adam in the Creation of Adam symbolize two aspects related to the Bible: the transition between the first and second circles of life (specifically, breaking the connection between humans and God) and God's reversal of creation of humanity in Chapters 6-9 in the Book of Genesis.
  • The Biblical flood: Jackson's son is named Noah, the cruise ship (where Adrian's father Harry performs) is called Genesis (the book in the Bible in which the account appears), and humanity is saved by the use of "arks". At one point we also see animals being lifted aboard the arks.
  • Jackson Curtis' name is 50 Cent's (Curtis Jackson) name backwards. Reportedly, Emmerich is a fan of him.

tropes.name: Skewed Priorities
tropes.html:
• When the Curtis family is frantically getting into the limo as Los Angeles is collapsing all around them, Lily looks back at the house in agony because she lost her hat collection. It takes her mother to snap her out of it and get in the limo.
  • When Adrian sees the luxurious accommodations on the Ark, he's obviously dismayed to realize how much priority Anheuser placed on creature comforts over saving more people.

tropes.name: Smug Snake
tropes.html: Yuri. He desmonstrates his lack of gratefulness for Sasha's sacrifice by bringing up that he knew he was Tamara's lover and giving a Large Ham, highly insincere "may God bless that poor bastard's soul!"

tropes.name: Spreading Disaster Map Graphic
tropes.html: Towards the end, on-screen graphics in the ark control room depict the massive waves closing in Asia and other continents.

tropes.name: Stealth Hi/Bye
tropes.html: Both of Jackson's kids appear to have perfected the art of teleportation. In two separate screens he explicitly tells them to stay put, and with no indication the kid have moved they abruptly appear next to him a few scenes later.

tropes.name: Stylistic Suck
tropes.html: Charlie’s video certainly has the vibes of the amateur video he says it is.

tropes.name: Super Cell Reception
tropes.html:
• A review in Empire Magazine includes this response to Emmerich's "wilfully ignoring science to keep the plot boiling": "For future reference, sudden continental drift probably will affect your cellphone reception." And even if it doesn't, good luck getting through when literally the whole world is trying to call someone.
  • A cell phone that gets reception from inside a metal ship buried under the Himalayas off in an undeveloped, rural corner of Tibet. After it has been explicitly stated that the apocalypse has knocked out nearly all communications.

tropes.name: Super Drowning Skills
tropes.html: Played straight with Tamara, who gets sealed in a room rapidly filling with water.

tropes.name: Take My Hand!
tropes.html: About a dozen times but the most notable one is when Jackson attempts to pull Yenzin and Gordon out of the gear shaft. Gordon doesn't make it.

tropes.name: Take That!
tropes.html: A very lazy shot at Arnold Schwarzenegger ("He's an actor - he's reading from a script!"). There is a veritable myriad of take-thats in the film, but there's so many that it's kind of hard to pinpoint them all. Civilization? Religion? Rich people? Poor people?

tropes.name: Take That, Critics!
tropes.html: A subtle one can be found in the adoration Jackson's Sci-Fi book gets. In the movie, the book sells barely 432 copies because critics found its ridiculously Cosy Catastrophe view of the world to be insufferable and unrealistic, yet major characters (the president's science adviser included!) find it be a source of great inspiration. Director Roland Emmerich also made The Day After Tomorrow, which was criticized for being offensively preachy and silly in the levels of Cosy Catastrophe it brought to the screen.

tropes.name: Talking Is a Free Action
tropes.html: Characters ramble on for minutes without any noticeable difference between the time they got started and the time they finished, usually minutes later. Standouts include Adrian's speech on the Ark and Jackson getting ready to unplug the gears.

tropes.name: Tempting Fate
tropes.html: Many times. See Dramatic Irony.

tropes.name: Teetering on the Edge
tropes.html: When the protagonists reach the China mountains, they have to make a rough landing due running out of fuel. Sasha stays on the plane to keep it level while everyone evacuates via the cars on the plane when it low enough to eject out the cargo hold safely. Sasha manages to land the plane safe enough that it skids to the edge of a mountain and stops. He himself chuckling at his good luck... then the plane proceeds to tilt over the edge, crash and explode; killing him.

tropes.name: Throw-Away Country
tropes.html: Sometimes played straight, sometimes subverted - e.g., India and China are given considerable focus beyond being nature's Butt-Monkey. Canada possibly fits this trope too. The world leaders conference at the beginning is held in British Columbia, and Canada is mentioned as having survivors on board one of the Arks.

tropes.name: Title by Year
tropes.html: 2009 Disaster Movie based on the prediction that the world would end on December 21st, 2012

tropes.name: 25th Amendment
tropes.html: Floated, then immediately ripped up.

tropes.name: Uncertain Doom
tropes.html: Various characters who aren't evacuated to the Arks. It does seem like a stretch that the various disasters killed every single other person on earth besides The Africans, but it's doubtful that there were many left. This is lampshaded after Tony loses connection with his son and granddaughter as an earthquake hits Japan and Harry tells him to hold out hope that they might have evacuated somewhere. And then there's the Genesis itself when it's hit, but not explicitly destroyed, by a giant wave just minutes later.

tropes.name: Ungrateful Bastard
tropes.html: Adrian accuses Anheuser of this after finding out that Satnam and his family, the ones who first discovered the danger in the first place and warned him, weren't evacuated, although there is some ambiguity over whose fault this was.

tropes.name: The Unmasqued World
tropes.html: The 2012 phenomenon and significance of the Mayan Long Count Calendar was considered a myth by everyone except world governments...until the apocalypse actually occurred.

tropes.name: Viewer-Friendly Interface
tropes.html: Both played straight (the computers on the arks with 3D, real-time representations of the gears for the doors) and averted (the scientist who discovers the end is near uses Vista, and everyone else who's not an Ark operator).

tropes.name: Well-Intentioned Extremist
tropes.html: Say what you like about Anheuser, but he genuinely wanted humanity and civilization to survive the planetary upset.

tropes.name: Wham Line
tropes.html: When West informs Adrian that the entire city of Pasadena, California had been destroyed after he asks what CalTech (located in Pasadena) thinks of the earthquake.

tropes.name: What Happened to the Mouse?
tropes.html: The president for some reason searches for a girl's father instead of seeing the full damage that happens to the capital. The girl's father gets forgotten a few minutes after he gets outside, not that it mattered with the wave.

tropes.name: What Measure Is a Mook?
tropes.html: Or an unnamed character.

tropes.name: What Measure Is a Non-Cute?
tropes.html: Averted with Tamara.

tropes.name: What You Are in the Dark
tropes.html:
• Tenzin, a worker on the Ark who made arrangements for a secret passage that would save his family, accepts putting the plan at risk when confronted with Jackson and his family when his grandmother points out that they are all children of God, when he could have argued that his plan was too risky even with just them never mind with more people involved.
  • Yuri may have abandoned his cheating mistress, but he acts to save his children over himself in the final moments.
  • Adrian Helmsley quotes Jackson when he observes that "The moment we stop fighting for each other, that's when we lose our humanity", reinforcing that what matters in a crisis like this is humanity's compassion for each other rather than making purely pragmatic choices, which inspires all the other world leaders to open the gates of the Arks and try and let more people in even if it puts their current passengers at risk.

tropes.name: You Have to Believe Me!
tropes.html:
Jackson: (having a phone conversation with Kate while speeding towards her home) Kate, stop what you're doing.
Kate: (confused) Jackson?
Jackson: Listen to me, I've rented a plane. Pack up the kids. I'll be there in five minutes.
Kate: (dismissive) What are you talking about? We're going about our regular Saturday. Noah has music at 2, and Lily has karate.
Jackson: Kate, California is going down! Pack up the kids, now!
Kate: They just got back! God, you sound like a crazy person; the Governor just said we're fine now.
Jackson: The guy's an actor; he's reading a script! When they tell you not to panic, that's when you run!
Kate: Look, call me back when you calm down, huh? (hangs up)

tropes.name: You Have GOT to Be Kidding Me!
tropes.html:
Laura: He's injured. Something must have gone wrong.
Anheuser: Something must have gone wrong? Something must have gone wrong?! ARE YOU KIDDING ME?!! OF COURSE SOMETHING WENT WRONG!!

tropes.name: Your Princess Is in Another Castle!
tropes.html:
Jackson, after finding out that the ships are in China.
Jackson: We're gonna need a bigger plane.

tropes.name: Accidental Pervert
tropes.html: Charlie walks in on Stella when she's in her underwear. While she's practicing cracking a safe.

tropes.name: Anti-Hero Team
tropes.html: The protagonists (sans Stella, a civilian) are very much professional thieves who at the start of the film are stealing for the riches. When Steve turns on them and kills their mentor, the team decides to steal their gold back while getting Steve to pay on a more personal level.

tropes.name: Armed Blag
tropes.html: The final heist involves targeting a safe inside a moving armored truck.

tropes.name: Artifact Title
tropes.html: Most of the movie takes place in Los Angeles, but it's all set into motion by The Job they did in Italy.

tropes.name: Artistic License – Cars
tropes.html: After Wrench modifies the cars, he and Charlie are walking past a shelf filled with what Wrench describes as "unnecessary engine parts". On that shelf are three exhaust headers and three crankshafts (along with many other parts) which are absolutely necessary for an engine to run.

tropes.name: Artistic License – Geography
tropes.html:
• The final heist in the movie is a 20-minute long application of this trope. The armored truck starts at Yucca and Vine,note near the Capitol Records building then appears a mile away and turns twicenote once from east to south, then from north to west through Hollywood and Highland. It then goes west past Grauman's Chinese Theater, the MINI Coopers drive off, and the van stops in front of the Chinese Theater again before the street collapses. Learning that the subway tunnel is blocked, Steve sends his men to Figureoa and 11th, which is nine miles away in Downtown Los Angeles. Charlie's team then drives 8 miles through the storm drain to the L.A. River,note east of Downtown L.A. emerges at the Sepulveda Basin Recreation Area,note 20 miles northwest of Downtown L.A. then go past Staples Centernote southwest of Downtown L.A.. Finally, after Steve loses his helicopter, he chases Charlie to Union Station by going west on Arcadia Street, even though Union Station is immediately behind them.note a road sign in the background points out the Union Station exit
  • When the MINIs are going down into the underground tunnels, they're supposedly at the Hollywood and Highland station. In reality, they are at the 7th and Metro station, stationed in Downtown Los Angeles, based on the fact that the MINIs jump into the tunnel in front of a Blue Line train (the Hollywood station only services the Red Line).

tropes.name: Artistic License – Physics
tropes.html: During the planning stages, the crew decides on using MINI Coopers because they fit in the hallways of Steve's house. The cars would fit, but they certainly wouldn't be able to turn the 90 degree corners.

tropes.name: Badass Pacifist
tropes.html: The team takes a certain pride in the fact that they pull off the titular heist without ever touching a firearm. The only time the protagonists fire a gun is a tear gas launcher that Handsome Rob uses on the armored car guards.

tropes.name: Black-and-Gray Morality
tropes.html: The protagonists are thieves, and not the "Robin Hood" kind, either (granted, they are originally stealing the gold from a bunch of Mafia gangsters, who are no saints themselves). However, Steve is a brutal thug with no sense of loyalty who casually murders friend and stranger to get what he wants.

tropes.name: Boring, but Practical
tropes.html: The "boring" part is emphasized later, as well: Steve's plan to steal the gold from the Italian job was to hire a bunch of mercenaries and ambush Bridger's team. They have no guns, while the mercs have guns. Easy-peasy.

tropes.name: Boring Insult
tropes.html: Steve is accused of having no imagination after stealing the gold, having spent it on all the things everyone else had said they would buy with their shares, and having had no better plan for said theft than getting some goons and waving a gun on the team's faces.

tropes.name: The Cameo
tropes.html:
Well, not quite. Steve is watching The Italian Job on DVD, but all we ever see is a part of Michael Caine so they wouldn't have to pay royalties by showing his face.
  • Also, that really was the creator of Napster playing himself stealing the idea from Lyle in college.

tropes.name: Caper Rationalization
tropes.html: "You know it was never about the gold, right?" The gang all acknowledge that they're very emotional about avenging John Bridger's death in going after Steve.

tropes.name: The Charmer
tropes.html: Handsome Rob.

tropes.name: Chekhov's Gun
tropes.html: The oxygen tanks and scuba gear they use in the opening heist saves the team's lives when their van falls off the bridge into icy water.

tropes.name: Chekhov's Gunman
tropes.html: Yevhen, the talkative jewelry store owner Steve is using to move the gold, first mentions his cousin well before it's obvious that the man is a powerful crime boss.

tropes.name: City of Canals
tropes.html: The titular caper is pulled off in Venice at the beginning of the movie.

tropes.name: Cold-Blooded Torture
tropes.html: Steve begs the Ukrainian crime boss not to shoot him. He doesn't intend to. Instead, he plans to show Steve the wonderful tools at his garage...

tropes.name: Cool Car
tropes.html:
The Aston Martin Vanquish that Handsome Rob plans to buy and that Steve does buy after he steals the money and kills Bridger.
  • Stella owns the same red Mini Cooper SS from the 1969 film.

tropes.name: Creative Sterility
tropes.html: Steve’s Fatal Flaw, as pointed out by Charlie (“No imagination”). Despite considering himself a master criminal, his plans always resort to either force or paranoid defense, and his one good idea throughout the film is easily figured out by the team. Ultimately, he always takes the easy or safe route, which leaves him incapable of effectively responding to Charlie’s sheer audacity and cunning.

tropes.name: The Crime Job
tropes.html: Not only the movie itself, but also its planned sequel The Brazilian Job.

tropes.name: Dead Star Walking
tropes.html: Donald Sutherland is only in the opening heist before Steve betrays the team and kills him.

tropes.name: Decoy Convoy
tropes.html: Steve uses three identical convoys of armored trucks with motorcycle escorts to hide the gold while it's moved to a more secure location. Lyle is able to figure out which one has the gold by seeing which one is weighed down since $27 million in gold is heavy.

tropes.name: Delivery Guy Infiltration
tropes.html: "Cable Guy Infiltration" variant. After the men recruit Stella, they set up a plan to infiltrate Steve's house. Handsome Rob first steals a cable company van by flirting with one of their employees, while Left Ear tampers with the cable box so that Steve's TV and modem will not work and Steve will be forced to call to set up an appointment. Once Steve's gate guard calls the cable company, Charlie calls back a moment later "claiming" that a technician of theirs has finished up on a call in the area and can make a quick detour. Stella drives in minutes later in the obtained work van, and using the name "Becky" (the name of the actual employee whose shirt Handsome Rob stole), she wears a mini-video camera disguised as a flag pin to allow the men to map up the house layout. When it's time for her to leave, Left Ear reconnects the cables that he pulled out to prompt Steve's call.

tropes.name: Double Caper
tropes.html: The titular "Italian job" (and actually called such by the characters) is the caper that opens the movie. The rest of it involves taking back the gold from traitorous member Steve and getting revenge for the death of John Bridger.

tropes.name: Down L.A. Drain
tropes.html: The film has the heroes driving through the viaducts in MINI Coopers as part of their getaway.

tropes.name: Draco in Leather Pants
tropes.html: In-Universe. Handsome Rob once took a stolen car across the country just so he could set the world record for longest freeway chase. He got legions of fangirls who sent fanmail to his jail cell.

tropes.name: The Dreaded
tropes.html: Steve, Skinny Pete, and Charlie's crew are all tough people. And they are all terrified of the Ukrainians.

tropes.name: Drill the Lock
tropes.html: Stella sort of does this when cracking safes. The hole she drills is for getting a borescope inside to have a look at the safe's locking mechanisms, though.

tropes.name: Even Evil Has Loved Ones
tropes.html: Mashkov is a ruthless Ukrainian gangster who is quite fond of torture and murder. He is devastated when he finds his cousin, the fencer Yevhen, murdered in his store, and brutally interrogates several underworld leads in order to find his killer.

tropes.name: Everything Is Online
tropes.html: Hacking the traffic light system of an entire city to cause a gridlock? Check. However, as Cracked points out, this is actually doable, though the extreme to which Lyle goes probably isn't.

tropes.name: Explain, Explain... Oh, Crap!
tropes.html: Yehven, Steve's fence, tosses gold trivia at Steve as they are negotiating the sale of a couple of bars… and Yehven mentions the history of the bars he is currently holding (with a dancer sigil on them) and that he heard of the Italian job. He noticeably hesitates when he reaches that part of the story, showing he finally figured it out, and his reaction becomes even more justified when Steve blows him away about a second later.

tropes.name: Five-Man Band
tropes.html:
• The Leader - Charlie (Red Ranger)
  • The Lancer - Handsome Rob (Black Ranger)
  • The Big Guy - Left Ear (Blue Ranger)
  • The Smart Guy - Lyle (Green Ranger, befitting it's Seth Green himself.)
  • The Heart - Stella (Yellow Ranger)

tropes.name: Fruit Boat
tropes.html: During the opening heist, a pursuing boat accidentally drives up another boat, is launched into the air, and lands in one.

tropes.name: Gag Dub
tropes.html:
Lyle (Seth Green) does this while Handsome Rob (Jason Statham) chats up a young woman with the aim of seducing her and getting her ID card. Bonus points in that Seth Green improv'd his dialogue.
  • Also counts as an Actor Allusion given Seth Green's Voice Actor credentials.

tropes.name: Good Hair, Evil Hair
tropes.html: C'mon, you knew Steve was a traitor just from that moustache-and-ratty-goatee combo alone.

tropes.name: Hack the Traffic Lights
tropes.html: Lyle creates a city-wide gridlock to control the green lights for their escape route.

tropes.name: Hate Sink
tropes.html: Steve Frazelli is a petty and smug member of John Bridger’s team of thieves who kills John, betrays and nearly kills the team and steals their haul of $35 million in gold bricks for himself just because "I wanted it". Arrogant and volatile, Steve also not knowing what he himself wants to do with all that gold uses about 8 million of it to mostly buy things other members of the team wanted instead. He blows away Yevhen, his fence, when he accidentally figures out the origin of the gold. Eventually, Charlie Croker and the rest of the team hand Steve over to Ukrainian mob boss Mashkov who intends to make Steve deservedly suffer as he kills him.

tropes.name: He Knows Too Much
tropes.html: Yevhen, while rambling about gold usage throughout history, stumbles upon the source of the gold Steve's been fencing through his shop. Steve kills him for it. Unfortunately, Yevhen is part of a local Ukrainian crime syndicate, which comes back to bite everyone later. Charlie deals with it easily enough; offering a share of the gold if they'll hide in earshot when Steve enters the train car, upon which Charlie will attempt an Engineered Public Confession. He pulls it off, and Steve is dragged to his fate by dozens of Ukrainians with SMGs to his one handgun.

tropes.name: Head-Turning Beauty
tropes.html: Stella, played by Statuesque Stunner Charlize Theron, predictably inspires this reaction from almost every male character she comes across.

tropes.name: Heel Realization
tropes.html: Bridger appears to have had one before the film began, as he talks to Charlie about how he regrets that his lifestyle prevented him from being a father to Stella and expressed a desire to make up for that before his death.

tropes.name: Helicopter Blender
tropes.html: Steve attempts this against Charlie, who's in a MINI, using the tail rotor. Charlie just barely manages to scrape by, but the rotor is ruined by the attempt and the helicopter is grounded, forcing Steve to jack a car to continue the chase.

tropes.name: Historical In-Joke
tropes.html:
Lyle was the real inventor of Napster, but Shawn Fanning was his roommate and stole his idea while he was napping at his computer.
Lyle: And then he's just the media darling... He's on the cover of all the magazines, I should've been on the cover of Wired Magazine. You know what he said? He said he named it "Napster" because it was his nickname because of the nappy hair under the hat. But he—it's because I was NAPPING when he STOLE it from me! He didn't even graduate!

tropes.name: Hollywood Density
tropes.html: Discussed Trope. They have to specially modify the cars to be able to handle the weight of the gold. Also, when the gold is being taken out of Steve's mansion, Lyle is able to figure out which of the three armored cars contains the gold because it's riding significantly lower than the decoys because of the weight of $27 million in gold bricks.

tropes.name: Impossible Mission Collapse
tropes.html: The original plan to storm Steve's mansion gets foiled by a cocktail party right across the street from the mansion's entrance, risking an awful lot of witnesses.

tropes.name: In Name Only
tropes.html: There is a theft in the movie that is actually called "the Italian job" by the characters. And Minis. And characters named "Charlie Croker" and "Bridger". Aside from that, yeah, everything's different.

tropes.name: Instant Seduction
tropes.html: Handsome Rob flirting with a cable girl so he can get her shirt and her truck to give to Stella so she can infiltrate Steve's house. Lyle tries to get an idea of what the conversation's going like by acting out both sides.

tropes.name: Invulnerable Knuckles
tropes.html: Averted. Charlie tells Stella that the reason he punched Steve instead of letting her do so is because her hands were too valuable. It's obvious that there are other reasons as well, but since he did in fact hurt his own hand, the explanation is good enough for them to let it go for the moment.

tropes.name: Ironic Nickname
tropes.html: Skinny Pete is actually quite obese.

tropes.name: It's Personal
tropes.html: While they all have an axe to grind with Steve, who tried to kill the team for the gold, Charlie and Stella are personally fueled by the murder of John, who was/was like a father to both.

tropes.name: Jerkass
tropes.html: Steve has absolutely zero redeeming qualities.

tropes.name: Lack of Imagination
tropes.html: This is Steve's (the movie's Big Bad) flaw, as while he managed to pull out swiping the gold from his fellow thieves and nearly killed them, his plan was simply to have a lot of goons with guns on his side. When he used the money, all he did was just mimic what everyone else had intended to use their share for. Charlie points this out to him, point blank telling him he has "no imagination" when finally confronting him face to face and citing that his brash actions ultimately make him panic when things don't go his way that he can't improvise on the fly. This is shown at the end where he's ultimately outgambited by Charlie's more creative heist to steal the gold from him and have a backup plan in case Steve manages to catch up (a plan that Steve himself unwittingly set up when he murdered a cousin of a very dangerous Ukrainian mobster).

tropes.name: Like a Son to Me
tropes.html: Charlie's relationship with John. Stella even notes that Charlie had a much closer relationship with her father than she did, although Charlie assures her that John regretted that he wasn't a better father to her.

tropes.name: The Mafia
tropes.html: The team originally steals to gold from a group of Italian gangsters in Venice.

tropes.name: The Mafiya
tropes.html: The Ukrainians.

tropes.name: Mission Control
tropes.html: Lyle, especially during the end chase.

tropes.name: Model Planning
tropes.html:
The thieves build a replica practice course in a warehouse to practice driving their escape route, and also have a CGI animation on their computer of the car as if it were traversing the actual route in real time for no apparent reason.
  • And then it turns out to be a "Shaggy Dog" Story when Steve alters his plans and so do they.

tropes.name: Noodle Incident
tropes.html:
Left Ear hates dogs.
Left Ear: This dude got dogs. I don't do dogs. I had a real bad experience, man.
Charlie: What happened?
Left Ear: I had a bad experience. Dammit, I'm deaf.

tropes.name: No Honor Among Thieves
tropes.html: The majority of the plot happens because of Steve being a backstabbing bastard who waited until the Italian Job was officially accomplished before stealing the gold and trying to kill the crew.

tropes.name: "No Peeking!" Request
tropes.html: Charlie walks in on Stella in her underwear and looks away so she can get dressed, but briefly tries to get a peek until she yells, "Don't look!"

tropes.name: Non-Indicative Name
tropes.html: The titular Italian Job is pulled off in the first 20 minutes, and then the entire rest of the movie takes place in the United States.

tropes.name: Oh, Crap!
tropes.html:
• Stella reacts this way when the crew open the truck and she sees that Steve has switched out the safe for one with extra security features to prevent her signature Drill the Lock technique.
  • Steve is justifiably panicked, unraveled, and helpless when the Ukrainian gangster whose cousin he killed shows up to take revenge on him and refuses to be bought off.

tropes.name: Plan B Resolution
tropes.html: Charlie and his crew initially attempted to infiltrate Steve's mansion and steal back the gold while he's out waiting for a date with Stella, but were forced to abort when they discover Steve's neighbors are throwing a party. Stella goes on the date to inspire a second one, but gives herself away. This leads to the climactic plan to make an unholy traffic jam in L.A. and lead the armored car with the gold to a location where they can raid it.

tropes.name: Pragmatic Villainy
tropes.html: When arguing against a shootout with armed guards, Handsome Rob doesn't argue morality. He just says "We'd lose." Fortunately, Charlie has another plan.

tropes.name: Precision F-Strike
tropes.html:
Steve when his armored truck is dropped into the subway tunnels.
Steve: What the FUCK happened to my truck?!

tropes.name: Product Placement
tropes.html:
The MINIs are the stars, sure, but while Stella drives an old one early in the movie (which almost could be considered a Mythology Gag), the climactic heist sees the use of then-recent models that see a lot of action.
  • The cover when sinking the gold down to the subway tracks involves using a giant Pepsi Blue sign to disguise the hole when Steve's sightline is obscured.

tropes.name: Pushy Gun-Toting Villain
tropes.html: One big sign of Steve lacking imagination as a criminal is that he is this trope while he assumes that bringing a gun along is what makes him clever.

tropes.name: Reality Is Unrealistic
tropes.html: People complained that hacking a traffic light system like in the film was highly improbable, turns out it IS quite possible in real life.

tropes.name: "The Reason You Suck" Speech
tropes.html: Steve gets a couple of these from Charlie, mostly focused on Charlie making it clear that Steve lacks imagination to the extent of only using the gold to buy what everyone else wanted rather than having any independent plans for it himself.

tropes.name: Refuge in Audacity
tropes.html: Charlie’s Plan B to get to the truck carrying the gold is to “Boost it in transit.” And by that, he means blow a hole in the street underneath it and drop it into the subway. It works.

tropes.name: Reluctant Fanservice Girl
tropes.html: Stella is upset when Charlie shows up while she's stripped down to her bra. She orders him to look away and quickly puts a shirt on.

tropes.name: Retirony
tropes.html: John Bridger is murdered shortly after completing his last job. Which makes this a variant, as he dies a few days after retiring instead of a few days before.

tropes.name: Ruthless Foreign Gangsters
tropes.html:
The Ukrainians. The moment it's discovered that they are interested on the heist (because of Steve killing Yehven, who was family of the local don), everybody goes Oh, Crap!. Thankfully, they are not ruthless enough that they cannot be negotiated with... which Charlie does, sealing Steve's final fate.
Skinny Pete: If there's one thing I know, it's never to mess with mother nature, mother-in-laws, and mother freaking Ukrainians.

tropes.name: Sadistic Thief
tropes.html: Discussed. John Bridger tells Charlie that there are two kinds of thieves in the world; the ones who steal to enrich their lives, and the ones who steal to define their lives. He tells Charlie not to be the latter because “it makes you miss out on what’s important in life.”

tropes.name: Screw the Money, This Is Personal!
tropes.html: Downplayed because Charlie made a deal with him first, but Mashkov, the leader of the Ukrainian Mafia, does not backstab the crew to get more of the gold and refuses Steve's proposal to be paid off because he wants revenge for Steve killing his cousin, along with a lot of tools he is looking forward to showing Steve…

tropes.name: Sequel Goes Foreign
tropes.html: Or rather remake, with the job of recapturing the gold taking place in the United States (original heist crew being British and all).

tropes.name: The Sixth Ranger
tropes.html: Wrench, a mechanic whom Rob recruits to modify the Caper Crews cars, later becomes an official part of the crew when they need additional support.

tropes.name: Smug Snake
tropes.html: Steve, full out. Even if the move with the 'shell game' was clever by Charlie's own admission, both the plan for his counter-caper and keeping the gold away from Charlie's crew come down to having more people using guns on his side (Charlie and Bridger, being both of the Con Man Gentleman Thief breed, absolutely refuse to use them on their plans), which Charlie points out completely 'lacks imagination'. Furthermore, he had no ideas for how to use the loot himself, and thus decided to copy everybody else's ideas. Finally, he tries to sell himself off as a master thief when he's only a trigger-happy idiot—this one comes bite him in the ass hard when he kills Yehven.

tropes.name: Something Only They Would Say
tropes.html: Steve realizes that he's on a date with Bridger's daughter when Stella uses her father's trademark phrase, "I trust everyone; I just don't trust the devil inside them."

tropes.name: Stealing from Thieves
tropes.html: In the form of a heist against a former member who stole the take from their previous heist and murdered their mentor.

tropes.name: Take Five
tropes.html: Skinny Pete tells his girlfriend, "Go relax, babe," when he wants to have a private meeting with someone.

tropes.name: Technical Pacifist
tropes.html: Charlie and company are proud of the fact that they steal without ever holding a gun. They'll use explosives to blow holes in buildings and streets, they'll go on dangerous car and boat chases, they'll gas people, and they'll hand Steve over to the much more violent Ukrainians, but they won't take any direct actions to hurt people.

tropes.name: There Are Two Kinds of People in the World
tropes.html: "There are two kinds of thieves in this world: The ones who steal to enrich their lives, and those who steal to define their lives. Don't be the latter. Makes you miss out on what's really important in this life." Sage advice from John Bridger to Charlie Croker. Pretty much the last one.

tropes.name: Thought-Aversion Failure
tropes.html: When meeting Skinny Pete, Charlie tells Left Ear to not "stare" at him. When Left Ear lays eyes on the colossal obesity of Pete, Left Ear struggles to even speak, let alone not stare.

tropes.name: Title Drop
tropes.html:
Charlie drops this when Handsome Rob shows concern about stealing the gold in transit, noting there's no way they could overpower armed guards in the truck. Charlie reminds him there's a way around a shootout (gas). It also describes how they pulled off the job in Italy: instead of breaking into the room with the safe, under guard by a lot of mooks with guns, they blow out the floor beneath it, causing the safe to drop where they can crack it open in safety. Doubles as a Call-Back when the team later does the same thing to drop the gold truck into the L.A. Subway, where Stella can crack it in safety like her dad did with the safe during the Italian job.
Charlie: We do it like the Italian job.

tropes.name: To the Pain
tropes.html: Steve's apparent fate once the Ukrainians take him away, though he is still likely Killed Offscreen.

tropes.name: Toyota Tripwire
tropes.html: Handsome Rob does this to a hapless mook during a car chase.

tropes.name: Turn in Your Badge
tropes.html: Parodied. Handsome Rob, whilst trying to drive through the city as fast as possible to time the fastest possible escape route, is the second car in line stopped in the left turn lane at a red traffic light (note, this is a green arrow only turn signal). Unfortunately, the driver in front of him is an actor rehearsing the phrase, "Give me your badge and your weapon; I don't want to see you anywhere near this case (pretends to crush cup)" in such a variety of different voices and emphases while reading off the script itself he fails to notice there's a green arrow, until the very last second when it's turning amber and Rob starts shouting "Hey! It's a green!" and honking at him, so he's the only one that gets to go through, with a very disgruntled Rob saying, "Unbelievable!" in disbelief. Also, bonus if you noticed that the actor copies Rob's accent and decides to use that accent for the audition.

tropes.name: Traitor Shot
tropes.html: Edward Norton is the only member of the team who never interacts with the others face-to-face during the opening heist, and when the others are celebrating afterwards, the camera holds on him mostly just staring at the others in silence. Is it any wonder he double crosses them later?

tropes.name: True Companions
tropes.html: Charlie's group may be thieves, but they're also family.

tropes.name: Villainous Virtues
tropes.html: Mashkov is a brutal torturer and murderer, but he clearly wants to be sure that he tortures and murders the right person. And when presented with an opportunity to use brute force to steal all the gold, he simply takes the case that Charlie has prepared for him and says "I have made my deal." Of course, the person suggesting it was the one who had murdered his cousin, but he could have taken his revenge and still stolen the gold for himself.

tropes.name: "Where Are They Now?" Epilogue
tropes.html: After the heist, Charlie narrates what happened to the others; Left Ear and Lyle got their dream house and stereo respectively, Handsome Rob went on his dream drive and got let off with a warning when he was 'caught' by the police, and Charlie is shown in Venice with Stella, musing that he's taking Bridger's advice by finding someone he loves that he will hold onto forever.

tropes.name: Xanatos Gambit
tropes.html: Either they steal the gold and get away, or Steve tracks them down and gets taken by the Ukrainians.

tropes.name: You Keep Telling Yourself That
tropes.html: Steve, ever the Smug Snake Jerkass, fires this at Stella when she defends stealing from him as justice for killing her father ("It's not about the gold." "Whatever helps you sleep at night, sweetheart!"). Stella punches him in the mouth in response, interrupting him before he can drop any further insults.

tropes.name: You Killed My Father
tropes.html: Stella's main reason for joining the heist is because Steve killed her father on his last mission and nearly drowned the rest of the team while stealing their gold.

tropes.name: Adaptational Badass
tropes.html: In the graphic novels, Kroenen is just a gas-masked Nazi with a Morally Ambiguous Doctorate. The movie turns him into a Surgery Addicted Clockwork Nazi Cyborg Assassin with a taste for arm blades...and a Morally Ambiguous Doctorate.

tropes.name: Adaptational Superpower Change
tropes.html: The movie gives Abe Psychic Powers.

tropes.name: Adaptational Ugliness
tropes.html: Abraham Sapien goes from reasonably handsome◊ (if fishy) in the comics and animated movies to a much more inhuman, fish-like appearance◊ in the films.

tropes.name: Adaptation Distillation
tropes.html:
• Hellboy is a rough condensation of the plots of Seed of Destruction, The Right Hand of Doom, and Box Full of Evil, with a sprinkle of Wake the Devil. Hellboy's character design was also slightly modified, as in the comics he has cloven hooves instead of feet.note  He still has cloven hooved feet, visible when John Myers first meets him, though it's difficult to see. The producers also worried about having to change the Right Hand of Doom to a Left Hand of Doom before casting Perlman, who is ambidextrous.
  • The Action Prologue featuring Hellboy's summoning is likewise condensed from the comic version which had the ritual and Hellboy's arrival take place in different locations. Here Bruttenholm and the U.S forces interrupt the summoning ritual. In addition minor comic characters like the Torch of Liberty and some psychics were cut entirely.

tropes.name: Adaptation Dye-Job
tropes.html: Liz has Selma Blair's natural black hair instead of auburn like the comics and animated movies.

tropes.name: Adaptation Expansion
tropes.html: Professor Bruttenholm's relationship with Hellboy (as father-son) gets a lot more focus here than in the comics.

tropes.name: Adaptation Relationship Overhaul
tropes.html: Ilsa and Rasputin are indicated in the film to be lovers. In Wake the Devil, Ilsa did indeed serve Rasputin, but her actual lover was Vladir Giurescu, who has been Adapted Out.

tropes.name: Adapted Out
tropes.html: While the film is inspired by Seed of Destruction and Wake the Devil, Vladmir Giurescu is absent. As are Hecate, the Women of Thessaly, and various other BPRD and Nazi characters.

tropes.name: Affably Evil
tropes.html: Rasputin allows Professor Bruttenholm a moment to prepare for his death and assures him that it will be quick, and it is. Kroenen generally prefers efficiency over sadism anyway, but still. Considering that the professor is terminally ill, it may even count as a Mercy Kill. Their little theology discussion beforehand, while decidedly antagonistic, is still very civilized.

tropes.name: Alien Blood
tropes.html: Behemoth bleeds a blue liquid as Hellboy chops down its Combat Tentacles and makes it blow up.

tropes.name: Alternate Continuity
tropes.html: Mignola said in one of his interviews that he felt that the way he did Hellboy was just one interpretation, and he didn't want the movie to be a rehash of that, so he let del Toro interpret the franchise his own way for the movies.

tropes.name: Angels, Devils and Squid
tropes.html: Hellboy's devilishness and the Lovecraftian elements are obvious. Angels don't appear directly, but their dried tears keep Sammael's essence restrained until his release, and religious icons possess holy power.

tropes.name: The Antichrist
tropes.html: Hellboy, though he's not too keen on the idea and becomes an Anti-Anti-Christ.

tropes.name: Art Imitates Art
tropes.html: A brief video clip of Hellboy copies the famous film footage of Bigfoot.

tropes.name: Artistic License – Geography
tropes.html: The Birgau Pass in Real Life Moldavia doesn't quite look like an imposing Mountains of Madness place to say the least.

tropes.name: Artistic License – History
tropes.html:
• Look closely at the soldiers in Professor Bruttenholm's taskforce as they take the picture at the start of the film; one is black, at a time when the forces were still segregated.
  • Rasputin's legendary Rasputinian Death is related by Bruttenholm as true, but there is actually scant historical evidence supporting this popular tale. He was simply shot three times, once to the head. Of course, Rasputin wasn't an immortal wizard who joined the Nazis either.

tropes.name: Ascended Extra
tropes.html: Bruttenholm and Kroenen get much larger roles here than in the original comics where Bruttenholm died at the start and Kroenen was just a minor Nazi flunky.

tropes.name: Asteroids Monster
tropes.html: Sammael. It lays a lot of eggs, and every time it gets killed, two of those eggs hatch and immediately grow to adulthood. Nothing short of firebombing all the adults and all the eggs simultaneously can stop them.

tropes.name: Audience Surrogate
tropes.html: Myers. Most viewers agreed that one was not necessary, hence his absence from the second film.

tropes.name: Badass Boast
tropes.html:
• Hellboy threatens hell itself in plain and matter-of-fact language: I said, "Hey, you, on the other side - let her go. Because for her I will cross over, and then you'll be sorry!"
  • Professor Bruttenholm gives a fantastic one while explaining the B.P.R.D.'s motto to Myers: see Badass Creed below.

tropes.name: Badass Bystander
tropes.html: The aggressive security guard on the train, who makes the unfortunate (albeit fairly understandable) mistake of thinking that Hellboy is a bad guy.

tropes.name: Badass Creed
tropes.html:
The Bureau naturally has one—"In absentia lucis tenebrae vincunt."note The version seen in the film is missing a couple of letters, but this is what it was aiming for.
Bruttenholm: In the absence of light, darkness prevails. There are things that go bump in the night, Agent Myers. Make no mistake about that. And we are the ones who bump back.

tropes.name: Badass Longcoat
tropes.html: Hellboy in the standard-issue B.P.R.D. trenchcoats. Kroenen in his black leather Nazi trenchcoat. Also Rasputin in his intricately embroidered coat.

tropes.name: Bad Moon Rising
tropes.html: After Rasputin forces Hellboy to use his giant right hand to unlock the Tunguska door by sucking out Liz's soul, the monolith sends some kind of Pillar of Light to the moon, which turns into a portal to let the Ogdru Jahad enter the world.

tropes.name: Bedtime Brainwashing
tropes.html: The villain does this to Liz, resulting in Liz burning the entire asylum.

tropes.name: Beethoven Was an Alien Spy
tropes.html:
• Grigori Rasputin as master mystic. Granted, even many of his contemporaries thought there was something weird about him.
  • Adolf Hitler as an accomplished mystic. Early in the movie, Bruttenholm briefs Myers on the Occult Wars which happened when the Nazis acquired mystical artifacts (such as the Spear of Longinus) and ended when Hitler finally died in 1958. Myers corrects him, saying Hitler died in 1945; Bruttenholm simply gives an amused "Did he now?"

tropes.name: BFG
tropes.html: One of the B.P.R.D. agents wields one, but by the time he charges it up, it's too late.

tropes.name: Big Bad
tropes.html: Grigori Rasputin, who spends the film trying to summon world-destroying Eldritch Abominations.

tropes.name: Bigger on the Inside
tropes.html: Rasputin's Tomb.

tropes.name: Big Eater
tropes.html: Hellboy, if the massive plates and bowls of food brought into his room six times a day are any indication.

tropes.name: Blade Below the Shoulder
tropes.html: Kroenen's preferred weapon.

tropes.name: Bloodless Carnage
tropes.html: During the fight scenes, Guillermo del Toro uses everything but blood: sweat, Sammael spittle, slime, gumballs, and coins from a pay-phone are just a few examples. The only bloodshed that occurs is symbolic.

tropes.name: Body Horror
tropes.html:
• Sammael. The very first one we're introduced to, after it escapes the train, falls onto the tracks. You get a nice visual of its legs and spine literally twisting around instead of it just simply rolling over to get up, complete with the sickening sounds of bones cracking.
  • Literally everything about Kroenen, when his body is fully stripped revealing a pale clockwork-powered corpse and we get the lovely sight of his unmasked Facial Horror.

tropes.name: Bodybag Trick
tropes.html: Used by Kroenen to infiltrate B.P.R.D. headquarters.

tropes.name: Bond One-Liner
tropes.html: Hellboy is fond of these. "I'm fireproof...you're not."

tropes.name: Bookends
tropes.html: Begins and ends with a monologue asking "What defines a man?"

tropes.name: Brains and Brawn
tropes.html: Hellboy is superhumanly strong and tough, while Abe is a psychic genius.

tropes.name: Bullying a Dragon
tropes.html: Yeah, throw rocks at the pre-teen pyrokinetic. Real smart, kids.

tropes.name: Burning with Anger
tropes.html: Liz, when she's angry at Hellboy. Or about to go whoop some ass. Either or.

tropes.name: Call a Smeerp a "Rabbit"
tropes.html: Sammael is called a hellhound. He does not resemble a dog in any way (except his canine teeth.)

tropes.name: Came Back Wrong
tropes.html:
Rasputin returns from the Void, though the extended cut shows he lost his eyes while being sucked into the Void. He also has an Eldritch Abomination in his stomach from the numerous times he died, although it's not technically "wrong" as far as he's concerned.
Every time I died, a little more of the master came back with me.

tropes.name: Chekhov's Apocalypse
tropes.html: It's eventually revealed that Rasputin's plans to free the Ogdru Jahad from their crystal prisons so they can end the world are still in play sixty years after they were first enacted, and Hellboy is the key. Given that actually killing them is implied to be impossible, the film features Rasputin giving Professor Broom a brief glimpse of the future to reveal what will happen when he's able to convince Hellboy to embrace his destiny, complete with cities laid waste and the Seven Gods of Chaos reigning unchallenged. In the finale, Hellboy is coerced into opening the portal to release the Ogdru Jahad, just long enough to see their tentacles reaching down from the sky, but he ultimately backs out once he's given a pep talk from Agent Myers... though the next film makes it very clear through another bit of storyboarding that Hellboy can't outrun his destiny forever.

tropes.name: Civilization Destroyer
tropes.html: Hellboy is apparently the Beast of the Apocalypse and is fated to destroy human civilization on Earth, which is what Rasputin wants.

tropes.name: Clockwork Creature
tropes.html: Kroenen is a clockwork Nazi.

tropes.name: Clothing Damage
tropes.html: Hellboy gets some clothing damage, mostly on his black shirts. The later half of the film has Hellboy’s trenchcoat eventually damaged too during battle.

tropes.name: Co-Dragons
tropes.html: Kroenen and Ilsa act as equal (yet separate in function, with Kroenen being the more physical enforcer while Ilsa is the more cerebral one) enforcers to Rasputin.

tropes.name: Color-Coded Characters
tropes.html: Hellboy has a red light on his communicator, Abe has blue. Those colors are also their B.P.R.D. callsigns.

tropes.name: Combat Tentacles
tropes.html: Behemoth uses them in its fight with Hellboy.

tropes.name: Comic Books Are Real
tropes.html: Hellboy is only known to the outside world as an urban myth and the star of a series of comic books. When John Myers meets the real Hellboy, HB himself complains that the comics never get his eyes right.

tropes.name: Composite Character
tropes.html: Rasputin takes Giurescu's role as Ilsa's lover.

tropes.name: Conveniently Distorted Evidence Footage
tropes.html: Discussed; Hellboy has become an urban legend over the course of his life and has attracted a lot of conspiracy theorists trying to get a photo of him, much to the annoyance of Tom Manning, who finds maintaining the Masquerade on the BPRD's behalf deeply annoying. Fortunately, the photographers somehow never manage to get a close-up shot of Hellboy, resulting in the usual Bigfoot-style out-of-focus photos, and when one such photo is shown to Manning on TV, he uses its blurry format as an easy means of debunking it.

tropes.name: Conservation of Ninjutsu
tropes.html: Hellboy spends a lot of the first act battling the first Sammael, but as the number of Sammaels grows, he has less difficulty with each one. Possibly justified, since he's learning to fight them more effectively.

tropes.name: Cosmic Horror Story
tropes.html: If anything, the movies are even more upfront with the Lovecraft influence: Mignola's Ogdru Jahad are reptilian, while del Toro's are betentacled crustaceans.

tropes.name: Couldn't Find a Lighter
tropes.html: Hellboy's first fight with Sammael leaves his right hand on fire. He lights a cigar with it before putting out the flame.

tropes.name: Covered with Scars
tropes.html: Kroenen, as a result of his addiction to surgery (though, being a century-old assassin, he's no doubt racked up a few battle scars as well).

tropes.name: Covert Group with Mundane Front
tropes.html: Played with. B.P.R.D.'s headquarters are very poorly disguised as a waste disposal facility, an elaborate, beautiful structure with impressive statues all behind a large entrance gate...and a tiny sign out front claiming it to be a waste disposal business. The transports for HB and Abe are disguised as garbage trucks.

tropes.name: Creator Cameo
tropes.html: Both original comic author Mike Mignola and director Guillermo del Toro appear, dressed as a knight and a dragon respectively, in the scene where a costume party is attacked.

tropes.name: Creepy Asymmetry
tropes.html: One of Wayne Barlowe's design considerations was that every Hell creature has an asymmetrical element to mark their otherworldly origin. Behemoth and the Ogdru Jahad both wrap their bodies in lopsided masses of tentacles, and in the latter's case crustacean claws. Sammael has two small eyes on one side of its face and a single large one on the other. And Hellboy himself has The Right Hand of Doom.

tropes.name: Crossover Cosmology
tropes.html: Much like the original comics. Devils, Lovecraftian horrors, fairy-tale creatures, and God are all implied to exist.

tropes.name: Crystal Prison
tropes.html: The Ogdru Jahad are contained within these.

tropes.name: Curse Cut Short
tropes.html: When Kroenen begins to Evil Laugh after getting beaten, Hellboy asks "What are you laughing at, you Nazi son of a..." before being cut off by the activation of the Trap Door beneath him.

tropes.name: Cute Kitten
tropes.html: Hellboy loves cats. There's even a scene where he goes out of his way to save a box of kittens from falling to their deaths during a fight with Sammael.

tropes.name: Dark Is Not Evil
tropes.html: Hellboy himself, though the villains try to convince him that he should be evil.

tropes.name: Deadpan Snarker
tropes.html:
• Hellboy's dialogue is laced with some of the snarkiest deadpanning of any film in the 21st century thus far. Professor Bruttenholm gets a pretty good one in 1944, so apparently that's where he got it from.
  • Liz also has rather snarky moments, and given her depressing background, this makes sense.

tropes.name: Deal with the Devil
tropes.html: Inverted: Hellboy briefly submits to his true form in order to get the love of his life's soul back (long story short, Grigori Rasputin steals her soul, stating that he can only get her soul back to her if he opens the gate).

tropes.name: Demon Slaying
tropes.html: One of the primary jobs of the BPRD.

tropes.name: Depleted Phlebotinum Shells
tropes.html: Hellboy's handgun shoots specially-made bullets with holy water, garlic, white oak, silver shavings... "the works".

tropes.name: Description Cut
tropes.html: Tom Manning states on TV that the B.P.R.D. does not exist. There's then an immediate cut to an establishing shot of B.P.R.D. headquarters.

tropes.name: Did You Just Punch Out Cthulhu?
tropes.html: Hellboy's standard M.O. Also, given Hellboy's true name and nature, this probably applies whenever someone punches him out.

tropes.name: Dies Differently in the Adaptation
tropes.html: Professor Bruttenholm is killed by Kroenen rather than a frog monster.

tropes.name: Distant Funeral Attendee
tropes.html: Following the murder of his beloved adopted father, Professor Trevor Broom, Hellboy has to discreetly attend the funeral while staying out of sight due to his inhuman appearance.

tropes.name: Doing Research
tropes.html: During Hellboy's fist fight with Sammael, Abe Sapien is researching Sammael and relaying information to Hellboy. He asks how to kill Sammael, and Abe replies that the book doesn't say how.

tropes.name: *Drool* Hello
tropes.html: Hellboy (and the audience) is introduced to the demon Sammael with a torrent of saliva falling down, from feeding on its latest victims.

tropes.name: Dull Surprise
tropes.html:
• Selma Blair's portrayal of Liz Sherman. Justified, as she's supposed to be depressed and heavily medicated due to her tragic past, and she gets much better in the second film, after she finally comes to terms with her emotions and powers.
  • Played for Laughs when Kroenen slices up Tom Manning's arm, the latter's reaction is to be taken aback before angrily yelling "Hey, what's wrong with you!?" as if Kroenen is some jerk who butted in line at a queue.

tropes.name: Elaborate Underground Base
tropes.html: Rasputin's crazy Clock Punk mausoleum.

tropes.name: Eldritch Abomination
tropes.html: The Ogdru Jahad, Sammael, and Behemoth (that thing that crawled out of Rasputin's stomach).

tropes.name: Emerging from the Shadows
tropes.html: Rasputin materializes from the shadows of Liz's asylum dorm room the moment the door is shut, which was achieved by a simple but effective Stop Trick.

tropes.name: Expy
tropes.html:
• The Sammael have similarities to the Frog Monsters, with their build, prehensile tongues and elongated faces. They are also amphibious and linked to one of the Ogdru-hem
  • The "Behemoth", the Eldritch Abomination that comes out of Rasputin to fight Hellboy in the ending is largely an expy of Sadu-Hem from the original Seed of Destruction comic.

tropes.name: Exploited Immunity
tropes.html:
The title character's immunity to fire comes up a few times:
  • Hellboy defeats a demon by grabbing a live subway rail. The electrical current is unpleasant for Hellboy, but fatal to Sammael.
  • When Hellboy is fighting swarms of Sammaels, Liz the pyrokinetic releases a fire blast that takes down all the Sammaels while leaving Hellboy intact.
  • Hellboy finally defeats Behemoth by pulling the pin on his grenades and jumping into its mouth. The ensuing explosion destroys Behemoth from the inside out, while Hellboy is Blown Across the Room but otherwise fine.
  • When Hellboy and Liz finally kiss, her powers light them both up in a flaming blaze. Scary to think what would've happened if poor Myers had been the one she fell in love with. Do you take your FBI agents medium or well-done?

tropes.name: Extra Eyes
tropes.html: Sammael has three eyes: two on the right side of its head, and one slightly larger on the left.

tropes.name: Extranormal Institute
tropes.html: The B.P.R.D.'s offices.

tropes.name: Even Evil Has Standards
tropes.html: Kinda. After revealing his plan to the Professor, as well as the knowledge that they would kill him afterwards, Rasputin assures him that his death will be quick and painless. Seconds later, Kroenen swiftly stabs him through the back of his neck, at the top of the spinal cord, killing him instantly.

tropes.name: Face Death with Dignity
tropes.html: Professor Bruttenholm doesn't struggle when Rasputin and Kroenen come for him, knowing that there's nothing he can do to escape them and nothing more he can do to foil their plans than he has already done.

tropes.name: Fanservice
tropes.html:
• Perlman mentions that all the female TAs were "smitten" with Hellboy, and suspects that many were crestfallen upon seeing him out of makeup and costume for the first time.
  • Abe Sapien spends the majority of time shirtless and is very fit.
  • In the movie, Liz apparently burnt all her clothes off before falling unconscious, so Rasputin kindly gives her a big blanket (and nothing else). On the movie case, she's also wearing a clingy black dress never seen in the film.

tropes.name: Feed It a Bomb
tropes.html: The death of the Behemoth.

tropes.name: Film Adaptation (Live-Action)
tropes.html: An adaptation of the Hellboy comics, includes an Origin Story.

tropes.name: Fire-Forged Friends
tropes.html: Hellboy starts out treating Myers like crap, partially due to him being a Naïve Newcomer and partially due to the Love Triangle between them and Liz. By the end of the film, he finally shows Myers some respect when he helps him realize he has control over his own destiny. Of course, then there's the fact that Hellboy had Myers literally Reassigned to Antarctica in the sequel.

tropes.name: Fish People
tropes.html: Abe is an Icthyo Sapien (thinking fish), an amphibious humanoid.

tropes.name: Foil
tropes.html: Rasputin is this to Hellboy. The latter is a demon who chooses to defend humanity, and prefers brute force and assorted guns to get the job done. Meanwhile, the former is a (undead) human who willingly chose to side with an Eldritch Abomination and is more skilled in the occult, relying on his underlings to do the dirty work. His final scenes show that he cares little for humanity, telling Hellboy that Earth's destruction will go unmourned by the rest of the universe.

tropes.name: Fold-Spindle Mutilation
tropes.html: Rasputin is sucked belly-first into the portal during the opening sequence, his already-liquefying body bending in half, backward (urk!).

tropes.name: Four-Fingered Hands
tropes.html: Hellboy's stone hand has only four fingers.

tropes.name: Friendship Moment
tropes.html: After Manning spends most of the movie complaining that Hellboy is an insubordinate menace, Hellboy saves his life from a death trap and then they team up to defeat Kroenen. Afterward, they have a friendly moment, which because it's Manning takes the form of him being a curmudgeon about the way Hellboy lights his victory cigar and teaching him how to do it properly, thus making the cigar actually taste better.

tropes.name: Funeral Banishment
tropes.html: While not formally kept from the procession, Hellboy is unable to attend the funeral of his adoptive father, due to his inhuman appearance, and can only watch it from a distance.

tropes.name: Gas Mask, Longcoat
tropes.html: Kroenen wears this combination in the opening scene when he's in Nazi uniform. Later, he just keeps his mask.

tropes.name: Gentle Giant
tropes.html: Hellboy loves cats and he doesn't mind the kid on the roof he meets while spying on Myers and Liz's date.

tropes.name: Ghostapo
tropes.html: The movie doesn't even start to show off the Nazis' capabilities with a Clockwork Nazi assassin. World War II was simply the public face of the decades-long "Occult Wars" which began shortly after World War I and lasted until the Allies finally killed Hitler in 1958. Only Mignola knows how America Saved the Day.

tropes.name: Gilligan Cut
tropes.html:
In the beginning, when Tom Manning is interviewed on TV.
Manning: — I want to tell you and I want to tell the American public one thing. This Bureau for...umm...
TV Anchor: — ...Paranormal Research and Defence.
Manning: — (looks towards camera) There is... No. Such. Thing.
[cut to properly subtitled facility of B.P.R.D]

tropes.name: Goggles Do Nothing
tropes.html: Averted, as Abe's goggles protect his aquatic eyes while also, as expected, looking really cool.

tropes.name: Good Hurts Evil
tropes.html: When Hellboy regrows his horns and is briefly evil, the crucifix from his rosary leaves a burn mark on his hand.

tropes.name: Greater-Scope Villain
tropes.html: The Ogdru Jahad, a team of Eldritch Abomination aliens worshiped by Rasputin, who tries to lay the world to waste by using Hellboy as a way of summoning them.

tropes.name: Green-Eyed Monster
tropes.html: Hellboy gets really upset about Liz going out for a coffee with Myers and overreacts about her doing things he deems romantic with him (like taking a photo of him, apparently). He throws a rock at Myers when he does the decisively more romantic Yawn and Reach move on her.

tropes.name: Groin Attack
tropes.html: When the Professor is recalling the history of Rasputin, he mentions that when Rasputin died the first time he was castrated as part of his death by Humiliation Conga.

tropes.name: Grudging "Thank You"
tropes.html: After dealing with Kroenen, Manning helps Hellboy light up his cigar properly before the two quietly exchange thank you's to one another.

tropes.name: Hand Cannon
tropes.html: Hellboy's enormous, customized "Samaritan" revolver, which holds four rounds and is made from consecrated materials such as iron from church bells and pieces of the True Cross. He uses two special types of rounds: "Whoppers" (explosive-tipped and filled with materials that can injure supernatural creatures) and "Trackers" (leave a dye trail that can be used to follow a wounded target).

tropes.name: Happily Adopted
tropes.html: Hellboy's fond memories of his surrogate father and his supportive childhood is a fundamental reason of why he keeps trying his best to do the right thing, as hard as it is.

tropes.name: Heart in the Wrong Place
tropes.html: Kroenen doesn't seem to have a working heart or blood in the film adaptation, but the clockwork device that keeps his body going...somehow...is in the upper left side of his chest where his heart should be.

tropes.name: Hellgate
tropes.html: Rasputin's portal to the Void.

tropes.name: Hellhound
tropes.html: Sammael. Though he looks more like a cross between a Thanator and a Predalien than an actual dog.

tropes.name: High-Voltage Death
tropes.html: Double Subverted when Hellboy is battling Sammael the first time. Hellboy grabs the third rail of a subway. He just gets jolted, but Sammael gets barbecued. Hellboy then lights a cigar off a flaming bit of Sammael stuck to his stone hand.

tropes.name: Historical Villain Upgrade
tropes.html: Rasputin in reality was little more than a weird, opportunistic fortune teller, while this story draws heavily from propaganda painting him as a malevolent wizard bent on domination.

tropes.name: Hit Me, Dammit!
tropes.html: When Liz is still having problems accessing her powers, she goads Myers with this.

tropes.name: Holy Burns Evil
tropes.html: When Hellboy embraces his demonic power during the climax, Professor Bruttenholm's cross burns his palm when Agent Myers throws it to him. However, during the rest of the movie, Hellboy has no problem with using holy objects such as the components of his Depleted Phlebotinum Shells.

tropes.name: Holy Water
tropes.html: One of the ingredients in the custom revolver rounds Hellboy creates for hunting demons, alongside white oak, silver shavings, and clover.

tropes.name: Huge Guy, Tiny Girl
tropes.html: Hellboy is said to be 6'5" and is a mountain of red muscle, while Liz has a slender and feminine frame.

tropes.name: Human Sacrifice
tropes.html: Done in order to bring back Rasputin in 2004. Kroenen kills the man who guided him and Ilsa to the ancient ruin in Moldavia and the guide's blood pools down into a basin at the centre of the temple from which a newly respawn Rasputin emerges.

tropes.name: I Call It "Vera"
tropes.html: Hellboy's Hand Cannon is named "The Samaritan".

tropes.name: Idiot Ball
tropes.html: In retrospect, leaving Kroenen's body unattended, and leaving all his gear in the same room, might not have been the best idea.

tropes.name: I Just Want to Be Normal
tropes.html:
• Hellboy. He sands down his horns to fit in and generally likes to pal around with the other B.P.R.D. agents when he's not working.
  • Liz resents her power, and Hellboy believes part of the reason she left the BPRD was because she felt like she wasn't a part of the normal world there.

tropes.name: I Know Your True Name
tropes.html: Invoked and played with, as Rasputin knows Hellboy's real name, Professor Bruttenholm most likely knows but refuses to say it, and the viewer is left wondering if Hellboy himself knows right up until his final confrontation with Rasputin. Turns out, Hellboy does know his demonic name: Anung Un Rama.note  It means "And upon his brow is set a crown of fire."

tropes.name: Ignore the Disability
tropes.html: Clay warns Myers not to stare at Hellboy's filed horns...with predictable result.

tropes.name: Impaled with Extreme Prejudice
tropes.html:
• Karl Ruprecht Kroenen is impaled against a column during the opening battle but survives it and disappears. In Russia he tries to make Hellboy fall into a Spikes of Doom-filled Trap Door... but ends up getting thrown into it himself, after which Hellboy drops a huge gear on top of him for good measure leaving him stuck in a And I Must Scream state if he's still conscious and unable to piece himself back together.
  • Rasputin gets a horn shoved into his belly after Hellboy snaps out of his control.

tropes.name: Implausible Fencing Powers
tropes.html: Kroenen is capable of deflecting bullets at his attackers and Diagonal Cutting stone statues.

tropes.name: In-Series Nickname
tropes.html: Hellboy has two: "H.B." and "Red".

tropes.name: In the Style of
tropes.html:
Hellboy reads a Jack Kirby-styled Hellboy comic book at one point. He considers it a Guilty Pleasure.
Hellboy: I hate those comics. They never get the eyes right.

tropes.name: Interspecies Romance
tropes.html: Hellboy (demon) and Liz (human).

tropes.name: Involuntary Group Split
tropes.html: When the agents enter Rasputin's Elaborate Underground Base, they're split into two groups by rising walls, literally seconds after stressing the importance of sticking together.

tropes.name: It Always Rains at Funerals
tropes.html: During Professor Bruttenholm's funeral.

tropes.name: "It" Is Dehumanizing
tropes.html:
• The Professor gently corrects Myers for referring to Abe as "it" instead of "he".
  • Tom Manning refers to Hellboy as "that thing" after being assaulted.

tropes.name: Jerkass Has a Point
tropes.html: Manning, regarding Hellboy's irresponsibility as a commanding officer. Such a good point, in fact, that the movie has him immediately follow it up with a bigoted rant so we don't stop thinking of him as a jerkass.

tropes.name: Kids Are Cruel
tropes.html: The children that gang up on Liz in her childhood memory go as far as throwing stones at her.

tropes.name: Kill It with Fire
tropes.html: Liz uses this a lot, obviously. Sometimes she's Wreathed in Flames for that extra boost of awesome.

tropes.name: Kindhearted Cat Lover
tropes.html: Hellboy's soft side is established early when he's introduced in a bedroom filled with pet cats. Hellboy also goes well out of his way to save some kittens during his fight with Sammael in the subway.

tropes.name: Kiss of Death
tropes.html: Rasputin gives it to Liz. It's not death for her but for all the other inmates of the looney bin she's in, because it makes her fire power go haywire and blow up the whole building.

tropes.name: Kiss of Life
tropes.html: Hellboy to Liz.

tropes.name: Lampshade Hanging
tropes.html:
At the library when Hellboy goes to face Sammael alone:
Myers: Hey, no one goes with him?! Jesus!
Abe: Hmm... no. He likes it that way. The whole "lonely hero thing"...

tropes.name: Lightning Bruiser
tropes.html: By human standards, Hellboy is definitely this, but since his actual fights tend to be against various supernatural creatures, he can be anything from a Fragile Speedster (compared to the Behemoth) to a Mighty Glacier.

tropes.name: Lip Losses
tropes.html: Karl Ruprecht Kroenen. On top of the many cybernetic modifications and acts of Self-Harm inflicted on his own body, he's also revealed to have sliced off his upper and lower lips by the start of the film - hence why he never speaks and usually wears a gas mask to cover the injury.

tropes.name: Living Labyrinth
tropes.html: Under the mausoleum in the film's final act.

tropes.name: Love Triangle
tropes.html: Between Liz, Hellboy, and Myers (who seems to vacillate between trying to reconcile Liz and Hellboy and falling for Liz himself).

tropes.name: Magical Weapon
tropes.html: The Spear of Longinus is said to make its wielder invincible, and to have caused Hitler's power to grow tenfold when he acquired it during his rise to power, though fortunately it's safely locked away in the B.P.R.D. and is not important to the plot.

tropes.name: Malevolent Architecture
tropes.html: Kroenen's Living Labyrinth (actually Rasputin's Tomb) comes complete with Spikes of Doom and Smashing Hallway Traps of Doom.

tropes.name: Masquerade
tropes.html: Hellboy, the B.P.R.D., and the occult are all kept secret from the public, and one of Tom Manning's jobs is to appear on TV and deny that they exist.

tropes.name: Mercy Kill
tropes.html: Kroenen delivers one to Professor Bruttenholm by stabbing him in the back of the neck on Rasputin's orders.

tropes.name: Meta Casting
tropes.html: When discussing the film, Mignola and del Toro were considering who should play Hellboy. They each said they had a particular actor in mind and decided to each write their choice down on a napkin and turn them both over at the same time. They had both written "Ron Perlman." Given that Perlman was large and deep-voiced, had extensive experience working in heavy prosthetic makeup, and was already a del Toro regular, the choice was rather obvious.

tropes.name: Mind Over Matter
tropes.html: Professor Broom concludes that there's nothing physically keeping Kroenen alive but sheer willpower.

tropes.name: Mistaken Death Confirmation
tropes.html: Dr. Bruttonholm's autopsy of Kroenen somehow overlooks that he's merely suspended the clockwork that animates him, which costs Bruttonholm his life.

tropes.name: Mistaken for Santa
tropes.html: Subverted — a patient with Down's Syndrome at Liz Sherman's sanitorium reports seeing a "big red guy" outside the window. One of the staff thinks she's talking about Santa, seeing as it's the Christmas season, but the patient confirms that what she saw wasn't Santa, and she's right- it's Hellboy himself, having stopped by the sanitorium to share drinks with Liz.

tropes.name: Mobile Fishbowl
tropes.html: Abe sometimes wears water goggles and water tanks when he is out of his tank. Based on the comics this is more to keep him from drying out than to help him breathe; he has both lungs and gills.

tropes.name: Muggles
tropes.html: Every supernatural entity's opinion of ordinary humans, including B.P.R.D. agents.

tropes.name: Mr. Fanservice
tropes.html: Abe and Hellboy are both quite muscular and both spend a lot of time shirtless.

tropes.name: Mythology Gag
tropes.html:
• Hellboy gets presented a comic book based on him, similar (but distinct) to his actual source material. In the cover you can see Von Klempt and one of his Krigoffs, characters from the comics that haven't made their way to the films as of yet.
  • Rasputin dubs Sammael "seed of destruction". This film (loosely) adapts the first arc of the comics, appropriately titled Seeds of Destruction.
  • The lightning and angles used for the scene Myers and a doctor discuss Liz from behind a glass are lifted almost directly from a similar scene in the comics arc titled Almost Colossus.
  • Roger the Homonunculus, a comics character, can be briefly glimpsed as a statue in the B.P.R.D lobby.

tropes.name: Naïve Newcomer
tropes.html: Myers, who doesn't know much about the supernatural and carries some naivete from his youth with him.

tropes.name: Names to Run Away from Really Fast
tropes.html: Karl Ruprecht Kroenen, the Ogdru Jahad, Anung Un Rama (the last a subversion...although it being a subversion depends entirely on whose side you're on).

tropes.name: Nazi Gold
tropes.html: The guide who led Ilsa Haupstein and Kroenen to the site where Rasputin could be resurrected is paid by them with a gold bar stamped with a swastika for his services... and then Kroenen promptly stabs him in the back.

tropes.name: New Era Speech
tropes.html:
Rasputin gives one of these just before carrying out a ceremony to release the Ogdru Jahad for the Nazis.
Rasputin: What I will do tonight can never be undone! I will open a portal and awaken the Ogdru Jahad, the seven gods of Chaos! Our enemies will be destroyed, and from the ashes, a new Eden will arise.

tropes.name: Nice Guy
tropes.html: Myers is said to be "pure of heart" by Abe, and he'd know.

tropes.name: Nice Job Breaking It, Hero!
tropes.html: Hellboy does this on several occasions, from causing Sammael to multiply each time he kills one of them (including the original Sammael, setting off the chain reaction), to getting several Red Shirts killed by running off on his own.

tropes.name: Nigh-Invulnerability
tropes.html: Hellboy can get hurt, but he's extremely durable.
