tropes.name: Ninja Pirate Zombie Robot
tropes.html: Kroenen is a Nazi clockwork zombie cyborg assassin who can sprout blades from his wrists sleeves.

tropes.name: Nurture over Nature
tropes.html: The core of Hellboy's character, as he was created to herald the return of various Eldritch Abominations but was raised by a good man.

tropes.name: One-Liner
tropes.html: "I'm fireproof. You're not," and, "I'm gonna be sore in the morning..." Made all the better because this was the last line Ron Perlman recited while working on the film. The cast and crew gave him a standing ovation.

tropes.name: Out of the Frying Pan
tropes.html: After resisting Rasputin's temptation to summon Eldritch Abominations to Earth, Hellboy kills Rasputin—which allows another abomination, hiding inside Rasputin, to begin wreaking havoc.

tropes.name: Pedestrian Crushes Car
tropes.html: Hellboy punches an oncoming car with his stone fist to save Myers who is lying in the road, causing it to flip over them both.

tropes.name: Piggybacking on Hitler
tropes.html:
Rasputin.
SS General: Five years of construction and research, Grigori! Five years! The Fuhrer doesn't look kindly on failure!
Rasputin: There will be no failure, General. I promised Herr Hitler a miracle... I'll deliver one!

tropes.name: Power Incontinence
tropes.html: Liz's pyrokinesis blows up an entire city block when she's eight years old. Later in life, Rasputin uses that memory to have Liz destroy the mental institution she's living in while she's asleep. It's the biggest reason she's afraid of her power.

tropes.name: Practical Effects
tropes.html: Used extensively and very effectively throughout, as is del Toro's tradition. Basically, any monster that's not running or fighting is a suit or animatronics rather than CGI. Even the Sammael had an actual physical suit built (complete with motorized tendrils!)

tropes.name: Pretentious Latin Motto
tropes.html: The motto of the BRPD is "In absentia luci, tenebrae vicunt." Or, "In the absence of light, darkness prevails."

tropes.name: Product Placement
tropes.html:
• Hellboy first bonds with Bruttenholm over Baby Ruth bars, which are shot in their original wrapper. Modern bars are seen in the modern scenes.
  • Hellboy steals a six-pack of Bud Light, which receives a lot of close-up camera attention.
  • Dunkin' Donuts boxes and coffee cups are seen scattered about Hellboy's room.
  • Hellboy sips on a can of Red Bull with the label facing the camera during one scene in his room. Feels amusingly fitting considering the color of the character and the last name of the director.

tropes.name: Promoted to Love Interest
tropes.html: Liz Sherman; she's more like a little sister to Hellboy in the comics. Played with when Liz tells Myers that she's known Hellboy all her life. In the original stories, Liz had a stronger romantic interest in Abe.

tropes.name: Protagonist Title
tropes.html: Hellboy, our hero.

tropes.name: Psycho Knife Nut
tropes.html: Kroenen. Not only does he love his tonfas (bladed tonfas at that), but when he's shown without his trenchcoat, he's got several knives strapped to his arms and legs.

tropes.name: Psychic Powers
tropes.html: Abe is telepathic and able to read the past of objects and places, probably to allow them to do an Infodump for the audience without it seeming too awkward.

tropes.name: Public Domain Artifact
tropes.html: The Holy Lance is prominently displayed in a glass case in the BRPD headquarters. According to Professor Bruttenholm, it was taken from Adolf Hitler's body.

tropes.name: Rasputinian Death
tropes.html: Rasputin, obviously...and he's still not technically dead.

tropes.name: Red-Flag Recreation Material
tropes.html: In the DVD special features, the characters are all given their own profiles, including likes and dislikes. The apocalyptic-minded Rasputin naturally enjoys Paradise Lost and the works of Modest Mussorgsky.

tropes.name: Red Shirt
tropes.html: The ordinary, unnamed human BPRD agents are in the movie mainly to get picked off by the bad guys at dramatically appropriate moments.

tropes.name: Removing the Earpiece
tropes.html: Done twice by H.B. The second time, it leads to several redshirts getting killed while he can't be reached.

tropes.name: The Right Hand of Doom
tropes.html: Hellboy's stone right hand is literally the Right Hand of Doom.

tropes.name: Roof Hopping
tropes.html: Hellboy does it when he spies on Liz and Myers having a date, and reveals his presence to a kid who was tending to a pigeon coop when he almost takes a deadly leap, but the kid isn't afraid and joins him at spying on the two after promising he won't tell anyone.

tropes.name: Rule of Cool
tropes.html: Anything Kroenen does runs on this. The museum fight is probably the best example, where he can spin his blades fast enough to deflect bullets and shoot them back at the guards.

tropes.name: Say Your Prayers
tropes.html: Rasputin allows Professor Bruttenholm a moment to do so before having him killed by Kroenen. If the rosary is any indication, he made use of it.

tropes.name: Screw Destiny
tropes.html: Hellboy was born to bring about the Apocalypse. After Myers reminds Hellboy that he has a choice, Hellboy tells Rasputin what he thinks of his destiny by ripping off his own horns and stabbing Rasputin in the gut with them.

tropes.name: Secret War
tropes.html: Professor Bruttenholm mentions in passing that World War II was merely the public face of the Occult War, which only ended with Adolf Hitler's real death in 1958.

tropes.name: See No Evil, Hear No Evil
tropes.html: Abe Sapien's introductory scene features rotten eggs which Myers smells and is repulsed by while in-frame, despite having been present in the scene for several minutes. Joked about on the commentary: "Is it too late to send this back to editing?"

tropes.name: Seen It All
tropes.html:
On Myers' arrival at the BPRD:
Clay: So you saw the fish guy, right?
Myers: Oh, yeah. That was weird.
Clay: [unimpressed] Yeah, right.

tropes.name: Self-Harm
tropes.html: According to Broom, Kroenen suffers from "surgical addiction", a severe form of masochism that made him mutilate himself and he survives all of that only thanks to some kind of black magic.

tropes.name: Sinister Subway
tropes.html: Hellboy fights Sammael on underground railroad tracks and later in the middle of a crowded subway station.

tropes.name: Shout-Out
tropes.html:
• The scene of Bruttenholm befriending "baby Hellboy" is very reminiscent of the Baby Ruth scene from The Goonies — including the yummy-sounds.
  • There are shoutouts to Mike Mignola scattered about - in Liz's flashback sequence, one of the buildings is called "Mignola Plaza", and one of the headstones in the Russian cemetery is inscribed with Mike Mignola's name in Russian.
  • Hellboy lives on the 51st floor of the BPRD HQ.
  • Hellboy calls Kroenen "Pinhead" in his Pre-Mortem One-Liner.

tropes.name: Shown Their Work
tropes.html: With Mignola and del Toro co-producing, it wasn't hard to squeeze in all kinds of obscure mythological references. Of course, it's a Fantasy Kitchen Sink, so...

tropes.name: Smoking Is Cool
tropes.html: Hellboy is constantly smoking cigars. It may double as a real-life Actor Allusion as Ron Perlman is an avid cigar aficionado.

tropes.name: Snowy Screen of Death
tropes.html: When Liz has her pyrokinesis fit in the psychiatric institution, the CCTV cameras go to full static as the fire wave destroys them, and again in the auction hall in TGA, along with the lights blacking out.

tropes.name: Spin to Deflect Stuff
tropes.html: Kroenen uses his blade-tonfas to block bullets and shoot them back at people.

tropes.name: Spy Catsuit
tropes.html: Abe's wetsuit is effectively this. Kroenen also wears one in several scenes, like the museum infiltration early in the film.

tropes.name: The Stinger
tropes.html: Halfway through the credits is the punchline of a Brick Joke.

tropes.name: Stock Scream
tropes.html: As an unnamed Nazi scientist is thrown against the portal in the beginning and reduced to a skeleton before disappearing, a classic Wilhelm scream is heard.

tropes.name: Stopped Reading Too Soon
tropes.html: A variation; Abe Sapien reads off the description for the Hellhound from a book to Hellboy. Hellboy supposedly kills the hellhound before Abe finishes, after which he mentions the last few sentences about resurrection.

tropes.name: Stop Trick
tropes.html: The moment that the door of Liz's asylum dorm room is shut, leaving it in shadow, Rasputin materializes out of the darkness. Del Toro pointed this out as one of the most effective special effects in the film, and it was achieved by a simple Stop Trick.

tropes.name: Storyboarding the Apocalypse
tropes.html: Rasputin gives Bruttenholm a vision of Hellboy causing the end of the world.

tropes.name: Stupid Evil
tropes.html: It's unclear just how intelligent the Behemoth is, but the fact Rasputin calls it "the master" is suggestive — in which case, it wasn't very smart of it to swallow Hellboy whole when he had a bomb on his person, which ultimately kills the beast from the inside. Possibly justified by a lack of familiarity with terrestrial technology.

tropes.name: Subhuman Surfacing Shot
tropes.html: Early in the film, Grigori Rasputin is resurrected for the second time by spilling the blood of an innocent guide in an ancient ritual circle, resulting in a pool of blood that he rises smoothly from as if levitating, firmly driving home the fact that Rasputin is even more unearthly this time around. For good measure, the deleted scenes featured Rasputin being resurrected without eyes, making the resurrection even more unsettling and forcing Rasputin to make use of glass prosthetics throughout the film.

tropes.name: Supernormal Bindings
tropes.html: Rasputin binds Hellboy in stocks and chains inscribed with Hellboy's true name. The only way for Hellboy to break these bindings is to say his name, tacitly submitting to his destiny as Prince of Hell and bringer of the apocalypse. Of course, making Hellboy fulfill this destiny is Rasputin's entire goal.

tropes.name: Tastes Like Friendship
tropes.html: Baby Ruth bars. Also, milk and cookies from a nine-year-old kid.

tropes.name: The Team Normal
tropes.html: John Myers is just a normal FBI agent thrust into the world of the supernatural.

tropes.name: Tempting Fate
tropes.html:
• "We'll be all right as long as we don't separate." Cue sliding walls rising up from the floor and splitting the group in two.
  • Before Hellboy goes into the final battle:
    Myers: Are you gonna be ok? Alone?
    Hellboy: How big can it be? (gets snatched by a giant tentacle) DAMN!

tropes.name: Things That Go "Bump" in the Night
tropes.html: They are quite real, as the Professor points out. The B.P.R.D.'s job is to understand them, and stop them from harming ordinary people.

tropes.name: This Is Gonna Suck
tropes.html:
Hellboy when about to be swallowed whole by the Behemoth while he's carrying a live bomb.
"Oh, this is gonna hurt."

tropes.name: Those Wacky Nazis
tropes.html: Ilsa, Kroenen, and von Klempt.

tropes.name: To Hell and Back
tropes.html:
Hellboy threatens it when he saves Liz.
Hellboy: I said "Hey, you on the other side; let her go. 'Cause for—[chokes back a sob]—for her I'll cross over...and then you'll be sorry."

tropes.name: Touch Telepathy
tropes.html: Abe Sapien can learn about objects or people by touching them. For example, he can touch a weapon left behind at a crime scene and see exactly how the crime happened — or he can touch a superior's hand and realize the man is dying of cancer.

tropes.name: A True Story in My Universe
tropes.html: We see some Hellboy comics on the actual Hellboy's legends.

tropes.name: The Tunguska Event
tropes.html: In the Director's Cut it's revealed that the large monolith Hellboy inserts his rock hand into to generate the Pillar of Light when he's under Rasputin's control was sent to Earth by the Ogdru Jahad, causing the Tunguska explosion in the process.

tropes.name: Two Guys and a Girl
tropes.html: Hellboy, Liz, and Abe are each supernatural and make up the core of the BPRD.

tropes.name: Underling with an F in PR
tropes.html: Hellboy is a Big Red Devil who's part of a secret government agency charged with eliminating supernatural threats before the public gets wind of them. Hellboy apparently didn't get the memo on that last part, because he enjoys having his picture taken with people, much to the director's chagrin. Note that in the comics, his existence is in no way a secret, and in fact nobody ever even bats an eye at his appearance.

tropes.name: Unexplained Recovery
tropes.html: Kroenen appears to have been mortally wounded in the prologue only to disappear, and according to his backstory his remains were later positively identified, yet he's alive again in the present. He does it again when he winds his heart to a stop to fool the BPRD agents, only to return to life hours later.

tropes.name: Unfazed Everyman
tropes.html: Myers. Once he adjusts, he's pretty much unfazed by the rest of the movie's events.

tropes.name: The Unintelligible
tropes.html: Ivan, the desiccated half-corpse Hellboy resurrects during the final act, talks with a fittingly dry, raspy voice and in (presumably) some form of Russian, which makes everything he says largely impossible to understand for the average western viewer. Hellboy and his team seem to understand him quite fine, though, if Liz's snickering when Ivan insults Hellboy is any indication.

tropes.name: Urban Legend
tropes.html: Hellboy and the B.P.R.D., until he goes public.

tropes.name: Villain Teleportation
tropes.html: Used by Rasputin.

tropes.name: Welcomed to the Masquerade
tropes.html: The movie begins with Agent Myers being brought in to the BPRD, a paranormal investigation unit. Downplayed in that his FBI skills don't do him any good against the various monsters and ancient evils they meet up with. He was only brought in to be a positive influence on the title character.

tropes.name: What Happened to the Mouse?
tropes.html:
• General von Krupt, the older Nazi who warns Rasputin that the Führer won't be happy if he fails, just oddly disappears, it's not shown whether he has fled or got killed during the battle.note In the screenplay, von Krupt goes down when Sgt. Whitman shoots him in the firefight.
  • We never do find out if Clay survives his stabbing (but Manning strongly implies to Hellboy that he won't).

tropes.name: When Things Spin, Science Happens
tropes.html: The Ragnarok Engine involves a series of revolving rings to create a portal to the prison of the Ogdru Jahad. Bonus points because Karl Ruprecht Kronen signals the scientist crew to start it up with the twirling-finger motion used to signal aircraft pilots to start their engines and "spin up" their propellers.

tropes.name: Window Love
tropes.html: A platonic variation between Abe and Liz when he gives her some words of advice and asks her to take care of Hellboy for him while he's stuck recovering in his medical tank.

tropes.name: With My Dying Breath, I Summon You
tropes.html: Rasputin summons the Behemoth this way - if it wasn't a case of the Behemoth simply being released by Rasputin's death, in which case, Nice Job Breaking It, Hero!.

tropes.name: Woobie, Destroyer of Worlds
tropes.html: Hellboy almost becomes this after Rasputin kills Liz in front of him and sends her soul into the Ogdru Jahad realm in order to force him to become the beast of the apocalypse and unlock the portal. The only reason H.B. doesn't is because Myers manages to get him to snap out of it by reminding him of what he once was and that he can choose his own destiny.

tropes.name: Would Hurt a Child
tropes.html: Kroenen in this incarnation is exponentially more despicable than his comic book counterpart. At one point in his Nazi days, he was in charge of Auschwitz, where a truly horrific amount of his victims in his twisted research were children.

tropes.name: Yawn and Reach
tropes.html:
Lampshaded
Kid: Hey! He's yawning! He's bored!
Hellboy: Yeah, the old "yawning" trick. Watch his arm...

tropes.name: You Are Better Than You Think You Are
tropes.html:
Invoked by Myers to convince Hellboy to refuse Rasputin's demand to free the Ogdru Jahad.
Myers: Remember who you are! [...] You have a choice! Your father gave you that.

tropes.name: You Are Worth Hell
tropes.html:
You Are Worth Hell
Ilsa: (to Rasputin, seconds before death) Hell will hold no surprises for us, my love.

tropes.name: You Killed My Father
tropes.html: Hellboy to Kroenen, after Kroenen kills Professor Bruttenholm. "You killed my father! Your ass is mine!"
The artificial heart ad displays the phone number 1-800-555-4444.

tropes.name: Abandoned Warehouse
tropes.html: The site of the first confrontation between Murphy and Boddicker's gang. Happens again in the last confrontation, though it also throws in abandoned factories to the mix.

tropes.name: Absurd Brand Name
tropes.html: There's a commercial advertising a huge car with terrible mileage called the "6000 SUX", mocking the Pontiac 6000.

tropes.name: Action Girl
tropes.html: Lewis is a police officer and helps RoboCop on two occasions.

tropes.name: After-Action Healing Drama
tropes.html:
• Murphy in the ER after he's shot. It doesn't work.
  • The scene in the abandoned steel mill after Murphy's escape from the OCP building also counts, though in that case it's makeshift repairs instead of healing.

tropes.name: All Crimes Are Equal
tropes.html: ED-209 advances dangerously on RoboCop for being illegally parked on private property at the end of the film, possibly having been deliberately programmed to be more aggressive than usual to protect the building due to the police strike.

tropes.name: All There in the Script
tropes.html: The script establishes that the film takes place in 2043, because in earlier versions, the news story that was shown following RoboCop's escape from the police and ED-209 had Casey Wong report to us that Sylvester Stallone had died at age 97 during a brain transplantnote Stallone was born in 1946 before the Kill Sat story was put in instead.

tropes.name: The Alleged Car
tropes.html: The S.U.X. 6000 travels just 8 miles to the gallon and has lousy build quality even when brand new. In the final chase, the hubcap of the one driven by Clarence falls off.

tropes.name: Amnesia Missed a Spot
tropes.html: After his transformation into RoboCop, what remains of Officer Murphy's mind experiences flashbacks of his prior life despite his memory being wiped.

tropes.name: Amnesiac Resonance
tropes.html: Murphy has no memory of his life before his death and resurrection, but begins to piece together that he Was Once a Man by how others react to things he says or does unthinkingly.

tropes.name: Anaphora
tropes.html:
When Ron Miller is holding City Hall hostage to get an old job back:
Ron Miller: And I want a bigger office! And I want a new car! And I want the city to pay for it all!

tropes.name: And I Must Scream
tropes.html: There are scenes where we see RoboCop's creation from his point of view. We see Bob Morton and Donald Johnson, the first complaining because the scientists have saved Murphy's left arm. After being asked if RoboCop understands what they're saying, he replies that it doesn't matter as they're going to wipe his memory anyway. This is followed by Morton asking Johnson if he thinks they'd remove the arm, to which Johnson replies that they should, given Murphy signed release waivers when he joined the force allowing OCP to do whatever they want to him when he dies. Ultimately, Morton orders them to remove the left arm and RoboCop is shut down for surgery.

tropes.name: Answer Cut
tropes.html:
An incredibly subtle, droll example occurs after Bob Morton secures approval for the RoboCop program and steps in to the elevator with his co-exec Donald Johnson.
Johnson: So, when do we start?
Bob Morton: As soon as some poor schmuck volunteers.
[cut to Alex Murphy flipping around his gun]

tropes.name: Arch-Enemy
tropes.html: RoboCop has Clarence Boddicker, the crime boss who killed him as a human.

tropes.name: An Arm and a Leg
tropes.html: Murphy's hand is blown off by a shotgun. Later, a scientist excitedly tells Bob Morton that they can save one of his arms, but Morton snaps that he wants all of Murphy's limbs replaced by bionics.

tropes.name: Armored Collar of Durability
tropes.html: The fact that beat cops have to go out wearing the realistic variant of this trope is meant to show just what a violent, lawless hellhole Detroit has become.

tropes.name: Armor-Piercing Question
tropes.html:
• After RoboCop's first nightmare about his death by Boddicker's gang, he gets up to leave his laboratory, apparently disturbed. Lewis stops him in a hall. During the conversation she says: "Don't you have a name?... Murphy, it's you." This startles him out of some of his amnesia, causing him to backpedal slightly, and marks the start of his personality returning.
  • In the Miranda rights scene, RoboCop throws Boddicker through numerous plate-glass windows, intent on hurting him or killing him. Boddicker confesses Jones' involvement in the plot, but RoboCop keeps going. Boddicker finally gets Robo to stop by saying "You're a cop!", reminding Robo that his first duty is to the law. RoboCop stops his Roaring Rampage of Revenge and arrests Boddicker instead.
    RoboCop: Yes, I am a cop.

tropes.name: Artificial Gravity
tropes.html: Played for Laughs. The President's first visit to the Star Wars Peace Platform (which is an orbital defense platform instead of the peaceful use of the ISS today) got off to a shaky start when power failed, causing a brief but harmless period of weightlessness for the visiting President and his staff. It's also Foreshadowing that, fitting the movie's themes, corners have been cut on the station, which later misfires and sets a large chunk of California ablaze.

tropes.name: Artistic License – Chemistry
tropes.html: Emil gets exposed to "toxic waste", from a disused steelworks, causing his body to literally melt apart. No substance in reality reacts with a human body, or organic matter period, in that gratuitously violent fashion. There's Hydrofluoric acid, which is nasty, but the damage and pain it causes is not evident until the day after, and you'd die long before of organ failure anyway.

tropes.name: Artistic License – Gun Safety
tropes.html:
• Played with early on. Murphy is doing trigger guard spins with his duty weapon, definitely unsafe. When Lewis remarks on his fancy moves, he puts the magazine back in the weapon, indicating that he was actually practicing with an unloaded weapon - before immediately doing it again, this time with a magazine in the weapon. This could be an aversion or played straight: either there isn't a round in the chamber (safe) or there was one in there all along (definitely unsafe). Either way, he's setting a very bad example seeing as how he's doing this in public. It's worse when he does it with the fully automatic Auto 9 as Robo.
  • Why exactly would they load up the ED-209 with live ammo for a demonstration in the executive board room? And give a loaded gun to Kinney to act out the demonstration? Kinney proceeds to recklessly point the weapon at Dick Jones, who should be far more outraged than he was. Also, why would they keep a box with a loaded handgun inside the OCP board room? Perhaps it would make sense if it was there just for the ED-209 demonstration, but it's still there a long time later at the end of the movie when RoboCop walks in on the board meeting. OCP's board of governors are stupid. On that point, the Desert Eagle that was used during the demonstration is still left loaded in the unlocked display case in the boardroom, as demonstrated when Jones grabs it during the finale. Of course, the answer is most likely, as with most of the problems present across the rest of the movie, sheer corporate stupidity.
  • During the Shooting Gallery scene that introduces RoboCop's Improbable Aiming Skills with his Auto 9, Lewis steps forward on the range. In any Real Life shooting range, this is a huge violation of gun safety and would get her kicked off the range and her gun taken away. To make this even more ridiculous, most of her fellow cops follow suit to see what she's looking at.
  • A particularly egregious example happens when RoboCop and Lewis are hiding out in the steel mill when RoboCop decides to recalibrate his targeting system and does so by shooting at some jars of baby food not a couple feet away from a sleeping Lewis.

tropes.name: Artistic License – Law
tropes.html: Legally speaking, a CEO cannot simply fire an employee on the spot, especially a senior executive like Dick Jones, without going through bureaucratic red tape and masses of paperwork. Luckily for the Old Man, RoboCop isn't that knowledgeable about employment contract laws, and it is adequate enough to remove the pesky Fourth Directive preventing him from arresting Dick Jones.

tropes.name: Artistic License – Law Enforcement
tropes.html:
• Most modern police stations have a sally port (a separate entrance for police vehicles only) where they load and unload prisoners. In this case, the police station does have a sally port. Lewis (and later RoboCop with Clarence) should have brought their prisoners in through the sally port, not into the lobby where they could have posed a threat to civilians.
  • RoboCop never once calls in his location to dispatch, whether it's a gas station robbery, apprehending a suspect in a dance club, or taking out an entire drug warehouse. Him being a bulletproof, super-strong cyborg wielding a hand cannon and a corporate product with a bunch of general directives gives him enough leeway to be above standard procedure, which dictates that officers must keep dispatch informed of their whereabouts and activities at all times; the most that can be said is that he seems to have some kind of tracker built into him. He also never does any paperwork, shoving Clarence at the Desk Sergeant with a simple "Book him." The proper response from the Desk Sergeant should have been "he's your collar. Book him yourself!", though the revelation that Clarence is a cop killer seems to matter more to those present.
  • In Real Life, there are very good reasons that cops don't work cases personal to them, especially in the event when a suspect tries to kill them. Boddicker's gang actually did kill Murphy. His hesitation at the gas station allows Emil to blow it up before RoboCop can apprehend him; it can also be argued that he uses excessive force against Leon Nash, and he later very nearly beats Boddicker to death at the cocaine factory. Possibly a Justified Trope because of how embattled and short-handed DPD was, and because nobody at the precinct even knew he was Alex Murphy (and OCP meant for RoboCop's human components to be a blank slate, so even he wasn't supposed to know he was Murphy; he definitely didn't while confronting Emil). If any of the Boddicker gang had lived, the court proceedings and lawsuits might have been very interesting.

tropes.name: Artistic License – Physics
tropes.html: RoboCop stops his first robbery by bending the barrel of the hood's gun while the criminal is holding it. Due to leverage mechanics, the goon would need to counter the inhuman force applied by RoboCop just to keep ahold of the gun. In reality, the gun would simply be ripped from his hands before it bends.

tropes.name: Ascended Fanboy
tropes.html: Subverted. Murphy himself isn't a fan of the Show Within a Show, T.J. Laser, evidently about a futuristic gunslinger, but his son loves it, and Murphy "gets a kick out of" trying to live up to the standard. Needless to say, he ends up succeeding in a way he doesn't expect.

tropes.name: Asshole Victim
tropes.html: Clarence Boddicker is a sociopathic gang leader who takes great delight in killing and causing suffering. Safe to say no one feels bad for him when RoboCop stabs him in the jugular.

tropes.name: As You Know
tropes.html: Jones says the trope verbatim when explaining that OCP has entered into a contract with Detroit to run local law enforcement as a part of his unveiling ED-209 to the other executives, who should know that already. Interestingly, the viewer is made aware of this fact via the news broadcast prior, so it feels a little more natural than most examples.

tropes.name: Attempted Rape
tropes.html:
One of the first crime victims rescued by Murphy after his transformation into RoboCop is a Damsel in Distress being threatened by two men. He disables the first with an iconic Groin Attack by shooting him through the woman's dress.
RoboCop: Your move, creep!

tropes.name: Author Avatar
tropes.html: The young gas station attendant with the glasses and the geometry book is a reference to a young Paul Verhoeven himself, who wears spectacles and studied Mathematics in the Netherlands.

tropes.name: Awesome, but Impractical
tropes.html:
ED-209 looks very intimidating, but is badly unsuited for law enforcement work and doubtful it could even perform well in the military. Lampshaded and justified by Dick Jones, who was motivated by profit far more than utility.
Dick Jones: I had a guaranteed military sale with ED-209! Renovation program! Spare parts for 25 years! Who cares if it worked or not!

tropes.name: Back from the Dead
tropes.html: The basic plot revolves around a murdered police officer who is resurrected, but begins to remember who he was before he was cyberized.

tropes.name: Bad Boss
tropes.html:
• After a member of his gang named Bobby burns the money they were trying to steal, leaving it marked and useless, and Bobby is subsequently wounded in a gunfight, Clarence Boddicker has him thrown out the back of the truck at the pursuing cops.
    Clarence: Can you fly, Bobby?
  • The higher-ups in OCP aren't much better. They're deliberately putting cops in danger to a) engineer the police strike that suits their agenda and b) get suitable candidates for the RoboCop program killed in the line of duty so they can harvest their brains. They treat the death of one of their own in an utterly stupid board room demonstration gone wrong as "life in the big city" and corporate infighting includes actual assassinations. The Old Man seems more pissed off than horrified by ED-209's Epic Fail during the demo.
    The Old Man: Dick, I'm very disappointed in you.

tropes.name: Barrier-Busting Blow
tropes.html: RoboCop punches through a wall to grab the disgruntled Ron Miller, who is holding the mayor hostage.

tropes.name: Bathroom Stall of Overheard Insults
tropes.html: Bob Morton insults Dick Jones in the bathroom only to discover he's been listening in the cubicle all along.

tropes.name: Bespectacled Cutie
tropes.html: Dr. Tyler, the scientist who leads the RoboCop project, is played by attractive French actress Sage Parker and wears notably large, thick-rimmed glasses.

tropes.name: Better Than New
tropes.html: After Murphy is pronounced dead, OCP takes his remains and resurrects him using cybernetic/robotic technology into the Nigh Invulnerable RoboCop. He'll never be human again.

tropes.name: BFG
tropes.html: Boddicker and crew eventually are supplied with the Cobra Assault Cannon. The props were built from Barrett Model 82 .50 caliber rifles, and they're quite explosive. They use the Cobra against RoboCop, and he takes one after they're defeated and uses it to blow up the ED-209 in front of OCP's headquarters.

tropes.name: Big Bad
tropes.html: A Big Bad Duumvirate between Clarence Boddicker, the crime boss of Old Detroit whose actions lead to Murphy becoming RoboCop, and Dick Jones, the vice-president of OCP who actively supplies Boddicker with his equipment and money.

tropes.name: Big Entrance
tropes.html: The producers were concerned that a simple open entrance could make RoboCop look silly; instead, Verhoeven had Robo's entrance teased out. RoboCop is delivered to the police station by a transport convoy. The support staff comes in first, and as the desk officer protests to Bob Morton, he is suddenly silenced by the sound of heavy mechanical footsteps of something non-human walking into the station, barely visible behind frosted glass. We follow this up with teasing looks of the thing that become more and more revealing until you are eagerly following the running cops through the halls trying to get a good look at this thing. At the end, you get to see RoboCop towering in his maintenance chair and looking completely kickass.

tropes.name: Bigger Is Better
tropes.html: Advertised in the commercial for the 6000 SUX, a car which has reclining leather seats, goes really fast, and gets really shitty gas mileage. Just don't be deterred by its 8.2 mpg rating. Inefficient engineering: An American tradition!

tropes.name: Black-and-Gray Morality
tropes.html: Dick Jones may be in cahoots with Clarence Boddicker, produces dangerously defective ED-209 droids, has Bob Morton killed, and takes the chairman of OCP hostage - but Bob Morton is no saint either, not caring much about Kinney's death and deliberately putting cops in harm's way to get a candidate for the RoboCop program. He's just far less of a total bastard than Jones.

tropes.name: Black Comedy
tropes.html:
• The newscasts cheerfully talk about awful things.
  • When asked to use gun "in a threatening manner", Kinney points it right at Dick's sternum, finger on the trigger... With a brief facial expression that indicates that intent was more than apparent.
  • The unlucky junior executive who gets killed during the demonstration of ED-209 is shot over and over with blood spraying everywhere until he's Deader than Dead. Morton calls for a paramedic anyway.

tropes.name: Body Horror
tropes.html:
• The first time RoboCop takes his helmet off, he says to Lewis, "You may not like what you're about to see." Murphy's face is the only visible organic part of him, and from the looks of his head, has been grafted onto a completely synthetic skull. And he still has a scar on his forehead from being shot there.
  • Boddicker's getaway driver Emil crashes the panel truck into an industrial-strength tank of acidic toxic waste. Unfortunately for Emil, he survives. He's melting as the acid eats away at his skin. Then he stumbles in front of a speeding car and gets utterly splattered.
  • The simple fact that Murphy, a nice guy with a wife and kid, wakes up to discover that he is now mostly a machine who can only "feel" his past without actually remembering it is just all kinds of nasty.

tropes.name: Bookends
tropes.html:
• The film begins and ends in the exact same boardroom, with an OCP executive being shot to pieces by a robot.
  • Murphy and Lewis chase Boddicker and his gang to an old steel mill, where they get separated and Murphy is executed by Boddicker. At the end Boddicker and his gang locate Murphy at the same steel mill packing military grade weapons, though this time Murphy and Lewis are able to work together to defeat them. Spiritually, the first time was when Murphy died and the second time RoboCop removes his helmet to become Murphy again.

tropes.name: Bond One-Liner
tropes.html: Boddicker chortles, "Give the man a hand!" after using his shotgun to shoot off Murphy's right hand.

tropes.name: Boom, Headshot!
tropes.html: Murphy dies after Boddicker pulls a pistol and shoots him in the head (which, after getting his entire right arm shot off, and being hit in the torso numerous times with shotguns, is almost a Mercy Kill).

tropes.name: Bottomless Magazines
tropes.html: Nobody is seen reloading in this movie except Murphy who does once, right before the Final Battle. The fictional stats for RoboCop's pistol states that it holds an implausibly huge 50-round magazine. When Boddicker shoots Lewis in the battle at the abandoned factory, he fires 10 rounds from his IMI Desert Eagle Mark I. This should have emptied the gun (10 rounds is the maximum amount it can hold), but the slide is not locked back after he is done shooting, indicating that the gun still has at least one more round in it.

tropes.name: Bowdlerise
tropes.html:
• Verhoeven was forced to tone down the violence in some spots to avoid an X rating in the United States. Most notably, the over-the-top death of Mr. Kinney by the malfunctioning ED-209 was trimmed to the point that it ironically became more disturbing than the original. Murphy's death was also toned down. The uncut version wouldn't be released until 1998 by The Criterion Collection, but it's now widely available.
  • The TV edit used for a ABC Sunday Night Movie in the early '90s cut half the movie and overdubbed the rest: "Ladies, leave!" and "You finked on the wrong guy." Emil also avoids getting ran over by Boddicker. The Arrow Video blu-ray release includes the TV cut as a bonus feature.
  • There was also a hilarious censor mishap on a Canadian showing which bleeped out "mother" but not "fucker".
  • The Mexican Spanish dub changes the references to a civil war in Mexico to a war in the Middle East (oddly, the original dialogue is uncensored in the subbed version).
  • Despite getting an 18+ age rating, Hungarian TV airings of the original dub cut a few seconds of Bob Morton doing coke in the company of two hookers. Bootleg versions circulating online splice in this bit from the later re-dubs. Also, most of the gratuitous swearing was removed or toned down ("fuck" is often replaced with "darn it", "shut up", "stop" or vague grunts).

tropes.name: Brick Joke
tropes.html:
• When RoboCop is first revealed to the rest of the police department, it's explained by the engineers that RoboCop eats a "rudimentary paste that sustains his organic systems". The OCP exec Donald Johnson tries some and immediately tells Morton it "tastes like baby food", and can't resist helping himself to some more. Later in the film, when RoboCop is hiding out at the steel mill waiting for Boddicker to show up, Lewis brings him his gun, a cordless drill... and several jars of baby food to eat.
  • Murphy, leaving the police motor pool, goes up the exit ramp too quickly and scrapes his rear fender on the cement. RoboCop later does the same thing.
  • One that can only be found in the script: when Dick Jones's Engineered Public Confession is exposed by RoboCop at the end of the film, the script comments that "having your cover blown is almost the worst thing that can happen to a Corporate Animal." A few lines later, after Jones gets blasted out the window, the script quips that "this is probably the worst thing that can happen to a Corporate Animal."
  • During the hostage situation scene at City Hall, councilman Ron Miller makes several demands. One of these is for a new car that "has reclining leather seats, goes really fast and gets really shitty gas mileage!" to which the negotiator offers the 6000 SUX (and even offers to throw in a Blaupunkt audio system). Later in the film, we are shown a commercial for the 6000 SUX in which terrified civilians are chased through the streets by a very shoddy stop motion T-Rex:
Commercial Announcer: It's back! Big is back, because bigger is better! 6000 SUX, an American tradition. [text appears across the bottom]: An American Tradition, 8.2 MPG

tropes.name: Bring My Brown Pants
tropes.html: After seeing that their insults were overheard by Jones in the bathroom, the sleazy corporate guy who was conversing with Bob Morton prematurely zips his pants up before he could finish urinating, resulting in a nasty wet spot on his pants.

tropes.name: Broken Record
tropes.html:
• "Hahaha! I'd buy that for a dollar!!"
  • "I know you. You're dead. We killed you. We killed you!" (RoboCop records and plays back) "You're dead. We killed you!"
  • "Murphy, it's you... Murphy, it's you..."
  • "I had to kill Bob Morton because he made a mistake. Now it's time to erase that mistake. I had to kill Bob Morton because he made a mistake. Now it's time to erase that mistake..."

tropes.name: Broken Faceplate
tropes.html: RoboCop's visor gets smashed open by ED-209, allowing the audience to see the fear and surprise on his face during a close-up.

tropes.name: Bubblegum Popping
tropes.html: Alex Murphy's partner in law enforcement, Anne Lewis, blows a bubble before trying to apprehend one of Clarence Boddicker's men. She fails and gets knocked out some minutes before Alex Murphy faces something much worse.

tropes.name: Bulletproof Human Shield
tropes.html: In the scene where Kinney is getting shot repeatedly by ED-209, there is tons of blood but the bullets should have realistically passed through his body and shattered the window behind him. And when RoboCop shoots Jones at the end of the movie, bullets are shown clearly going through his body, but the window behind him doesn't show any damage until Jones falls through it.

tropes.name: Bulletproof Vest
tropes.html: Murphy, wearing full body armor, is shot dozens of times and the vest gets shredded from it. It keeps him alive, but in horrible agony long enough for Boddicker to finish him off (temporarily) with a headshot.

tropes.name: Callous Demonstration of Power
tropes.html: While making a deal with another mob boss, Boddicker casually puts his hand in the other man's glass of wine. While Boddicker is a sadist who loves doing things For the Evulz, in this case it's simply to demonstrate to the other man who the bigger fish is.

tropes.name: Came Back Strong
tropes.html: Murphy is killed in the line of duty and is resurrected as an armour-plated heavily-armed cyborg.

tropes.name: The Cameo
tropes.html: Voice actor Bill Farmer, best known for being the official voice for Goofy, makes a brief cameo as a reporter.

tropes.name: Can't Use Stairs
tropes.html: The ED-209, ostensibly built for urban law enforcement, lacks the mobility to navigate a simple staircase. Justified in-story, as it was intentionally written as a poorly-conceived design in several ways (spotty AI, major weak points, seriously overarmed), which is why the project was abandoned in favor of the titular character.

tropes.name: Capitalism Is Bad
tropes.html:
A villanous corporation runs the show in the name of profit, and even the plain old crooks get on it.
Emil: No better way to steal money than free enterprise.

tropes.name: Car Chase Shoot-Out
tropes.html: Murphy shoots at Clarence Boddicker's gang from the car after they try to shoot him from their getaway van. It is implied that he's the only police officer who does this and other reckless things such as Gun Twirling.

tropes.name: Car Fu
tropes.html: Emil should have known not to play Car Fu around vats of industrial chemicals. After getting horribly disfigured by the stuff, he's finished off by getting run over himself and bursts into noxious slime.

tropes.name: Casting Gag
tropes.html: Just before meeting with Dick Jones, Boddicker hits on one of Jones' secretaries, who makes no effort to hide her disdain for him. She's played by Joan Pirkle, Kurtwood Smith's real-life wife.

tropes.name: Chekhov's Gun
tropes.html:
• During the ED-209's first presentation, an OCP executive is asked to brandish a loaded gun. In the final scene of the movie, Dick Jones grabs the same gun and uses it in an attempt to take the Old Man hostage.
  • RoboCop's classified 4th Directive. It turns out to be the restriction in RoboCop's system that prevents him from arresting Jones, or any OCP executive, after being revealed to aid Boddicker with impunity for his numerous felonies.
  • The Cobra assault cannons supplied to Clarence's gang. During the Final Battle, Lewis grabs Clarence's weapon and uses it to kill Leon. After that, RoboCop takes the same weapon with him and uses it to destroy an ED-209 guarding the entrance to OCP.
  • The data interface spike that emerges from RoboCop's fist and which he uses to dispatch Boddicker in the final act.

tropes.name: Chekhov's Skill
tropes.html: When RoboCop is first seen arriving at DPD, the scientists run a few checks on his systems. Among them, introduced to the audience is RoboCop's ability to record both audio and video and replay it. Later, when Dick Jones confronts Boddicker, he's enraged that the latter tells RoboCop he (Boddicker) works for him (Jones), because as a cyborg RoboCop can record the conversation and his memory is admissible as evidence. At the climax, RoboCop uses that exact capability to replay Dick's confession of Morton's murder to the OCP board.

tropes.name: Children Are Innocent
tropes.html: In a Flashback where Murphy walks in on his son, Jimmy, watching a TV show and sees The Hero twirling his gun, Jimmy asks Murphy to do it. Gun Twirling is risky because of the danger of an accidental discharge of the gun, but most kids wouldn't know that.

tropes.name: Climactic Elevator Ride
tropes.html: RoboCop takes one just before he confronts Dick Jones about his complicity with the crimes of Clarence Boddicker, but this isn't anywhere close to his final confrontation with either.

tropes.name: Cluster F-Bomb
tropes.html: The convenience store robber, upon RoboCop's entrance: "Fuck me! Fuck me! Fuck me!" This doubles as an Oh, Crap! moment; the robber is screaming this because his gun has proven useless against RoboCop.

tropes.name: Collateral Damage
tropes.html: Gang leader Sal is not killed by RoboCop but by one mook who keeps pulling the trigger of his submachine gun while dying at the hands of the nigh-indestructible cyborg.

tropes.name: Comically Small Demand
tropes.html:
The voted-out politician holds the city council hostage, demanding three things: "I want a recount. And then I want my old job back." Which would make the recount superfluous. And, of course, he also wants the new 6000 SUX that has reclining leather seats, goes very fast, and gets really shitty gas mileage.
Lt. Hedgecock: Let the mayor go, we'll even throw in a Blaupunkt.

tropes.name: Complexity Addiction
tropes.html: Leon arrives above the muddy terrain where his boss Clarence is being cornered by Murphy. Instead of just blasting Murphy on the spot, from a safe distance, firing his Cobra Assault Gun, he drops his perfectly functional weapon (tailor-made for the task), and instead runs to access and operate a crane to dump a load of scrapped metal onto RoboCop, which does ultimately nothing but briefly trap and incapacitate the cyborg. Oh, and he gets blasted to smithereens by Officer Lewis for his trouble.

tropes.name: Conditioned to Accept Horror
tropes.html: Everyone's blasé reaction to Kinney being killed by ED-209. Johnson and Morton brush it off as just an ordinary part of life in their city while the Old Man is more angry at the ED-209's poor performance.

tropes.name: Continuity Nod
tropes.html: RoboCop screams as Boddicker stabs him in the chest in a similar manner to when he gets shot by Boddicker's gang at the beginning of the film.

tropes.name: Cop Killer
tropes.html: Clarence Boddicker has killed 32 police officers before he got to Alex Murphy. However, his murder of Murphy comes back to bite him in the ass when Murphy is resurrected as the titular cyborg.

tropes.name: Corporate Conspiracy
tropes.html: There's a vice-president willing to make a deal with a crime boss to start a crime spree so that OCP can step in and offer to privatize the police force — and all of this to demolish Detroit and rebuild it as Delta City.

tropes.name: Corrupt Corporate Executive
tropes.html: Everyone who works for OCP is greedy, apathetic, and/or evil. In the first film, Dick Jones hires gangsters to bump off rivals.

tropes.name: Creator Cameo
tropes.html: Paul Verhoeven plays a dancer at a disco, and executive producer Jon Davison is the voice of ED-209.

tropes.name: Create Your Own Hero
tropes.html: Again, Boddicker and his men killing Murphy came back to haunt him as Morton used Murphy's remains to make RoboCop.

tropes.name: Credits Gag
tropes.html: The copyright notice in the end credit has "This motion picture is protected under the laws of the United States and other countries and its unauthorized duplication, distribution or exhibition may result in civil liability and criminal prosecution by enforcement droids."

tropes.name: Crooks Are Better Armed
tropes.html: Dick Jones, an exec in OCP which owns the police, wants RoboCop destroyed, so he supplies Clarence's gang with "the Cobra Assault Cannon", a .50 caliber rifle firing armor-piercing explosive rounds. RoboCop uses one to completely destroy an ED-209 guarding the entrance to OCP headquarters. In RoboCop 2, the same gun only knocks RoboCain off balance for a moment without doing any damage, showing just how tough RoboCain is.

tropes.name: Cruel and Unusual Death
tropes.html:
• Clarence Boddicker and his gang don't even try to make Murphy's death swift and painless, at one point even shooting off his hand and joking about it.
  • Emil later suffers a similar fate himself when he begins to melt and dissolve when he comes in contact with toxic waste. Clarence then makes him explode when he runs him over.

tropes.name: Crucified Hero Shot
tropes.html: Murphy's death, even though he doesn't have his arms splayed, is more or less a re-enactment of the Crucifixion. The RoboCop = cyborg!Jesus metaphor is extended throughout the film (see: getting pierced by a spear, walking on water).

tropes.name: Cruel Mercy
tropes.html: Boddicker stops Emil from killing Murphy right away, just so the whole group can give him a sadistic, drawn-out death.

tropes.name: Curb-Stomp Cushion
tropes.html: ED-209 largely dominates the initial battle with RoboCop. However, RoboCop does manage to rip off one of ED-209's arms.

tropes.name: Curb-Stomp Battle
tropes.html:
• RoboCop versus all the thugs in the cocaine-production facility.
  • RoboCop versus the ED-209 near the end of the film. Especially satisfying because their earlier fight wasn't concluded.

tropes.name: Cutting the Knot
tropes.html: RoboCop cannot do anything to Dick Jones because of Directive 4, even as he is holding The Old Man at gunpoint. The solution? The Old Man tells Dick that he's fired, thus he's no longer an executive of the company and Directive 4 no longer applies, so RoboCop is free to do as he pleases.

tropes.name: Cyberpunk
tropes.html: Gritty crime, greedy megacorps, and futuristic cybernetics.

tropes.name: Cyberpunk Is Techno
tropes.html: The soundtrack blends traditional orchestral music with electronic music and synthesizers. The movie's director says this was meant to symbolize RoboCop's dual nature as both man and machine.

tropes.name: Cyberpunk with a Chance of Rain
tropes.html: The battle at the film's climax takes place outside (one of the few scenes that isn't set at night) where it's cloudy and grey, and there are puddles of water everywhere.

tropes.name: David vs. Goliath
tropes.html: RoboCop vs. the hulking ED-209.

tropes.name: Dead Man's Trigger Finger
tropes.html: During the drug lab shootout, one mook gets shot by RoboCop and whirls around, still firing from his assault rifle, which spectacularly takes out his own boss.

tropes.name: Deadpan Snarker
tropes.html:
The hostage negotiator vs. Ron Miller in the city hall hostage situation:
Lt Hedgecock: Okay Miller! Don't hurt the mayor! We'll give you what you want!
Ron Miller: First, don't fuck with me. I'm a desperate man! And second, I want some fresh coffee. And third, I want a recount! And no matter how it turns out, I want my old job back!
Lt. Hedgecock: Okay.
Ron Miller: And I want a bigger office! And I want a new car! And I want the city to pay for it all!
Lt Hedgecock: What kind of car, Miller?
Ron Miller: Something with reclining leather seats, that goes really fast, and gets really shitty gas mileage! All right?
Lt Hedgecock: How about the uh, 6000 SUX?
Ron Miller: Yeah! Okay, sure! What about cruise control? Does it come with cruise control?
Lt. Hedgecock: Hey, no problem, Miller. You let the Mayor go, we'll even throw in a Blaupunkt!
  • Brick Joke when a commercial for the SUX is shown and we see it has an 8.2 mpg rating.

tropes.name: Death Glare
tropes.html: Johnson shoots one of these at Jones upon learning that it was the latter man who killed his friend Morton. After RoboCop kills the bastard, Johnson gives him a heartfelt thumbs-up.

tropes.name: Destination Defenestration
tropes.html:
• The hostage-taker at City Hall is grabbed and punched through a window by RoboCop.
  • After RoboCop shoots up the cocaine-production facility and corners Boddicker, he throws the latter through several windows while reading the Miranda Rights. He only stops when Boddicker reveals that he is working for Jones.
  • Jones' death at the end of the film. After holding the president of OCP hostage and getting fired, he's blown out the window by RoboCop and plummets to the ground.

tropes.name: Destroy the Product Placement
tropes.html: The 6000 SUX, driven by Clarence Boddicker, is crashed prior to the last part of the final confrontation. It's a Brand X of the Taurus' competitor, the Pontiac 6000. Earlier Boddicker blows up another 6000 SUX demonstrating his new gun.

tropes.name: A Dick in Name
tropes.html:
• Dick Jones gets an underling killed by accident in his opening scene and dismisses it as a "temporary setback," not to mention has people killed as he amasses more power and attempts to take over the company he works for. Clarence Boddicker puts special emphasis on his name when addressing him ("Look what he did to my face, Dick.") until Jones cuts him a very sweet deal for taking out RoboCop, at which point Boddicker is suddenly fine with just calling him "Richard".
  • Clarence is a cop-killing career criminal, sadistic misogynistic psychopath and all-around scumbag; he has "dick" in the middle of his last name.

tropes.name: Did You Actually Believe...?
tropes.html:
Dick Jones says this to RoboCop when he tries to arrest him in his office, and informs him about the hidden Directive 4 that prevents this very contingency from happening.
Dick Jones: What did you think? That you were an ordinary police officer? You're our product. And we can't very well have our products turning against us, can we?

tropes.name: Didn't Think This Through
tropes.html: Dick Jones programs Directive 4 into RoboCop to make it impossible for him to arrest a senior officer of OCP. And when it all goes to hell, he takes the Old Man at gunpoint, too arrogant to realize that the Old Man has the authority to terminate his employment, with predictable results.

tropes.name: Disastrous Demonstration
tropes.html: ED-209 malfunctions at an OCP board meeting and reduces a junior executive to Ludicrous Gibs.

tropes.name: Disney Villain Death
tropes.html: Happens to Dick Jones after getting shot by RoboCop a few times and falling a couple hundred feet out of the building.

tropes.name: Distract and Disarm
tropes.html: When Murphy and Lois go into the old steel mill, Lois finds Joe Cox (one of Clarence Boddicker's thugs) peeing in a corner. When she tells him to put his hands up and turn around, he does. As she holds him at gunpoint, she tells him he's under arrest, and he asks if he can "zip it up," and glances down. When she also glances towards his groin region, Joe slaps the gun out of her hand, and pushes her off the balcony they're standing on. As she lies stunned on some rubbish, Joe laughs and zips up his pants.

tropes.name: Distracted by the Sexy
tropes.html:
• A female-on-male example as Murphy and Lewis pursue a gang of crooks. Lewis catches one criminal urinating in a corner and holds him at gunpoint. He smugly puts his hands up and turns around (without pulling up his pants). Even though Lewis knows he's trying to distract her, she can't resist taking a peek downward. As soon as she does, the crook knocks her gun away.
  • Whilst RoboCop is going after Boddicker after going through his first dream sequence. The OCP scientist Roosevelt is flirting with a female cop, whose jacket zipper is way down.

tropes.name: Doomed Supermarket Display
tropes.html: A variant. During RoboCop's first patrol, a thug walks into a small convenience store and demands the owner empty the cash register and open the safe. The owner protests they don't have a safe. The thug kicks a large pyramid of beer cans, which collapses to reveal the safe.

tropes.name: The Dragon
tropes.html: Boddicker is a Psycho for Hire version, acting as the nefarious Jones' muscle in return for cash.

tropes.name: Dramatic Gun Cock
tropes.html:
• When Murphy and Lewis are chasing Boddicker's gang after the bank robbery, Murphy racks the slide on both his and Lewis' sidearm. Implying the cops in this crime-ridden Detroit still carry their sidearms in Condition 3.
  • After Emile spots them on their tail, the gang is heard pumping their shotguns 3 separate times before they kick open the door.
  • Averted with RoboCop's Auto-9, despite gratuitous twirling, it's never seen being loaded or cycled.

tropes.name: Dramatic Unmask
tropes.html: RoboCop removing his helmet. "You may not like what you're going to see."

tropes.name: The Dreaded
tropes.html:
• Dick Jones. When Morton starts talking shit about him in the bathroom, everybody bolts out knowing that Jones is there.
  • Clarence Boddicker is the most feared crime boss in Old Detroit, and deservedly so. He's a ruthless amoral killer.
  • RoboCop becomes this once he's known to criminals.

tropes.name: Drugs Are Bad
tropes.html: The scene in the drug factory is almost painfully '80s, what with the close-up shots of RoboCop's metallic feet trampling on the vials of cocaine after blowing away bad guys.

tropes.name: Dub-Induced Plot Hole
tropes.html: In the Russian dub of the movie, the plot-relevant line "You're fired" (which leaves the Big Bad unprotected by the RoboCop's directives) was translated as, approximately, "You've got burned up."

tropes.name: Eagle Land
tropes.html: Produced in the United States, RoboCop is described by its creators as an external critique of America, made possible by granting Dutch director Paul Verhoeven authorial freedom in his first American movie, allowing him to infuse the film with his outsider perspective and tone. This results in a sharp satire of ultra-capitalist America, where violence is depicted both as a consequence of societal collapse and, paradoxically, as a sanctioned solution to systemic dysfunction. Verhoeven was not attempting to make a political commentary, only to portray his vision, and the outcome is a corporation-run dystopia, where media manipulation, unchecked corporate power, and privatized policing converge in grotesque, exaggerated forms. The film’s signature dark humor, graphic violence, and faux TV commercials underscore the absurdities of Reagan-era neoliberalism and consumer culture. In his analogy of RoboCop as an American Jesus, Verhoeven muses that his messianic, action-driven hero aligns with the evangelical figure transplanted into modern America and its gun culture.

tropes.name: Egopolis
tropes.html: The Old Man calls Delta City, his development project for the Detroit metropolitan area, his "dream", and everything about his company, Omni Consumer Products, indicates that he's only really building it because he has the means, not for any improvement for the average citizen's quality of life.

tropes.name: Enemy Eats Your Lunch
tropes.html: Boddicker creepily dips his fingers into Sal's wine glass at the drug factory and then sniffs them to intimidate him. It doesn't work with Sal casually drinking from the same glass.

tropes.name: Engineered Public Confession
tropes.html: "I had to kill Bob Morton because he made a mistake. Now it's time to erase that mistake." This ends up biting Dick Jones in the ass. What makes this particularly stupid on his part is that he knows damn well RoboCop is capable of recording everything he says (he even bitches out Boddicker for telling RoboCop about his involvement in the first place), but he didn't expect him to survive his ensuing fight with ED-209, the SWAT team and Boddicker's gang.

tropes.name: Epic Fail
tropes.html: The ED-209 attempts to descend a set of stairs in the OCP building, despite the fact that its feet are too big to go down the steps.

tropes.name: Equal-Opportunity Evil
tropes.html: Clarence Boddicker's gang is very ethnically diverse: generic white (Boddicker, Leon Nash), black (Joe Cox), Asian (Steve Minh, Chan in the script), and Slavic (Emil Antonowsky).

tropes.name: Even Evil Has Standards
tropes.html:
• When Boddicker, a slimy murderer, enters Bob Morton's house to assassinate him, Morton is in the company of two hookers. Clarence orders them, "Bitches, leave!" and lets them flee the scene unharmed.
  • The Old Man may be the CEO of one of the most corrupt corporations in all of fiction, but he and his board are clearly horrified and angry when ED-209 kills a fellow board member.

tropes.name: Everyone Calls Him "Barkeep"
tropes.html: The name of the CEO of OCP is never given. He is simply called "The Old Man".

tropes.name: Evil Cannot Comprehend Good
tropes.html: When RoboCop breaks up a cocaine factory to arrest Boddicker, after shooting two dozen criminals he's ready to just kill him to save the trouble. Boddicker tries to threaten him explaining he works for Dick Jones at OCP and OCP owns the police. RoboCop doesn't care about that but Boddicker repeatedly saying "You're a cop!" only reminds RoboCop of his duty as a law enforcement officer, and takes Boddicker to be booked.

tropes.name: Evil Gloating
tropes.html:
• Boddicker's gang loves this.
  • OCP Prez Dick Jones isn't above indulging in some of this either, when RoboCop shuts down when he tries to arrest Jones, and even confesses to having Bob Morton killed. This comes back to haunt Jones in a huge way.

tropes.name: Evil Has a Bad Sense of Humor
tropes.html: Clarence Boddicker isn't above the occasional violence-based pun.

tropes.name: Exact Words
tropes.html:
• Seems to be the case with ED-209. It directs Kinney to, "Please put down your weapon." It clearly specifically means "gently place the gun on the ground," not "throw the gun away from your hand".
  • Directive Four:
    • "Any attempt to arrest a senior officer of OCP results in shutdown." The Old Man is quick to realize this and promptly fires Dick Jones thus no longer being a senior and is subject to arrest or escalation of force.
    • Subverted up to a point when RoboCop tries to arrest Dick Jones in that violating the directive doesn't trigger an actual shutdown, he is just seriously hindered but still able to function afterwards.

tropes.name: Executive Meddling
tropes.html: In-universe, the Directive 4, which Dick Jones describes as his "own little contribution."

tropes.name: Executive Suite Fight
tropes.html:
• After finding out his connection with Boddicker, RoboCop storms into OCP's headquarters in an attempt to arrest Jones, who sics ED-209 on him.
  • At the end of the film he returns and blows up the ED-209 guarding the building, then walks into an OCP board meeting and shoots Jones when he tries to hold the Old Man hostage.

tropes.name: Extreme Melee Revenge
tropes.html: After tracking down Boddicker, RoboCop gets his revenge by casually throwing him through several panes of glass.

tropes.name: Failed Future Forecast
tropes.html: The movie is set at some unclear future date after 1987, and implies that the Cold War is still going on, with references to SDI and the MX missile. The latter, which became the Peacekeeper, has now been scrapped. References are also made to the South African apartheid government which is not only still in power (albeit reduced to a single city-state), but actively threatening to deploy a Neutron Bomb against insurgents, thus promoting them from racist assholes to cartoonish supervillains (although, in Real Life, they did have nukes).

tropes.name: Failed State
tropes.html: The city of Detroit still has a government and a police force, but both are seriously undermanned and underfunded. As a result, crime is running wild in the city, which is nearing total collapse. The outsourcing of law enforcement to Omni Consumer Products is what kicks off the events of the movie.

tropes.name: Fake Platform
tropes.html: During the warehouse shootout, Clarence Boddicker attempts to leap from a catwalk onto the roof of an office, but it's one of those false, suspended ceilings that instantly collapses under his weight, causing him to fall painfully onto the concrete ground below.

tropes.name: Failsafe Failure
tropes.html: The attempt to have the ED-209 perform a test of a crime situation ends up having it kill the man simulating a hostage situation. Even though the programmers have a control console in the room, they are unable to shut down the robot before it riddles the target full of bullets.

tropes.name: False Flag Operation
tropes.html: Dick Jones hires criminals and gives them military weapons to increase crime and kill police officers, just so he can sell his ED-209 as the solution.

tropes.name: Fanservice Extra
tropes.html: Twice. Apparently cops in the future have co-ed locker rooms. Later on, when RoboCop goes into a club to collect Leon, a woman is seen dancing topless.

tropes.name: Fauxrrari
tropes.html: The 6000 SUX is a Pontiac 6000 with modified front and back to make it look "futuristic". It boasts itself on being "An American Tradition. 8.2 MPG".

tropes.name: Filling the Silence
tropes.html: The creative team wanted a full 10 seconds of silence and blank screen between the moment of Murphy's death and the first flash of static marking the start of his resurrection. The executive team had other ideas.

tropes.name: Finger-Twitching Revival
tropes.html: When RoboCop wakes up and leaves the police station.

tropes.name: Fingore
tropes.html: Among the many mutilations inflicted on him before his death, Boddicker's crew starts out by blowing off Murphy's right hand with a shotgun.

tropes.name: Firing Day
tropes.html: Dick takes the Old Man hostage, but RoboCop is unable to act due to his directive against acting against an OCP employee. So the Old Man fires Dick and Robo shoots him out the window.

tropes.name: First-Person Dying Perspective
tropes.html: Alex Murphy's death is largely shot from his perspective as his life flashes before his eyes, from Alex interacting with his wife and son, the criminals who attacked him, and the paramedics trying to save his life as he's bleeding out on the operating table. Everything goes black and fades away, but then an operating system and a Robo-Cam starts back up...

tropes.name: Flashback Nightmare
tropes.html: After his first successful deployment, RoboCop is recharging in his chair, when he starts having a nightmare of the day that Boddicker and his gang emptied their guns on him. When the dream ends with Boddicker shooting him in the head, RoboCop marches out of the room and goes on patrol.

tropes.name: Flipping the Bird
tropes.html: Implied to a degree, RoboCop's six-inch data jack emerges from his fist and he brandishes it to a computer tech when he tries to stop Robo accessing files on his own death and Boddicker's gang.

tropes.name: For the Evulz
tropes.html: While Boddicker and his gang are interested in turning a profit, but they also enjoy the more violent aspects of their job like going completely overkill just for a good laugh.

tropes.name: The Foreign Subtitle
tropes.html:
• Austria: RoboCop: The Law of the Future
  • Brazil and Portugal: RoboCop: The Cop from the Future
  • Mexico: RoboCop: The Defender of the Future

tropes.name: Foreshadowing
tropes.html:
• The artificial heart advert between the opening news reports foreshadows Alex Murphy losing ties with his family after his life-saving transformation into RoboCop.
    Doctor: Is it time for that operation? This may be the most important decision of your life.
  • RoboCop holsters his Auto-9 after test-firing it with a twirling flourish, an early indicator that the attempts to erase Alex Murphy didn't quite take.
  • RoboCop shoots a man's dick early in the film. The film ends with him shooting Dick.

tropes.name: Form-Fitting Wardrobe
tropes.html: Averted. Officer Lewis' body armour looks exactly like everyone else's, with no accomodation for boobage.

tropes.name: Full-Conversion Cyborg
tropes.html: The movie doesn't go into extreme detail over what remains of Alex Murphy, but largely implies all that remains is his brain, his face and some minimal organs in the chest. Even the rest of his skull is obviously metallic, face aside. In the second movie he gets dismembered but survives with only his head and half his torso intact.

tropes.name: Funny Background Event
tropes.html: During his house call to Bob Morton's house, Boddicker helps himself to some of the cocaine that's laying around before pulling out a grenade.

tropes.name: Futile Control Fiddling
tropes.html: During the demo of ED-209, when it continues its countdown after Kinney drops the gun, the project team immediately realize ED-209's malfunctioned and open its control panel to start trying to disable it, but to no effect. The countdown expires, ED-209 starts shooting the junior VP, and doesn't stop until one of the techs breaks the control panel by yanking out some wires, shutting the robot down.

tropes.name: Future Society, Present Values
tropes.html: The newscast at the beginning of the film depicts South Africa still under Apartheid. Three years after its release, the National Party began deconstructing the Apartheid system and transitioned to majority rule in 1994.

tropes.name: Gaia's Lament
tropes.html:
• The ozone layer is long gone and twenty seconds of exposure to direct sunlight in California is considered too much. Sunblock 5000 is provided as a way to protect people for hours at a time...but frequent use will also cause skin cancer.
  • The news segments also mention that a nuclear plant in the Amazon experienced a meltdown, irradiating the rainforest.

tropes.name: Gangsta Style
tropes.html: Boddicker's getaway driver Emil holds up a gas station by holding a SMG this way.

tropes.name: Gangster Land
tropes.html: Crime-ridden Detroit is going to be superseded by Delta City, a reboot of the town designed by OCP to be a feast for corporate and blue-collar crime alike.

tropes.name: Gone Horribly Wrong
tropes.html: ED-209's first demonstration not only fails to register a "hostile" surrendering, it can't be stopped from firing unless its plug is pulled. This is why the Old Man is so eager to hear about the RoboCop program.

tropes.name: Good Night, Sweet Prince
tropes.html: Joe Cox says this with a sarcastic tone as Boddicker and rest of his gang leave the steel mill after shooting Murphy to death with their shotguns.

tropes.name: Gorn
tropes.html: A notorious movie for it, so much so that it initially got slapped with an X rating by the MPAA for violence alone, and had to be re-edited eleven times before it finally got an R-rating. ED-209's demonstration, Murphy's death and Emil's acid bath are the worst offenders.

tropes.name: Greater-Scope Villain
tropes.html: The Old Man is the true head of OCP but he's not involved with Dick Jones' Evil Plan. While OCP is satirically presented as a major cause of the Wretched Hive Detroit has become the Old Man himself appears benign, indicating more Inherent in the System (though sequels demonstrate him being just as bad).

tropes.name: Grew Beyond Their Programming
tropes.html: RoboCop gradually starts to recover his memories of being Murphy, and starts to behave more human-like. He even confronts Dick Jones knowing full well his programming will not allow him to bring the corrupt executive to justice, but neither will he allow him to escape his sight either for want of upholding the law. There's also the final showdown with Clarence Boddicker, where RoboCop tells the surrendering felon, "I'm not arresting you anymore!"

tropes.name: Groin Attack
tropes.html:
Groin Attack
  • You're trying to take down a would-be rapist who's holding his victim hostage. He's using her as a human shield. You are RoboCop and so you have Improbable Aiming Skills. What do you do? Shoot between the hostage's legs and neuter the guy.
  • When RoboCop is apprehending him at the club, Leon makes an ill-advised attempt to kick the cyborg between the legs, with predictably self-defeating results.

tropes.name: Gosh Dang It to Heck!
tropes.html: In the TV edit Dick tells Bob Morton he just "finked" with the wrong guy.

tropes.name: Got Volunteered
tropes.html: Following the ED-209's shooting of an executive assistant Morton swoops in to talk to the Old Man about his project, which the Old Man promises to approve after a presentation in his office. Outside the shot up board room, Morton tells Jones that his project is ready to go, all he needs is a candidate to "volunteer." Following his brutal murder, Murphy, thanks to his stellar police record, has his brain incorporated in the project's cybernetic body, and comes online a year later as RoboCop.

tropes.name: Guns Akimbo
tropes.html: Human Murphy tries to shoot up the Boddicker gang's panel truck this way, with his own pistol and Lewis's sidearm. He fails spectacularly by only managing to hit Bobby in the leg.

tropes.name: Gun Twirling
tropes.html: Murphy's signature Character Tic, as he copies a move from his son's favorite TV show T.J. Lazer. He explains to Lewis in the scene prior to the car chase that he does this because he knows he's his son's role model. (The gun safety issues of doing this are averted by the fact that Murphy only does that trick after unloading the weapon. When he's doing it with Lewis prior to chasing down Boddicker, he reloads his pistol afterwords.) After Murphy is killed and Bob Morton's team turns him into RoboCop, part of the process is that Murphy's memory is erased. However, it turns out the memory-wiping process is not perfect, as demonstrated when Morton shows off RoboCop's Improbable Aiming Skills at the firing range. After finishing his magazine, RoboCop twirls his Auto 9 on his right hand before putting it in his leg holster. Lewis sees this, immediately realizing that RoboCop is Murphy. He does do it again at the end of the film before tucking his gun into his holster and confidently walking away, like a hero in a Western.

tropes.name: Helmets Are Hardly Heroic
tropes.html: Robo removes his helmet near the end of the film, apparently deciding he would rather show his real face to the world than wear it. (Besides, it was damaged.)

tropes.name: Helpless Observer
tropes.html: Officer Anne Lewis watches in horror from a safe distance as her partner is brutally dismembered with shotguns.

tropes.name: The Hero Dies
tropes.html: And is reborn as an inexorable chrome crime-fighter.

tropes.name: Heroic Willpower
tropes.html: Directive 4 is explicitly stated to cause full system shutdown. And while it inhibits RoboCop's functionality, he manages to power through it and remain functional.

tropes.name: High-Speed Missile Dodge
tropes.html: RoboCop does this a few times during his Executive Suite Fight with ED-209 in OCP headquarters.

tropes.name: History Repeats
tropes.html: Happens several times. When Murphy first encounters Clarance and his gang, he's outnumbered, unarmed, and wearing body armor that is not able to withstand multiple close-range shotgun blasts. The second time, he's in a bulletproof cyborg body and wielding a Hand Cannon, and methodically dispatches all of them except Clarence and Cox. The third time, his armor is damaged and they've got much more powerful weapons, but he's got a partner to provide backup and uses the terrain to his advantage, so he comes out on top.

tropes.name: Hoist by His Own Petard
tropes.html:
• Dick Jones and his Directive 4. Since he is the "number 2 guy around here," he tries to take the one guy who could terminate him hostage. "Dick, you're fired!" takes on a whole new meaning.
  • Dick Jones also screwed himself over when he taunts a fallen RoboCop by confessing that Jones had OCP exec Bob Morton killed, knowing full well that the cyborg can record everything he says, and it is admissible as evidence in a court of law. Jones even chewed out Clarence Boddicker for this shortly before.

tropes.name: Hollywood Acid
tropes.html: Boddicker's henchman Emil attempts to crush Murphy with his car, only to miss Murphy and drive straight into a tank full of corrosive toxic waste. He survives, but undergoes a horrific and agonizing injury as his skin rapidly erodes via the acid, and is shortly killed outright when Clarence accidentally runs him over.

tropes.name: Hollywood Board Games
tropes.html: Played for Laughs in the In-Universe commercial for Nukem, a board game that can be better described as Battleship with nukes. Instead of two navy fleets facing each other, the players are each one side of a worldwide nuclear war. The commercial wouldn't be out of a place for a themed Battleship, what with the characters hammy shouting that x territory is being threatened or smugly bragging when their tactics prove successful.

tropes.name: Hollywood Fire
tropes.html: Robo survives being caught in a gas station explosion with only a little soot on his improbably shiny armor.

tropes.name: Hollywood Silencer
tropes.html: When Boddicker shoots Morton, he fits a silencer first so his pistol is barely audible; he even uses a different pistol with an extended barrel in this scene. Since he then blows up the house, it's unclear why he used a suppressor in the first place.

tropes.name: Hookers and Blow
tropes.html: Plenty of both, particularly at Morton's house right before his death scene where he snorts the stuff off a hooker's breasts.

tropes.name: Hospital Gurney Scene
tropes.html: Murphy being airlifted to the ER where a trauma team makes a last-ditch effort to save him.

tropes.name: Humanity Is Infectious
tropes.html: The movie is about a police officer who loses his humanity by becoming a cyborg only to later gain it back.

tropes.name: Hummer Dinger
tropes.html: The 6000 SUX has reclining leather seats, goes really fast and gets really shitty gas mileage(!), specifically, 8.2 MPG! It became even funnier once Hummer SUVs started hitting real life American streets.

tropes.name: Hydrant Geyser
tropes.html: When the Boddicker gang are playing around with their Cobra Assault Cannons, one blows the top off a fire hydrant causing a geyser.

tropes.name: The Hyena
tropes.html: Joe Cox distinguishes himself among the thugs by his cackling laugh.

tropes.name: I Surrender, Suckers!
tropes.html: Attempted by Boddicker at the end of the final showdown. He tosses his gun aside and says he gives up... while his buddy is preparing to drop a load of scrap onto Murphy.

tropes.name: I Was Just Joking
tropes.html: Sal uses the "I was just kidding" justification to defuse the armed standoff with Clarence gang. It works, only for RoboCop to barge in at that moment.

tropes.name: Identity Amnesia
tropes.html: Alex Murphy forgets everything about his past life when he's killed, including his real name. Over the course of the film he regains his identity and gets his revenge on the people who wronged him.

tropes.name: Idiot Ball
tropes.html:
• We don't see the decision on screen, only its consequences, but whoever it was who decided to load a prototype law enforcement robot that the design team had to know was flaky and unreliable with live ammo for a demonstration in front of the OCP board of directors cannot be the brightest bulb on the company's Christmas tree.
  • There was no possible good outcome in Lewis and Murphy trying to follow Clarence's gang into the steel mill after tracking down their van, being heavily outnumbered in the enemy's territory.
