From that moment, Hannah's life was changed forever. She reappears in "Tape 7, Side A" when asked regarding her last talk with Hannah.

tropes.name: Space Whale Aesop
tropes.html:
• In Season 3, it's wrong not to feel sad that a serial rapist Bryce) has died because he was capable of being a partially sympathetic person sometimes.
  • Season 3: it's okay to murder a rapist, providing you can pin it on another rapist...but only if he's already dead. If he's still alive, this is wrong.

tropes.name: Spotlight-Stealing Squad
tropes.html: Ani, who is first introduced in season three yet in that season becomes the new main character, appearing in what seems like 80% of all the scenes. She is also the one who saves the day at the end of the season by concocting a story to frame Monty for Bryce's murder. Oh, and she's the new narrator as well.

tropes.name: Star-Crossed Lovers
tropes.html: Over the course of the series it's made very clear that Hannah had reciprocating feelings for Clay, so much so that it was one of the "11 Reasons Why Not", she just never acted on them. And there in lies the tragedy, they were Star-Crossed without even getting the chance to be Lovers.

tropes.name: Surprisingly Happy Ending
tropes.html: For a show that was consistently grim to the point of being a near-constant Trauma Conga Line for the cast, the ending of Season 4 managed to be surprisingly positive. Although Justin tragically dies (which had been set up from the first episode of this season), everyone else is moving on to a bright future, having gotten into college and/or getting the careers they wanted, have found love or the promise of a new relationship, they don't have to deal with Liberty High anymore and none of them face any legal consequences for the various laws they've broken, up to and including murder.

tropes.name: Surprisingly Realistic Outcome
tropes.html:
• After all the drama in the first three seasons, there is a significant uptick in student security by the school administration (via more security guards and metal detectors) and parents (who begin monitoring their kids’ messages and social media). After the death of four students (one of which was a much-publicized suicide), various felonies and scandals and dozens of fights in-the-school, it’s only natural the adults would start to crack down on kids who (whether sympathetically or not) have a history of lying and covering up.
  • Clay's first-time having sex hilariously averts Idealized Sex and he lasts as long as you would expect an 18-year-old virgin to.
  • Hannah’s tapes do her memory more harm than good in the long run. Once revealed to the public, instead of bringing Bryce Walker to justice (which was why Porter was the last one on the list), the school’s attorney is able to use them to paint Hannah as a vindictive narcissist and habitual liar.

tropes.name: Suspiciously Similar Substitute
tropes.html: In Season 3, we discover a young geeky girl with few secrets hidden to her mother who is the omniscient narrator during this season and stunningly also a Love Interest to Clay. It's not Hannah but Ani.

tropes.name: Take That!
tropes.html: At the start of season 2, the school board's latest obviously boneheaded move is to completely ban discussion of suicide, in what feels very much like a jab at the people who accused the show of glamorizing suicide simply by bringing it up at all.<!--* TalkingDownTheSuicidal: [[spoiler:Hannah wants Mr. Porter to do this to her, although it is ambiguous whether she set him up to fail. [[ForegoneConclusion He fails hard.]]]]-->

tropes.name: Teens Are Monsters
tropes.html: While all the teenagers in the show have issues and/or Fatal Flaws, some of them stand out for being total Hate Sinks such as Bryce Walker, his comrades and Montgomery de la Cruz.

tropes.name: Teen Pregnancy
tropes.html: Chloe reveals she's pregnant with Bryce's baby in "Bye." She has an abortion in season 3.

tropes.name: That Makes Me Feel Angry
tropes.html: In "Tape 6, Side A," and since the ending of "Tape 5, Side B," the dialogue keeps trying to pretend Clay "killed" Hannah, with even him saying it, when it's pretty obvious he... didn't.

tropes.name: Their First Time
tropes.html:
• Subverted in "Tape 6, Side A." Clay is about to lose his virginity to Hannah, but the trauma of all her other experiences causes her to drive him away.
  • Clay tries again at the start of season 2 with Skye. It is subverted again; this time, it is he who is too traumatized to go through with it.
  • Finally played straight in season 2, when it is revealed that Hannah and Zach lost their virginity to each other in a summer fling. It appears to have been such a positive experience that, despite including Zach on her tapes for not recognizing her loneliness, she never directly referenced it for others to hear.
  • Halfway through season 4, Clay successfully has sex for the first time, at a house party, with a girl he barely knows, who happens to be the daughter of the local sheriff, and who, afterwards, turns out to have a boyfriend... who Clay beats the shit out of.

tropes.name: There Are No Therapists
tropes.html: Averted. Barely. Despite references to Mr. Porter not being a real therapist, like in the book, after Hannah's suicide, Clay's parents discuss sending Clay to go talk to his old therapist. He refuses, and though it's brought up again after that, nothing comes of it until the audience meets Clay's therapist Dr. Ellman in season 4, played by Gary Sinise. In season 2, Cyrus says that he sees a therapist.

tropes.name: Time Skip
tropes.html: Each season represents a school semester. The first season is fall 2017. Season 2's present day picks up five months after (March 2018) the end of season 1 (November 2017/Freeze-Frame Bonus to the deposition tapes showing the date of November 2017); "Bye" takes place a month after "The Box of Polaroids." Season 3's present is the following fall semester (September/October 2018) with Flashbacks to April. Season 4 opens around June 2019, and the main narrative is the six months prior to then.

tropes.name: Title Drop
tropes.html:
• In "Tape 7, Side A," when Clay gives the tapes to Mr. Porter and explains what's on them.
  • Every third season episode title is a line dropped at some point, usually by Ani.

tropes.name: Token Evil Teammate
tropes.html: While the people who led Hannah to commit suicide aren't saints and have done and/or said some pretty messed up things, and have tried to escape blame from their partial responsibility, Bryce takes this position as he raped Hannah (and before her, Jessica) and shows no remorse over his heinous actions.

tropes.name: Token Good Teammate
tropes.html: Scott Reed, one of only two jocks on the baseball team who doesn't actively condone the actions of his teammates, and wants to distance himself from their reputation as rapists (or rape apologists). The other one is Zach. Neither are willing to publicly stand up at first, as Zach decides to work as a sort of double-agent, supplying Clay with proof of the team's activities. Scott also makes rape jokes in the beginning of the season, but as time goes on he feels more compelled to distance himself from their actions and eventually joins forces with Clay, Tony and the rest.

tropes.name: Token Minority Couple
tropes.html: Courtney surfaces with a black girlfriend in the season 2 finale.

tropes.name: Tragic Aids Story
tropes.html: Justin, having been homeless on multiple occasions and selling his body for drug money, is revealed in the series finale to have contracted HIV, which, because he declined to get tested, evolved into AIDS. His body is too far gone and he dies from the disease.

tropes.name: Troubled, but Cute
tropes.html: Justin through and through. With a difficult home life and some Jerk Jock behavior, but Hannah and Jessica are still drawn to him. Clay lampshades this in "The Box of Polaroids," telling Imaginary!Hannah that girls always go for that sort of thing.

tropes.name: Troubled Teen
tropes.html: Almost every single main character is this to a degree, the straightest examples are Justin (homeless and living on the streets, abuses drugs), Tyler (bullied and isolated as well as being raped, and brings weapons to the school with the intent on causing a mass shooting), and Hannah (being torn down bit by bit by bullying before being raped and later taking her life).

tropes.name: True Companions
tropes.html: Despite all of arguments and drama between them and this trope was downplayed at the end of Season 2, the main cast (more prominently Clay, Justin, Jessica, Tony, Alex , Zach, and later Tyler) are always there for each other. Lampshaded by Ani in the third season finale.

tropes.name: Turn the Other Cheek
tropes.html:
• Bryce is easily forgiven for his terrible crimes by Ani in Season 3, and even Clay, though marginally less easily than Ani, thinks that it was wrong not to grieve Bryce at all.
  • Tyler for the shooting. Yes, he has serious problems, but he still tried to commit mass murder at the school dance, but he still remains good friends with Clay and most of the main cast.
  • Justin is viewed as this in-universe once he gets back together with Jessica because he was responsible for her being raped.
  • In the eyes of the law, his school and his friends, Clay's delusions cause him to hurt numerous people, beat people up, crash Zach's car and leave him for dead and even light a car on fire and he is never charged, gets into an Ivy League school and is chosen as class speaker.
  • Winston quickly accepts Monty's apology for beating him up, and invites him over to his house for a second hookup.
  • Alex is Bryce's killer, but in the end, not that many people seem to care – his father isn't even that conflicted about covering it up, and Sheriff Diaz seems to know what really happened, but implies to Bill that he's also complicit in the cover-up. Charlie, his new boyfriend is pretty fine with it and willingly enters into a relationship with him, and even when he confesses to the one person who was most hurt by it (Winston), he doesn't seem to mind that much. In the end, he doesn't even seem to feel that guilty, and no one in the core group is uncomfortable around him or concerned about him.

tropes.name: Two Guys and a Girl
tropes.html: Clay, Justin and Jessica fit the trope. After the focus shifts away from Hannah, they are the most focused characters. In Season 2 and 3, Clay is The Hero, Justin is The Lancer and Jessica is The Heart. The finales of seasons 2 and 3 end with them on the last scene.

tropes.name: Two Girls and a Guy
tropes.html: Hannah, Jessica and Alex, before their friendship falls apart.

tropes.name: Understatement
tropes.html: At his deposition, Marcus, due to his inability to admit his faults, can only state that he might have hurt Hannah's feelings at their so-called "date." You ''think'', mate?

tropes.name: The Unfair Sex
tropes.html:
• Despite their close relationship, Hannah constantly chides Clay for the apparent faults she finds with his character — all delivered with a cheery smile. But heaven help Clay if he reciprocates, which usually leads to emotional histrionics or her storming off. For example: in "Tape 1, Side B," she asks Clay if he thinks that Hannah can be as pretty as Jessica. Clay is baffled by the question and, before he can formulate an answer, she already takes his silence as an insult. When he honestly says that Jessica is pretty, but Hannah is special (which sounds like he is trying to weasel his way out of having to admit that Hannah is not beautiful), she takes it as "special needs"/'retarded' and is insulted. Than she blames his lack of social skills, even though she is the one who asked a question where there is no right answer and jumped to the worst conclusion.
  • There's also the fact that the entire series is Hannah's mental torment of Clay, despite the fact that even she knew he did nothing wrong, because telling her story the way she wanted was more important than not destroying his mental health.

tropes.name: Unresolved Sexual Tension
tropes.html:
• Clay and Hannah in their Will They or Won't They? relationship. They were attracted by each other but due to his fear of being rejected and her "I don't deserve him" insecurity, they couldn't be officially together and with Hannah's death, their story remains unfulfilled.
  • Justin and Jessica in Season 2. They're still in love with each other and almost Everyone Can See It. But Jessica doesn't forget that he let Bryce rape her, tries to stay away of him, and like Hannah above, Justin feels he doesn't deserve her. It's really and finally resolved in mid-season 3.

tropes.name: Unwitting Instigator of Doom
tropes.html: Kat moving away and having Hannah pursue Justin is the first of the thirteen reasons.

tropes.name: Urban Legend Love Life
tropes.html: Hannah has an infamous reputation as the "class slut," but seemingly remains a virgin up until a summer fling with Zach, ironically one of the only jocks who didn't claim Hannah was trying to sleep with him.

tropes.name: Used to Be a Sweet Kid
tropes.html: Played with during season 2. At the beginning of "The Box of Polaroids," a flashback is shown of eight-year-old Bryce befriending Justin, who wore the same clothes everyday, was foul smelling, and was teased and bullied by classmates because of it. However, it also showed that Bryce used fear and intimidation even back then.

tropes.name: Victorian Novel Disease
tropes.html: Alex has a rare present-day example that manifests as painful stomach cramps and requires daily medication.

tropes.name: Vomit Indiscretion Shot
tropes.html:
• After being forced to chug a 40 oz malt liquor bottle by Justin, Zach and Bryce, Clay goes home drunk and spews all over the family dinner while being admonished by his parents.
  • Hannah vomits quite violently into the the waste basket after seeing Bryce raping Jessica. At Jessica's own party for that matter.
  • In season 2, Justin's withdrawal symptoms involve a lot of vomiting, and all on screen.

tropes.name: Wham Episode
tropes.html:
• Any episode from 10 on can count, but "Tape 7, Side A" is infamous for containing Hannah's very graphic suicide (although it was later removed) among other things.
  • The season 2 finale, "Bye," likewise contains the graphic sexual assault of Tyler by Monty with a mop handle, it being the last straw for Tyler who enacts his plan to shoot up the school by the episode's end. It (both directly and indirectly) puts much of the "bitter" in the Bittersweet Ending.

tropes.name: Wham Line
tropes.html:
• There are quite a few of these, and most of them come from Tony. At the end of "Tape 1, Side A," Tony meets Clay at Eisenhower Park. They talk for a minute, and Tony goes to leave. Before that, though:
    Tony: Eisenhower Park? That must mean you're about ready for side two.
  • After Tony's been following Clay around for episodes, hounding him about his set of tapes, Clay gets frustrated and snaps at him, wondering how Tony fits into everything. He then states that there probably isn't even a second set of tapes like Hannah said. Tony gets into his car, turns on a cassette, and:
    Hannah: Hey, it's Hannah. Hannah Baker. That's right. Don't adjust your... whatever device you're hearing this on.
  • Also worth mentioning is the final scene before Clay's episode. Tony finds Clay sitting at the park from the first tape, and tells Clay that his tape is next. Clay asks him if Clay's the reason that Hannah killed herself. Tony tries to explain that he thinks everyone contributed to her death. Clay interrupts him and asks:
    Clay: Knowing what you know, and believing what you believe, did I kill Hannah Baker?
    Tony: Yes.
  • Not the line itself, but the circumstances of it: Tyler blurts out about the tapes during his deposition, ending any chance of them not going public.

tropes.name: Wham Shot
tropes.html:
• A lower level of Tyler's photography case reveals a number of boxes of ammunition as well as a pistol, a rifle and a shotgun, heavily implying that he'll shoot up the school.
  • Later on, Tyler examining photos of people that he'll target in the shooting. He removes Alex for standing up to Montgomery for him but Clay is still on there.
  • Season 3's trailer has one major one at the end, establishing the new season arc. The second-last shot is of most of the main characters at a funeral, and the camera pans over to a picture near the coffin, identifying who the deceased person is. It's Bryce.

tropes.name: What Happened to the Mouse?
tropes.html:
A few characters disappear suddenly with maybe a short mention, but no follow-up:
  • Cyrus tells Tyler that Marcus is suspended, but it is not depicted onscreen, nor is he mentioned afterwards.
  • Jackie, who stayed at the Bakers', suddenly left after Tony's hearing and only left a goodbye note. The contents (and probably her motivation) are not shared with the viewer.

tropes.name: What the Hell, Hero?
tropes.html:
• Tony gives a few of these to Clay, including one for taking a sensitive photo of Tyler and spreading it around, arguing that through seeking justice for bullying with more bullying he only fed the vicious cycle instead of breaking it.
  • Sheri also gives one to Clay when he asks why the girls in the Polaroids got themselves into bad situations.
    Sheri: Clay, you don't know what was happening in this photo, and you don't know what happened after.
    Clay: But clearly no one's forcing her to be there.
    Sheri: Look, girls don't just "get themselves" into bad situations. Guys make the situations bad. You don't know what it feels like, to be a girl in that room.
  • In Season 3 Jessica gets this from a lot of people when she leaves Alex and goes back to Justin. Especially, given the reason she does it, because Alex isn't as good at sex as Justin is.

tropes.name: Whodunnit?
tropes.html: The third season's central plot is the murder of Bryce Walker.

tropes.name: Who Murdered the Asshole?
tropes.html: A major plot in Season 3 is who killed Bryce. Considering he's more or less the Big Bad of the first two seasons and has managed to seriously harm and/or screw over the majority of the cast, that's a lot of potential suspects. Somewhat subverted in that Bryce spends a lot of season 3 attempting to atone for his actions in the previous two seasons.

tropes.name: Who's Laughing Now?
tropes.html:
• It was heavily implied by the end of the first season that Tyler is planning a school shooting to get back at his bullies. Lo and behold, in the Season 2 finale, he was ready to carry it out before Clay and Tony stepped in and prevented it.
  • Hannah mentions at least once that she expects the tapes to have consequences and the last person supposed to listen to them was the school counselor anyway, pretty much guaranteeing it.

tropes.name: With Friends Like These...
tropes.html: Justin and his posse were all relatively close, but as the season progresses, Justin was left with no one; understandable considering Reason #10 reveals he let Bryce rape Jessica.

tropes.name: Woobie, Destroyer of Worlds
tropes.html: Tyler. Pretty much everything that happens to Tyler following Hannah's suicide drives him deeper down the path to a place of no return.

tropes.name: World of Snark
tropes.html: Nearly everyone is prone to some level of snark, but most notably Clay, Hannah, Alex, and Ani.

tropes.name: Yank the Dog's Chain
tropes.html: Hannah. Constantly. Unlike in a lot of stories like this, her problem isn't that she has a Friendless Background, but that nearly every damn friend she makes either turns out to be a Bitch in Sheep's Clothing or an Innocently Insensitive idiot who inevitably screws her over or pushes her away.

tropes.name: You Have GOT to Be Kidding Me!
tropes.html:
Hannah gives this reaction when Mr. Porter says that if Hannah is not comfortable naming her rapist, which would allow formal and even legal steps to be taken, the only option for Hannah is to move on from her rape.
Hannah: Are you fucking kidding me!?

tropes.name: Action Film, Quiet Drama Scene
tropes.html: Brian explaining himself after it emerges that Letty was his informant. He also tells Mia the reason why he allowed Dom to escape, despite feigning ignorance earlier.

tropes.name: Anachronism Stew
tropes.html: During the scene where Brian has his pick of impounded cars, an R35 GT-R is shown. While available at the time the movie came out, within the series timeline it shouldn't exist, as one character mentions it's been 5 years since the first movie, making the film take place in 2006. (The GT-R became available starting 2007.) The same goes for Brian's final car, which is a 2009 Subaru WRX STI.

tropes.name: Armour-Piercing Question
tropes.html:
Mia to Brian when they're talking in the cafe.
Mia: Maybe you're lying to yourself. Maybe you're not the good guy pretending to be a bad guy. Maybe you're the bad guy pretending to be the good guy. You ever think about that?

tropes.name: Artistic License – Cars
tropes.html:
• David Park introduces his car as a 1998 Nissan 240SX. The car actually used is a Nissan Silvia S15.note The given year of 1998 would have been correct if David's car was an actual 240SX, with '98 being the last year the 240SX (and its parent Nissan S-platform, for that matter) were sold in North America. Apparently, director Justin Lin loved the Silvias from the previous film so much that another Silvia was used as David's car in this. 
  • In the opening heist scene, the crew unhooks the gasoline trailers and reconnects them to a tow truck. Simply unhooking a tractor trailer and dragging it away would not work, as the air line needs to be connected for the brakes to release.
  • During the chase to bring Braga back from Mexico, Dom takes out several of Braga's goons by blasting their tires out with a shotgun and sending them cartwheeling end over end. Artistic License – Physics is also in full effect, as a flat tire would only slow a car down, not catapult it into the air.

tropes.name: Artistic License – Chemistry
tropes.html:
Brian escapes Braga's mooks after the tunnel run by rigging his cockpit to fill with nitrous oxide and detonating it with his car's cigarette lighter. The problem is that nitrous oxide is not a flammable gas, but an oxidizer, which aids engine output by decomposing into oxygen inside the engine's combustion chamber.
  • Dom is able to tell Fenix's car runs on nitromethane by looking at a yellowish powdery residue on the road. Nitromethane does not create yellow soot when it burns, and any fuel left on the road would have long evaporated by the time Dom came along.

tropes.name: Artistic License – Engineering
tropes.html:
• During the first helicopter scene, the pilot calls over the radio that he is "at angels 5", meaning he is at 5000 feet altitude. The helicopter is much lower, so the term should be "cherubs" 5, or about 500 feet.
  • During the final chase scene through the tunnels, the tunnels appear to be 1 to 2 miles in length. While not impossible to build a 2 mile tunnel through a mountain, it is practically impossible to build one through a mountain of stone without using some sort of technology that would give the position of the tunnel away, making it unlikely that the tunnels could exist without the U.S. and Mexican governments knowing about it.

tropes.name: Artistic License – History
tropes.html: Agent Penning says about Arturo Braga that "he's moved more heroin across the border than Escobar did in 10 years," referencing the notorious Colombian drug cartel leader Pablo Escobar. However, Escobar and his Medellin cartel primarily trafficked in cocaine, not heroin.

tropes.name: Artistic License – Medicine
tropes.html: When Mia is treating Dom's gunshot wound, she says the bullet is not inside, which means there should be an exit wound. However, Dom doesn't appear to have one.

tropes.name: Asshole Victim
tropes.html:
While Fenix does suffer a horrendous death at the end of the film, he's a cartel lieutenant who antagonizes Brian and Dom and personally executed Braga's last batch of drug runners.
  • Dwight is a cocky drug runner for Braga's cartel who is constantly antagonizing Brian for driving a Nissan and taunts him after Dom spins him out in the audition race. It's hard to feel sorry for him when Brian brings the DEA into his house while he's filming a sex tape and has him arrested to take his place in Braga's organization.

tropes.name: Author Appeal
tropes.html: Although he isn't a big car guy, director Justin Lin expressed his appreciation for the Buick GNX, and urged the car coordinators to have Dom drive one at the start of the movie as it fit his character and because it had barely been used in movies.

tropes.name: Arc Villain
tropes.html: Arturo Braga, though It's Personal with the Dragon, Fenix Calderon, for seemingly killing Letty.

tropes.name: Awesomeness by Analysis
tropes.html: Dom shows incredible detective prowess, instantly knowing not only exactly what went down at Letty's crash site, but walked out with a vital clue apparently even the FBI missed.

tropes.name: Backhanded Apology
tropes.html: Mia gives one to Brian while they're talking in the cafe, "apologising" for the fact that Brian had to come to their house and pretend to love her.

tropes.name: Back from the Dead
tropes.html: You know that 1970 Dodge Charger (which was wrecked by his father and rebuilt before the first film's events) that Dom wrecks in the first film? It's back in this film. And it gets wrecked and rebuilt again.

tropes.name: Bookends
tropes.html:
• The movie begins with Dom and his gang hijacking a gasoline truck and ends with him getting rescued from a prison bus by Brian, Mia and his gang from the beginning. Also counts as a Bolivian Army Ending.
  • Also invoked with Fenix. Earlier in the movie Dom sees Fenix standing over Letty before killing her in some sort of guilt induced hallucination. At the end, Fenix stands over Brian in much the same way before Dom swoops in for the rescue.

tropes.name: Boom, Headshot!
tropes.html: Fenix kills the drug runners this way after they're finished doing the job.

tropes.name: Call-Back
tropes.html: A pretty grim one. When Dom is arrested and sentenced in the final act, the judge sends him to Lompoc prison. All the way back in The Fast and the Furious (2001), Dominic told Brian that he did two years in that prison and "(He'd) die before going back". The look on Dominic's face shows exactly what he feels.

tropes.name: Chekhov's Gun
tropes.html: During the initial U.S. - Mexico border run, Dom notices several propane tanks in the tunnels. Later on, he uses this to kill one of Braga's henchmen and collapse the tunnels

tropes.name: Conveniently Empty Roads
tropes.html: Played straight. When Brian and the crew break Dom out of the prison transport, there are no other vehicles around. The same is true during the opening gas truck heist.

tropes.name: Curb-Stomp Cushion
tropes.html: Dom attacking Brian. Brian is obviously not as strong as Dom and gets knocked around, but he manages to fight off Dom even when he is downed, blocking most of his punches, and even manages to get his legs around Dom's head to hold him back, with Dom having to put in real effort to get out of it. While he didn't fight Dom head-on unlike the likes of Hobbs, Jakob, Deckard, and Owen, he still does a lot better than anyone else apart from those four when pitted against Dom's wrath, and he did held back, as he acknowledged he deserved to be beaten down and just tried to calm Dom down without actually trying to fight back.

tropes.name: Darker and Edgier
tropes.html: Fast & Furious compared to the other films. It has a much grimmer atmosphere with both Brian and Dom investigating who was behind Letty's (apparent) death and Dom personally seeking revenge.

tropes.name: Dropped a Bridge on Him
tropes.html: Letty has all of five minutes of screentime, and the next thing we know, Mia calls up Dom to tell him that Letty has been killed by Fenix. We get to see what happens later, at least, but it's still awkward, especially since Michelle Rodriguez has her name on the posters.

tropes.name: Extreme Sports Plot
tropes.html: Explanation is same as 2Fast 2Furious (undercover cop and an ex-convict become street racers in order to get hired as drivers for a drug lord so they can infiltrate his operation) and the added twist that Dom is also going undercover on his own initiative to get revenge on the man who killed his girlfriend.

tropes.name: Fanservice
tropes.html: The film has moments of hot girls kissing during club scenes.

tropes.name: Femme Fatale
tropes.html: Zigzagged with Gisele, a mysterious woman who serves Braga and makes advances on Dom but ultimately sides with Brian and Dom.

tropes.name: First Girl Wins
tropes.html: Mia for Brian.

tropes.name: Friendlessness Insult
tropes.html: Dom is interrogating a man named David Park who has a connection to the murder of Dom's girlfriend Letty. Brian arrives and offers to help Dom solve Letty's murder, stating that Letty was his friend too. Dom cynically responds that Brian "isn't anyone's friend".

tropes.name: GPS Evidence
tropes.html: Dom examines the crash scene where Letty apparently died, found evidence of a certain kind of nitro booster, and knew exactly who installed it. Not only are there likely to be several garages in a city the size of Los Angeles that would do that particular mod, the fact that Dom hasn't been there in five years means that his knowledge of local garages is rather out of date. He still gets the right garage on the first try.

tropes.name: Hero Killer
tropes.html: Fenix supposedly to Letty, subverted since he didn't quite finish the job.

tropes.name: Hidden in Plain Sight
tropes.html: Where does Brian hide a car containing $60 million in smuggled drugs where the cops and gangs won't find it? The police impound lot.

tropes.name: High-Altitude Interrogation
tropes.html: Dom does this to one of Braga's informants.

tropes.name: Incredibly Obvious Bug
tropes.html: Brian's superiors plant a beeping tracking device with a bright red light in the center console of Brian's Skyline. He rips it out and destroys it before the cartel can search his car.

tropes.name: It's Personal with the Dragon
tropes.html: Braga might be the Big Bad, but Fenix is the one who Dom and Brian really hate throughout the film.

tropes.name: The Man in Front of the Man
tropes.html: The front man for the drug running ring appears to be working for an unseen boss. The boss turns out to be a decoy and the front man is the actual boss and Big Bad.

tropes.name: Mass "Oh, Crap!"
tropes.html: Every at the exchange (including Dom and Brian) all react this way when the FBI attack the area where the exchange is happening in an attempt to apprahend Braga.

tropes.name: Misplaced Retribution
tropes.html: Brian gets put on suspension for the raid to grab Braga going bad, despite the fact that he wasn't responsible - one of his colleagues jumped the gun and launched the raid before Brian gave the go signal, and told them to grab the wrong man.

tropes.name: The Mole
tropes.html: Letty went undercover for the DEA in Braga's organization, mainly in order to try and get a pardon for Dom.

tropes.name: Near-Villain Victory
tropes.html: Fenix manages to catch up to Brian's car and overturn it, allowing him to recover Braga. Just as he's about to finish him off, Dom comes busting out of the tunnels and guns straight for him. Fenix tries to shoot him but Brian grabs his leg, distracting him long enough for Dom to crush him against Brian's totaled car.

tropes.name: Non-Action Big Bad
tropes.html: Braga is good at planning and scheming, not so much on the action side.

tropes.name: "Not So Different" Remark
tropes.html: Braga gives one to Dom, claiming that neither of them are "heroes".

tropes.name: Oh, Crap!
tropes.html:
Oh, Crap!
  • Dom has this reaction during the truck heist at the start when he notices that they've been spotted by the truck's driver. The truck driver, himself, also has one when he realizes that he's driving towards a cliff, and decides to jump out of the truck with his pet iguana.
  • Brian after hearing his phone ringing and seeing Letty's name on the screen, realising that Dom just figured out that the former was the one who put Letty undercover, and is clearly pissed.
  • Agent Trihn has this reaction when she finds that Ramone Campos is actually Arturo Braga.

tropes.name: Only a Flesh Wound
tropes.html: A mook shoots Dom directly in his shoulder. The look on Dom's face made it clear he was more worried about his nice jacket than any damage done to his actual person. Oh, and Dom proceeds to beat the mook damn near to death, with both hands. And doesn't so much as flinch while Mia patches up the wound.

tropes.name: The Only One Allowed to Defeat You
tropes.html: Dom with Fenix Calderon.

tropes.name: Outrun the Fireball
tropes.html: Dom when the propane tanks in the tunnel explode. Also inverted at the beginning, where Dom runs towards the fireball.

tropes.name: Product Placement
tropes.html: Subaru donated the Impreza WRX STIs.

tropes.name: Real Men Wear Pink
tropes.html: Subverted. The fact that Braga, a man who supposedly clawed his way up from "varrio enforcer" to "ruthless drug kingpin", came to a drug deal wearing a salmon pink silk tie is immediately taken by Dom and Brian as evidence that the man is not the real Braga.

tropes.name: Secret Underground Passage
tropes.html: Braga's men use a hidden tunnel wide enough to drive through to smuggle drugs across the US Mexico border.

tropes.name: Sequel Hook
tropes.html: Dom's escape from the prison bus, revealed at the beginning of Fast Five.

tropes.name: Smug Snake
tropes.html:
• In the climax, Braga constantly keeps mocking Brian as Dom and he are trying to outrun Braga's men, so much so Brian finally gets fed up and punches him to shut him up. And again In the sixth movie, since he has muscle by his side, he thinks he can take Brian while he's in prison. Brian easily handles them and get the information needed out of him.
  • Fenix taunts Dom about killing Letty, and instead of killing Brian outright at the end, kicks him around a few times before pointing his gun at him. This eventually became his undoing.

tropes.name: Surprisingly Realistic Outcome
tropes.html:
• Dom and Mia don't trust Brian for betraying their trust in the first film and it takes almost half the movie for them to forgive him and start trusting him again.
  • Despite helping to arrest a wanted drug lord and aiding a federal agent, Dom is arrested and sentenced to 25 years to life for his previous crimes. Thankfully, Mia, Leo and Santos, and Brian get ready to break him out...

tropes.name: Tempting Fate
tropes.html:
Brian and Dom kidnap Braga in order to forcibly take him back to the United States.
Brian: Where your boys at? Huh? They gonna show up, or what?
(Braga's men come swarming in from everywhere)
Braga: Careful what you ask for!

tropes.name: That's What I Would Do
tropes.html: Brian tries to narrow down a list of suspects with the same name to figure out which one is involved with street racing. He has his FBI partner read off a list of the suspects' cars. After hearing about a Nissan 240SX with an illegal modification, he remarks that he's the one. His partner asks how he knows this and he replies "Because that's what I'd drive."

tropes.name: Third-Person Person
tropes.html:
Dwight.
Dwight: Dwight likes this foot a lot.

tropes.name: Trailers Always Lie
tropes.html: Mia driving in the trailer. She only drives at the very end, a minute before the credits.

tropes.name: Tranquil Fury
tropes.html: When Dom gets the maximum sentence (a life sentence of which he must serve at least 25 years), Brian doesn't say anything, but you can tell that he is pissed.

tropes.name: Unresolved Sexual Tension
tropes.html: When Brian and Mia see each other again, Mia hadn't yet forgiven him for his role as an undercover cop five years earlier. Naturally, this is followed by a Relationship Upgrade.

tropes.name: What the Hell, Hero?
tropes.html:
• Mia gives one to Brian while talking in the Cafe for lying to her and her family during the events of the first movie.
  • Dom, after discovering that Brian put Letty undercover is understandably pissed, asking why he never told him about Letty.

tropes.name: You Have Outlived Your Usefulness
tropes.html: Braga has all his drivers for the border crossing run executed after completing a single run.

title: How to Lose a Guy in 10 Days
original_title: How to Lose a Guy in 10 Days

tropes.name: Alliterative Name
tropes.html: Both protagonists: Andie Anderson and Benjamin Barry.

tropes.name: Baby Talk
tropes.html: Andie uses goo-goo lingo as one of the methods to make men run away fast.

tropes.name: Back-to-Back Poster
tropes.html: The poster has the romantic leads leaning on each other and looking snide at the other. Fitting, since they don't start out really liking each other and are both secretly fake dating the other for their own agendas.

tropes.name: Based on an Advice Book
tropes.html: The film is adapted from a short cartoon book of the same name by Michele Alexander and Jeannie Long.

tropes.name: Becoming the Mask
tropes.html: Ben comes to fall for Andie once her former persona (the "good Andie") comes back. He even loves her so much that when he learns she loves him back, he doesn't want to go out with the woman who made the bet with him in the first place.

tropes.name: Best Friend Manual
tropes.html: Ben's mother lets slip that Andie is the first girl Ben ever brought home. It's not exactly advice, but it's a "heads up" insight that lets her see the context.

tropes.name: The Bet
tropes.html:
• Andie makes one with her boss. Ben makes one with his boss. Note that the woman is only doing it out of creative integrity, while the man is doing it just for money. Interestingly her so-called "creative integrity" leads to her manipulating a guy because she originally sees him as nothing more than a means to get some creative freedom. Ben, by contrast, is just doing his best to be charming (which isn't outside the realm of normal dating) and not giving up on Andie, to win a lucrative account for his company. Basically, both of them have to learn to stop manipulating the other just to get what they want. Of course, Andie's boss then reneges on the deal, saying that Andie can write about anything she wants... as long as it's trivial. Andie quits on the spot.
  • Ben's company already has the advertising contract; he just wants to be assigned to the account and break away from his usual assignments of "sports and beer". In a way, he also wants some creative integrity.

tropes.name: Bland-Name Product
tropes.html:
• Andie writes for a women's magazine known as Composure. It's very unlikely that this is a coincidence with Cosmopolitan, another women's magazine. Her boss states that "serious journalism", things "that matter" to Kate Hudson, such as politics, the environment, and foreign affairs are inappropriate for a women's magazine mainly comprised of things such as how-to's, make-up, and fashion.
  • DeLauer resembles DeBeers, a diamond company that owns most of the world's diamond business.

tropes.name: Chekhov's Skill
tropes.html: It's earlier in the film that Andie can talk her way out of a speeding ticket. It hints how she's going to convince Ben she's a vegetarian. She later she uses the same sweet talk to convince the taxi driver to pull over while they're on a bridge.

tropes.name: Chick Flick
tropes.html:
• A romcom starring two attractive actors as antagonist fake-daters who fall in love.
  • In-universe, they attend a Chick Flick Marathon, consisting of Sleepless in Seattle, Fried Green Tomatoes, Mystic Pizza, and When Harry Met Sally.... Pretty sure this constitutes Cold-Blooded Torture.

tropes.name: Couple Theme Naming
tropes.html: It's probably not a coincidence that the lead couple both has Alliterative Names.

tropes.name: Crying After Sex
tropes.html: Michelle admits that she cried after she and her now-ex-boyfriend had sex for the first time. When Andie and Jeannie push for more details Michelle admits that it wasn't a Single Tear but full on weeping, and they'd only been together for two days.

tropes.name: Deathbringer the Adorable
tropes.html: Krull the Mister Muffykins, looking natty in his Burberry sweater!

tropes.name: DEFCON-5
tropes.html: "I have to crack this guy. I mean, this is Defcon Five, and I have to do something truly appalling. It's not funny." Possibly makes sense in this context, however, as their situation is going rather well due to Ben doing everything in his power to not break up with her, while she's trying to make things worse until he does.

tropes.name: Diagonal Billing
tropes.html: A more subtle example than most but during the opening credits Kate Hudson's name is on the right-hand side of the screen and slightly higher while Matthew McConaughey is on the left and slightly lower.

tropes.name: Everyone Loves Blondes
tropes.html: The golden-haired Andie Anderson is considered so gorgeous she 'could throw up on a guy and he'd say, "Do it again."'

tropes.name: Female Gaze
tropes.html: Ben spends a lot of the movie sans shirt, and catches some women at his office staring.

tropes.name: Fiction Business Savvy
tropes.html: Ben thinks a great new slogan for the diamond industry group is "Go frost yourself." Lampshaded when his boss, agreeing this to be an excellent idea, shouts it out the window, only for someone to shout back "Frost this!"<!--* FlorenceNightingaleEffect: [[LampshadeHanging Lampshaded in dialogue]].--><!--* FourthDateMarriage: It's not exactly love at first sight.-->

tropes.name: Girly Girl with a Tomboy Streak
tropes.html: Andie is a feminine writer who goes around New York in pretty dresses, but she loves sports and bacon and has no problem getting covered in mud.

tropes.name: Hysterical Woman
tropes.html: Michelle, who is Prone to Tears (including after sex), gets attached way too quickly and thinks she's too fat. Andie exploits this behavior for her column — she thinks that acting hysterical (i.e. like Michelle) — early in a relationship is a great way to drive men away. She also blurts out while in a restaurant out of nowhere that her boyfriend thinks she's fat.

tropes.name: I Call Him "Mister Happy"
tropes.html: Hilariously subverted by having the girlfriend naming her boyfriend's penis "Princess Sophia". He complains by saying that, if she has to name his parts, it should be a more masculine name, "something like Spike, or Butch, or Krull the Warrior King!" The last of which is what she names her Chinese crested (which is a small, mostly hairless breed of dog that can conceivably be mistaken for a chihuahua.)

tropes.name: Jerkass Has a Point
tropes.html: Andie's boss at the magazine. It's a magazine devoted to fashion, makeup, and how-to articles. Why would Andie think "serious journalism" has a place there? Didn't she read the magazine before she took the job? The movie inadvertently implies she's either an entitled idiot who felt she could write whatever she wants despite her workplace's needs, or was not a good enough writer to land a job at the sort of "serious" publication she obviously wanted but still entitled enough to think the "trivial" magazine should let her do as she pleased.

tropes.name: Karaoke Bonding Scene
tropes.html: Done when Andie and Ben, who are sort-of in a fake relationship (it's complicated), perform an inebriated rendition of "You're So Vain" by Carly Simon at karaoke, which signifies how they're finally airing out their respective grievances.

tropes.name: Mean Boss
tropes.html: Lana is framed as this because she insists on Andie finishing her piece despite her misgivings, and because she objects to Andie's desire to write about politics.

tropes.name: Meaningful Echo
tropes.html: Towards the end, when Ben calls Andie's bluff about 'not running away' by using a term from the game his family plays. What makes it more meaningful is that earlier, Ben explained that his mother was bad at bluffing because she was "pure of heart".

tropes.name: Men Buy from Mars, Women Buy from Venus
tropes.html: The modus operandi at Ben's advertising agency is to assign accounts based on gender, under the assumption that men simply cannot understand the needs of female consumers and vice-versa.

tropes.name: Mister Muffykins
tropes.html: Invoked. In order to seem spoiled and shallow, Andie gets her and her new boyfriend a Chinese Crested dog that wears sweaters and pees everywhere. To his credit, Ben appears to become genuinely attached to it.

tropes.name: No Periods, Period
tropes.html: Ben reacts to the tampons Andie slips into his medicine cabinet as if they were live tarantulas.

tropes.name: Please Dump Me
tropes.html: Andie's project is to act horribly enough to drive a man away. The only reason it fails is that Ben has to keep her to get a promotion.

tropes.name: Race for Your Love
tropes.html: Andie is about to leave New York for a new job forcing to Ben to chase after her taxi on his motorbike. He catches up to the taxi on the bridge out of the city but the driver refuses to pull over until Andie tells him she feels like she's about to be carsick.

tropes.name: Rage Quit
tropes.html: Ben has one during a game of Bullshit at his parents' home on Staten Island, when he discovers his family has been helping Andie cheat the game. Though, he does it rather playfully.

tropes.name: Real Men Cook
tropes.html: One of the ways Ben attempts to get Andie to fall in love with him (to win a bet) is by cooking for her. His friends call it "bringing out the big guns". Unfortunately, Andie is working on the eponymous article and is actively doing everything she can to get Ben to dump her. So as soon as he brings out the lamb, she breaks down into fake tears, "revealing" that she's vegetarian (which the viewers know to be false since she was eating a burger earlier).

tropes.name: Romantic Fake–Real Turn
tropes.html: Andie and Ben both have their ulterior motives for dating each other: Andie to write an article; Ben to win an advertising contract. Despite both of them becoming bitter once the truth is revealed, Andie writes her article stating how much she regrets the deceit, and Ben upon reading this chases, catches up with, and kisses her.

tropes.name: Sexy Backless Outfit
tropes.html: Andie's yellow gown for the party is backless. She does a twirl in it and Ben can't take his eyes off her.

tropes.name: Shirtless Scene
tropes.html: And in the bathroom, no less. Ben also gets one early in the movie when he changes shirts.<!--* SimpleYetOpulent: Andie's fabulous yellow gown.--><!--* StrictlyFormula: No surprises in the plot, but still a good romantic comedy.-->

tropes.name: Suddenly Shouting
tropes.html: "Are you saying I'm some kind of... MENTAL PERSON?!?"

tropes.name: Those Two Guys
tropes.html:
Supporting characters show up in pairs to comment on how Andie's and Ben's deceits are going:
  • Judy Spears and Judy Green, Ben's rivals and co-workers.
  • Tony and Thayer, Ben's friends and co-workers.
  • Michelle and Jeannie, Andie's friends and co-workers.

tropes.name: Two First Names
tropes.html: Benjamin Barry.

tropes.name: Urine Trouble
tropes.html: The movie has Krull the Chinese crested peeing on a pool table.

tropes.name: 0% Approval Rating
tropes.html: Absolutely no one in the British Army has anything kind to say about Tavington. Cornwallis himself doesn't show any sympathy for him when Benjamin kills him.

tropes.name: Affably Evil
tropes.html: General Cornwallis comes across as cordial, diplomatic and more honor-bound than the likes of Colonel Tavington. He even gives Benjamin his genuine gratitude for retrieving his two great Danes unharmed and healthy.

tropes.name: And Starring
tropes.html: The opening cast roll ends with "and Tom Wilkinson".

tropes.name: Anyone Can Die
tropes.html: Benjamin's words prove true: "The innocent will die along with the rest of us". Blatantly proven when Tavington's men slaughter much of the side characters and love interests.

tropes.name: Appeal to Force
tropes.html: Col. Tavington in his introductory scene. When Martin tries to reason with him about his brutal conduct by citing the rules of war, Tavington responds by aiming a pistol at his head (an unarmed civilian, natch) and asks him if he would "like a lesson in the rules of war". Then he points it at Martin's children. Completely deconstructed when it's shown Tavington's superiors hate him for this approach because it violates the rules of war, inspires rebellion against Tavington's cruelty, and tarnishes the desired reputation of Officer and a Gentleman that his fellow soldiers like his superiors wish to maintain.

tropes.name: Artistic License – History
tropes.html:
Aside from most of the battles depicted, about two thirds of the movie. Specifically:
  • The timeline that the film tries to present doesn't jive with historical chronology, even though the film also presents these real events both on-screen and through monologue. The film opens in 1776, and the conversation at the South Carolina Assembly indicates that the Continentals "expect a Declaration of Independence," so it can be safely assumed that it is June or early July by that point. After Gabriel enlists and parts ways with his family, the audience hears his monologue-by-letter which reveals that Charles Town (modern-day Charleston, SC) fell to the British (12 May 1780) and his best friend "fell at Elizabethtown (part of the Battle of Springfield (23 June 1780))". The following scene with Benjamin and Thomas has Thomas stating that "it's already been two (years)". It's unclear if he means two years since the start of the war or since the levy vote, but either explanation is historically inaccurate. This also makes it difficult to determine just how bad the film's Not Allowed to Grow Up sin really is.
  • The film has the militia headquartering at the ruins of a Spanish mission. In real life, the Spanish did build and abandon a settlement, Santa Elena, in the lands that would later become South Carolina, but it was way larger than a single mission and was located more to the south, around modern-day Parris Island.

tropes.name: Ax-Crazy
tropes.html:
• Tavington, Tavington, Tavington. Most of the atrocities committed in the film are because of him, and he actively makes Cornwallis's job more difficult because of his needless cruelty.
  • Benjamin lapses and gives us a literal example (he's wielding a tomahawk) during his assault on the British detachment that took Gabriel. He brutally dispatches every redcoat that gets in his way with his tomahawk, and after taking down the last one standing, he savagely starts hacking away at the guy, driven into a blind, grief-filled rage. The sight of their father butchering a man while yelling and covered in blood understandably freaks out his two young sons (who he brought along to provide support fire).

tropes.name: Back from the Dead
tropes.html: John Billings is seen killed in the first redcoat volley at the climactic Battle of Cowpens. This is several months after he committed suicide. Also counts as a Blooper.

tropes.name: Badass Preacher
tropes.html:
Reverend Oliver is recruited for the militia by Gabriel.
"A shepherd must tend his flock...(snatches off wig and puts on black, broad-brimmed hat) and at times, fight off the wolves."

tropes.name: Batman Gambit
tropes.html:
• After taking a supply convoy full of Cornwallis' personal effects (and two prized Great Danes), which include numerous officers' uniforms, Martin rides into Cornwallis' base for formal parlay, claiming he's captured eighteen officers. The talks quickly turn to prisoner exchange, and Martin offers the officers (really just stuffed dummies) for the members of his militia, who were captured earlier. He then whistles on his way out, prompting the great danes to leave Cornwallis and run back to Martin.
  • Tavington defeats Martin's partisans, because he correctly guesses that they will try to attack another convoy, so he orders soldiers to hide in the wagons, while he is hiding with his dragoons behind a hill, ready to attack.
  • The Continental's strategy at Cowpens relies on Cornwallis's disgust with militia and their tendency to retreat during traditional battles. Martin leads the Continentals with his militia forces at the center of their ranks and orders a retreat after the British's second volley. Cornwallis orders his entire battalion to chase after the militia and slaughter them, unaware of the much larger Continental force behind the hill the militia were retreating to.

tropes.name: Battlefield Flagbearer
tropes.html: At the end of the film, when the Battle of Cowpens is at its peak, most of the resistance militia are cut down by British Dragoons, including their flagman. Benjamin Martin, realizing his men are fleeing, manages to rally his army by grabbing the dropped flag and using its pointed tip to skewer some enemy mooks. Then he starts waving it high, raising the militia's morale enough to fight back and eventually win the war.

tropes.name: Berserker Tears
tropes.html: At the end of the ambush, in slow motion.

tropes.name: Big Bad
tropes.html: General Cornwallis is the highest officer in the British Army seen during the movie, leading the Southern theater against the Continental Army to quell the revolution. He is later reduced to a more minor threat as Tavington is given free rein and becomes more brutal, committing civilian atrocities with glee and systematically hunting down Martin's guerillas. Martin's personal objective becomes killing Tavington, with defeating Cornwallis a secondary mission. Ironically, Martin only succeeds - and the tide turns - after he changes that and sacrifices a chance to kill Tavington in order to save the Continental Army from collapse. Though this being Hollywood, he gets a second go at Tavington just a few minutes later.

tropes.name: Big "NO!"
tropes.html: Gabriel yells this when his friend Peter Cuppin is shot by the British and his comrades are pulling him back to retreat. He repeats it much louder and longer when Tavington shoots his brother Thomas.

tropes.name: Black-and-White Morality
tropes.html: British = Evil, American = Good, nothing in between, no ambiguity. Though most of the British show redeeming qualities, with only Tavington being irredeemable and totally evil.

tropes.name: Blood from the Mouth
tropes.html: Captain Borden does so after Gabriel stabs him.

tropes.name: Blood Is the New Black
tropes.html: At the end of Martin's first guerilla engagement with the British, he kills the last soldier with a tomahawk, before proceeding to have at the corpse in bloodthirsty rage over the immediately preceding execution of his son Thomas. Martin's remaining sons look on in shock until their father eventually emerges with his face covered completely in blood.

tropes.name: Blood Knight
tropes.html: Despite his comments that he finds war an "ugly business", it's clear that Tavington enjoys his work as a soldier way too much and longs to kill as many enemies as possible to build himself up as a legend.

tropes.name: Boom, Headshot!
tropes.html: At the Battle of Camden, a cannonball is fired and bounces off the ground. An unlucky rebel soldier takes it right in the face. It doesn't turn out so great for him.

tropes.name: Brick Joke
tropes.html:
• Benjamin's inability to build a rocking chair. He finds one in Cornwallis' headquarters and tries to examine it until Cornwallis catches him.
  • Early in the film, Anne says that she remembers Gabriel because he had slipped ink into her tea years ago, so that her teeth remained black for several days. Later, when they become engaged and Gabriel sleeps at her parents' house, she prepares tea for him. When Gabriel leaves the house, his teeth are black.

tropes.name: Call to Agriculture
tropes.html: After experiencing the horrors of the French and Indian War, Benjamin took up farming (and apparently carpentry), and he refused to fight in the American Revolution, at first.

tropes.name: Canine Loyalty
tropes.html: Played With. Cornwallis' two Great Danes seemed happy enough with him, but almost immediately decide Benjamin Martin was a more preferable owner after spending just a few days in his militia's captivity. It seems they enjoyed the freedom of running unbound through the fields and prairies with Martin compared to their previous well-fed but sheltered ownership.

tropes.name: Card-Carrying Villain
tropes.html:
William Tavington forcibly conscripts plantation workers into the British Army, orders the execution of wounded American prisoners, burning Ben's home, murders one of his sons and orders the execution of another one. And that's just in his first few minutes of screen time!
"You know, it's an ugly business doing one's duty... but just occasionally, it's a real pleasure."

tropes.name: The Cavalry
tropes.html: The French making the save at the Siege/Battle of Yorktown to stop the British retreat.

tropes.name: Chekhov's Gunman
tropes.html: Jean Villeneuve, on behalf of the French; they promised their navy and ten thousand soldiers.

tropes.name: Cheese-Eating Surrender Monkeys
tropes.html: Averted. Maj. Villeneuve is a stalwart ally to the Colonials and an all-around badass, and the French army shows up at the end to play The Cavalry and force the British to surrender. Which actually is historically accurate.

tropes.name: Cold-Blooded Torture
tropes.html: In the French and Indian War, Martin and his men caught up to a group of French soldiers who had massacred and raped a town of civilians. Enraged, they killed the French slowly by means of torture and dismemberment.

tropes.name: Combat Pragmatist
tropes.html: Martin learned about hit-and-run guerrilla tactics employed by the Indians and later explained that his unit during that time period would respond in kind. In his first engagement in the movie, he instructed his sons to target the officers, shoot the soldiers from back to front (while he went front to back), stay low to the ground and hidden behind logs, trees and small hills. This was all reflective of the time period-the American Revolution was the first war to edge away from typical open field, lines of soldier's confrontations (at least, the first one since the advent of firearms - even then, before barrel rifling was devised, snipers were not nearly as helpful or useful in wars). Colonial troops had already long taken up what would now be called guerrilla warfare that they learned fighting various native tribes.

tropes.name: Composite Character
tropes.html: Both Martin and Tavington were a combination of several colonial militia leaders and brutal commanders.

tropes.name: Concepts Are Cheap
tropes.html: All the talk of freedom often amounted to just that, as Gabriel notes. It's his hope that after winning their independence the Americans will have a chance to make them a reality.

tropes.name: Create Your Own Hero
tropes.html: Benjamin Martin was actively trying to avoid becoming involved in the Revolutionary War for the sake of his family. He only starts a guerilla movement to oppose the redcoats after Colonel Tavington burns down his home and shoots one of his sons in front of him.

tropes.name: Cute Mute
tropes.html: Susan is very adorable and does not speak for the first half of the film.

tropes.name: Curb-Stomp Battle
tropes.html: The first one seen in the film has the British wiping the floor with the rebels. Also, later on when Ben and two of his sons slaughter the redcoats to rescue Gabriel.

tropes.name: Deadpan Snarker
tropes.html: Tavington is a very dark example.

tropes.name: Defensive Feint Trap
tropes.html: The Battle of Cowpens starts with the Continentals pulling this, taking advantage of the British's low opinion of militia and their tendency to flee under fire to lure the British into running right into the rest of the army for a counterattack. Truth in Television, as it happens.

tropes.name: Disproportionate Retribution
tropes.html: As part of Col. Tavington's Establishing Character Moment. A neutral family helps any and all wounded soldiers after a battle on their farm? Torch the buildings, kill the livestock, and steal the horses, since they had the audacity to help the rebels along with your own troops.

tropes.name: Doomed Hometown
tropes.html: Benjamin's house is burnt down by Tavington's men shortly after Thomas is killed and Gabriel is captured.

tropes.name: The Dragon
tropes.html: Capt. Borden is this to Col. Tavington, as his second-in-command.

tropes.name: Dragon-in-Chief
tropes.html: Col. Tavington takes his orders from General Cornwallis and is his direct subordinate, but he's by far the biggest threat in the film to Martin and the militia, a viler villain, and much better at hunting them down.

tropes.name: Dressing as the Enemy
tropes.html: The militia dress up as redcoats and blow up a munitions ship.

tropes.name: Driven to Suicide
tropes.html: John Billings shoots himself in the head after his family are murdered by Tavington. He does so within seconds of learning of their deaths, in full view of the minister and other rebels.

tropes.name: Dual Wielding
tropes.html:
• Tavington wields his saber in one hand and an empty pistol in the other when Gabriel's men ambush his dragoons.
  • The climax fight scene features Tavington wielding a sword and unfixed bayonet while Ben uses his Cherokee tomahawk in one hand and an empty pistol and seconds later a dagger in the other.

tropes.name: Elite Mook
tropes.html: The British Dragoon units led by Tavington, which leads the lesser redcoats in battle, and can be identified by the green stripes on their uniform and headgear.

tropes.name: Enemy Mine
tropes.html: The French aren't about American independence as much as they are seeing their old rivals, the British, humiliated. Personified by the relationship between Benjamin Martin and the Frenchman Jean Villeneuve. Martin is well-known to have massacred and mutilated a French force during the French and Indian War.

tropes.name: Even Evil Has Standards
tropes.html:
• Cornwallis is an honorable British general who respects the laws of warfare and simply wants to reestablish British rule. He also wants to maintain good, if not peaceful, relations with the colonials. Partly because of this, he is appalled at Tavington's brutal tactics and rightly faults him for the increasing resistance against the British from the American militia. Eventually though, he recognizes that Martin is a problem that needs to be dealt with urgently and gives Tavington permission to use whatever methods are necessary to hunt him down.
  • Captain Wilkins complains that there's no honor in burning down a church full of civilians, and is clearly reluctant to follow his orders to do so. Earlier, when Tavington finally clarifies Martin's identity, Wilkins looks noticeably disturbed that the first thing the colonel does is ask after his children. He hesitates before finally answering him, and in both instances his fellow Dragoons look to him with a cold, judging stare, showing they're just as troubled by Tavington's dishonorable methods even if they cannot insubordinate by speaking up.
  • When Tavington orders the unnamed British Captain to have the wounded rebels executed, the latter has a Jaw Drop. He looks ashamed and disgusted as his men carry out the Colonel's order.

tropes.name: Evil Brit
tropes.html: Again, Tavington is spot on. To a much lesser extent General Cornwallis, his staff and Tavington's loyalist aide-de-camp. Yet, they all belong to the least sympathetic characters of the story, mainly because Aristocrats Are Evil.

tropes.name: Evil Counterpart
tropes.html: William Tavington serves this role to Benjamin Martin.

tropes.name: Expy Coexistence
tropes.html: It requires both a fairly thorough knowledge of the war and careful attention to dialog, but apparently the main historical inspiration for Tavington, Banastre Tarleton, exists in the universe of The Patriot alongside Tavington. When Gabriel returns home wounded, he talks about the Green Dragoons "falling on the Virginians", an apparent reference to the Waxhaws Massacre, where Tarleton's soldiers thought that the Americans pulled an I Surrender, Suckers! and killed Tarleton while surrendering, note Accounts of the event differ, but the rough consensus is that some elements of the American forces were starting to surrender and others were still fighting when the white flag went up. Soon after the Americans put up the white flag, Tarleton's horse was killed and he was trapped beneath it, which led Tarleton's men to falsely believe that Tarleton had been killed. This sent them into a bloody rage, and the British proceeded to kill or injure most of the Americans before order could be restored.

tropes.name: Fatal Flaw
tropes.html: To defeat Cornwallis in the climactic battle, Martin takes advantage of Cornwallis' pride and penchant to ignore the fighting ability of American militia.

tropes.name: Faux Affably Evil
tropes.html: Tavington is usually quite polite, even as he's mocking a man about killing his son, or informing a building full of civilians that they're about to be burned alive.

tropes.name: Fire-Forged Friends
tropes.html: Dan and Occam. Dan repeatedly insults Occam because he's a black slave, but after Occam saved Dan's life during a battle, Dan softened on him. After the war, they work together to help rebuild Benjamin's house. Occam was a free man by that time, voluntarily staying with the militia even though he no longer owed them service.

tropes.name: Forgotten Fallen Friend
tropes.html: Thomas is only mentioned once after his death.

tropes.name: French Jerk
tropes.html: Major Jean Villeneuve is a subversion. At first he seems like a snobbish sort who treats Colonel Benjamin Martin with contempt (though not without reason, as Martin killed a lot of Frenchmen in the French and Indian War), which Martin dismisses as typically French. However, Villeneuve later reveals that his family was killed by British soldiers, his countrymen keep their word about the ships he promised, and he and Martin become Fire-Forged Friends by the end.

tropes.name: Four-Star Badass
tropes.html: "Lord Cornwallis knows more of warfare than we can hope to learn in a dozen lifetimes."

tropes.name: General Failure
tropes.html: Although we don't see him onscreen, General Horatio Gates is very much this as he was in real-life at the battle assumed to be the disastrous Battle of Camden. Benjamin comments to Gabriel that his strategy of engaging the British out on an open battlefield doomed his army from the very start, as their lines quickly dissolve as they fall into a bloody retreat. It's then mentioned that Gates had fled from the battle on horseback and left his men to fend for themselves, again true to the actions of the real-life Gates.

tropes.name: Gentleman Snarker
tropes.html:
Several, with special mention to Benjamin Martin.
Lord Cornwallis: (regarding Martin's threatening to kill 18note 19, if he hangs Martin with his men of Cornwallis' officers if Martin's men are not released) This is hardly the conduct of a gentleman.
Benjamin Martin: If the conduct of your officers is the measure of a gentleman, I consider that a compliment.

tropes.name: Gideon Ploy
tropes.html: Inverted. Benjamin Martin and his men dress up scarecrows as redcoat officers and hold them at gunpoint within full view of General Cornwallis' camp, specifically to convince Cornwallis that they held a large number of English officers captive so they could exchange the "officers" for Colonial prisoners Cornwallis had. It works, much to Cornwallis' later consternation.

tropes.name: Give Me a Sword
tropes.html: After getting shot, Reverend Oliver throws his musket upwards to Gabriel so he can kill Tavington.

tropes.name: Glory Hound
tropes.html: Lord Corwallis is one, but Tavington is a more blatant and eager example. As part of a Freudian Excuse, Tavington is overzealous to prove himself and gain riches through brutality due to his father squandering all of his inheritance and leaving him with nothing, while Cornwallis seeks to only rein in Tavington's brutality to maintain his reputation and advance his military career. Both end up paying the price for their desire of fame in war.

tropes.name: Good Shepherd
tropes.html: Reverend Oliver joins the patriots to defend his flock after many in his parish join the militia.

tropes.name: Greater-Scope Villain
tropes.html: The unseen King George III, ruler of the British Empire. He's only ever referred to in passing, but Cornwallis and the other Generals ultimately answer to him. And Tavington is such a central figure Cornwallis himself might count as this.

tropes.name: Guns Akimbo
tropes.html: Tavington is shown wielding a pistol in each hand when Gabriel's revenge party ambushes him. He then drops one of the pistols and draws his saber.

tropes.name: Harmful to Minors
tropes.html: One of Benjamin Martin's sons is shot in front of the rest of his children, and then he takes two of the remaining boys—aged between nine and twelve—and slaughters the British soldiers responsible. Their horror as they walk back to their torched house is apparent.

tropes.name: Heel–Face Door-Slam
tropes.html:
• The British lieutenant who thanked Martin for helping British soldiers after the first battle is shown to look horrified at the shooting of Thomas and the massacre of the enemy wounded. And then the movie has him become one of the first to die when Martin and his sons rescue Gabriel.
  • Then there's Wilkins, who protests the burning of the church and looks visibly upset by it, but nothing is ever done with it and he is forgotten about during the final battle, with no real resolution to his character. The novelization gives him an extra scene at the Battle of Cowpens as a payoff, where he almost intervenes in the fight between Benjamin and Tavington in the final battle, only to decide that Tavington isn't worth it. He defiantly stares Tavington down, lowers his loaded pistol and rides away even as Tavington orders him to shoot Martin.

tropes.name: Hero Killer
tropes.html: Tavington ruthlessly kills a lot of sympathetic characters, most notably Thomas, Gabriel, and Reverend Oliver - though in all fairness, the latter two were trying to kill him. Not to mention Anne, her parents, and pretty much everyone else burned alive on his orders.

tropes.name: Highly Conspicuous Uniform
tropes.html: Part of historical fact, but especially for the well-dressed French soldier. When Martin takes note of Villeneuve in his proper uniform just before a large battle, the Frenchman insists that if he is to die, he is going to die well-dressed. Also used for military purposes in the movie itself, as during Gabriel's rescue Martin shoots the more-conspicuously uniformed officers first, then goes to work on the grunts.

tropes.name: Historical Hero Upgrade
tropes.html: Martin is chiefly based on Francis Marion, the Swamp Fox, the foremost guerrilla fighter of the Revolution. Unfortunately, Marion had no qualms about slavery (he certainly didn't free any of his slaves) allegedly raped some of the women, and committed atrocities. Hence, to make Martin more sympathetic to modern audiences, Martin is made to reflect the anti-slavery sentiments of John Laurens, a South Carolina Revolutionary leader who was anti-slavery.

tropes.name: Historical Villain Upgrade
tropes.html:
• Although Banastre Tarleton, the prototype for Tavington, was a rather nasty individual (to clarify, note his actions at the Waxhaws Massacrenote and even then, it was arguably more his troops' fault than his own and his fervent support of the slave trade as an MP), he was not nearly as bad as the film would have you believe. Many of the things Tavington does, such as locking up villagers inside their church and then setting it and them on fire were based on German war crimes from World War II like the Oradour-sur-Glane massacre (though the English did do similar things to the Irish during the 1641 rebellion note  as did Irish rebels to English and Scottish settlers , even if more than 100 years beforehand).
  • The British in general get this, but Big Bad Charles Cornwallis definitely does. While in the movie he is still portrayed as a Noble Demon in comparison to Tavington's plain demon, he still holds the colonists in open contempt and disdain. In reality Cornwallis was a Whig who was sympathetic to the colonials, and before the war was an MP who voted on their behalf several times (notably, he was one of only five MPs to vote against the Stamp Act, predicting exactly the hostile response it generated). After Britain's defeat at Yorktown Cornwallis refused George Washington's demand that all slaves liberated by the British be returned to their American owners, instead evacuating them to freedom in Canada and Britain's Caribbean colonies. He was also an effective governor of Ireland and India after the war, effecting major changes in both parts of the British Empire despite his defeat in the Revolution.

tropes.name: Home Guard
tropes.html: Both Patriot and Loyalist varieties show up in this film.

tropes.name: Icy Blue Eyes
tropes.html: Tavington.

tropes.name: If Only You Knew
tropes.html: When Tavington explains that Benjamin's militia are more than just "farmers with pitchforks" (as Cornwallis puts it) thanks to their commander who is the "Ghost", Cornwallis is annoyed at the mention of this "Ghost", and expresses that it was Tavington who ended up creating the Ghost by using such brutal tactics, which has swelled the Ghost's ranks further. Although Cornwallis is already correct that Tavington's brutality is certainly boosting the Ghost's forces, he is unaware of Tavington's actions that led Benjamin to become the Ghost once more, which would make Cornwallis' statement even more accurate.

tropes.name: If You're So Evil, Eat This Kitten!
tropes.html:
Tavington occasionally pulls this on his men, Captain Wilkins learned this the hard way:
Capt. Wilkins: (after locking townspeople in a church) Ready to fire the town on your order, sir.
Col. Tavington: (Evil Laugh) The town? Burn the church.
Capt. Wilkins: There's no honor in this.
Col. Tavington: Didn't you say "All those who stand against England deserve to die a traitor's death"? Burn the church, Captain.

tropes.name: I'll Take That as a Compliment
tropes.html:
Gen. Lord Cornwallis: This is hardly the conduct of a gentleman!
Col. Benjamin Martin: If the conduct of your officers is the measure of a gentleman, I'll take that as a compliment.

tropes.name: Immune to Bullets
tropes.html: Tavington, to Gabriel's horror. The latter gets a spot-on shot on the former, and it does not affect him one bit. Also during the climactic duel, Benjamin's pistol shot does nothing to Tavington, and the former could only beat the latter through a series of stabs.

tropes.name: Impoverished Patrician
tropes.html: General Cornwallis gives a dressing-down to Colonel Tavington, trying to shame him that his brutal conduct on the battlefield hardly befits a man from a family as noble as his. Tavington doesn't bat an eye, snarking that since his father left his noble family dirt-poor, the only way for him to survive, much less prosper, is to win at any cost.

tropes.name: Improbable Aiming Skills
tropes.html:
• When Tavington shoots a fleeing revolutionary from a hundred yards away with a flintlock pistol while on horseback.
  • * Martin shoots a soldier on horseback at approximately 100 yards using a flintlock pistol. This would be extremely difficult using even a modern pistol, much less a period pistol, which had a maximum effective range of twenty feet.
  • When Benjamin ambushes the patrol to save Gabriel, he shoots a redcoat in the head while running and from the hip with a pistol from about 30 yards away.
  • Pretty much anyone who is not a regular grunt just can't miss.

tropes.name: Impromptu Tracheotomy
tropes.html: At the end of the film, Benjamin uses a bayonet to fatally stab Tavington through the throat after his Inertial Impalement, avenging his sons' deaths.

tropes.name: I Need a Freaking Drink
tropes.html: And in Tavington's case, it's from a clearly modern martini-style glass.

tropes.name: Inertial Impalement
tropes.html: In the second half of the film, Tavington fatally stabs Gabriel in the gut with his sword. Then, by the end of the Battle of Cowpens, Benjamin does the same to Tavington himself, this time with a bayonet.

tropes.name: Inexplicable Cornered Escape
tropes.html: The British dragoons under Tavington have just burst into Martin's sister-in-law's mansion looking for his family. One of Martin's younger sons is hiding under a dining room table as Tavington is searching the room. When he goes to look under the table, it appears that the boy will be discovered, but it turns out he crawled out while Tavington was briefly distracted by one of his men.

tropes.name: Innocence Lost
tropes.html: The Martin kids witness their brother die and their home burned. Two of them are forced to kill.

tropes.name: Innocently Insensitive
tropes.html:
Major Jean Villenueve is initially polite, if curt when first introduced, but he stalks off in a huff when Benjamin casually asks if he has and children of his own. One could infer that his exploits in the French and Indian War are the only reason Jean acts so prickly towards him, but he later reveals during an argument that the answer to Benjamin's question was "yes", but his daughters and wife were killed when the British naval fleet fired upon their ship.
Jean: "Violette was 12 and Pauline 10. They had green eyes."
Benjamin: "...I'm sure they were lovely."
Jean: "Yes. They were."

tropes.name: Insult Backfire
tropes.html:
• See the first Ironic Echo example below.
  • Near the end of the Battle of Cowpens, a presumably-incapacitated Benjamin Martin watches the battle as he writhes in pain, having been slashed by Tavington's sword. Tavington, who is right behind him, insults Martin by declaring: "Kill me before the war is over, will you? It appears that you are not the better man." Just as Tavington is about to behead Martin, Martin dodges the killing blow and grabs a bayonet to stab Tavington in the stomach. As Tavington falls, Martin holds the bayonet on Tavington's neck and responds to his insult by concurring with him, declaring that his sons were better men, right before delivering the killing blow to Tavington.

tropes.name: Ironic Echo
tropes.html:
• Cornwallis calls Martin and his militia "a bunch of farmers with pitchforks." After Benjamin Martin's gambit (see above), Tavington comments, "Quite impressive for a farmer with a pitchfork, wouldn't you say?"
  • A variant of this trope occurs during Benjamin's gambit. Tavington confronts him and insults his sons, after which Benjamin warns the Colonel, "Before the war is over, I'm going to kill you." In the Battle of Cowpens, an incapacitated Benjamin Martin is confronted yet again by Tavington, who remarks, "Kill me before the war is over, will you?" This later ends up backfiring on Tavington.
  • Capt. Wilkins, a Loyalist, answered Tavington's question on why he should trust a man who'd "betray his neighbors" with "Those neighbors of mine who stand against England deserve to die a traitor's death". Later on, Tavington orders Capt. Wilkins to burn his said neighbors to death inside the church. When Capt. Wilkins says there's no honor in it, Tavington coldly throws his words back at him to make him do it anyway.

tropes.name: It Has Been an Honor
