When Joel finally meets the President after he is captured by the WF, he is dishevelled, unshaven, hyperventilating and terrified, begging for his life on the floor of the Oval Office.

tropes.name: Genre Throwback
tropes.html: As Alex Garland's love letter to the traditional, pre-digital era style of journalism, the film is also a throwback to 1980s war thrillers about journalists reporting on foreign conflicts such as Under Fire and The Year of Living Dangerously, with the twist that it's being set in the journalists' home country.

tropes.name: Gentle Touch vs. Firm Hand
tropes.html: Lee tries to teach Jessie through Tough Love by telling her the hard truths of being a journalist and making her confront the horrors of war head-on, while Sammy tries to guide her more gently and tries to get Lee to back off. Joel is somewhere in the middle, gently chiding Lee for being too harsh and acting as something of an older brother figure to Jessie, but ultimately leaves her to her own devices for the most part.

tropes.name: Going for the Big Scoop
tropes.html: The journalists racing to interview the president before the rebels reach Washington, knowing that they will be traveling through active war zones and that loyalist forces shoot journalists on sight.

tropes.name: Go Out with a Smile
tropes.html: As he dies, Sammy watches embers flying in the air as the group drives through a burning forest and smiles at the beauty of it.

tropes.name: Group Picture Ending
tropes.html: A variation: the movie ends with a picture not of the main characters, but of the Western Forces squad who have executed the President of the United States and are posing with his body, with the implication that this photograph would become the defining image of the Second American Civil War.

tropes.name: Gunship Rescue
tropes.html: During the invasion of Washington, D.C., a team of WF soldiers are pinned down as they advance towards Pennsylvania Avenue by Loyalist soldiers with machine guns who have a height advantage. Cue the entry of a WF Apache helicopter, which flies low between buildings and makes quick work of the Loyalist vantage points with its 30mm chain gun and missiles, allowing the troops to press on to the White House.

tropes.name: Helmets Are Hardly Heroic
tropes.html: Despite establishing the importance of journalists wearing kevlar and helmets, the film has our character forego helmets in the final act without any stated reason. And notably, they DO wear helmets during the first skirmish they cover during the movie.

tropes.name: Heroic BSoD
tropes.html:
• During the final assault on Washington, D.C., Lee has a PTSD attack and must be literally dragged along by Joel.
  • Nearly getting killed by a white nationalist who already killed two of his colleagues and Sammy's subsequent Heroic Sacrifice take its toll hard on Joel, who becomes more withdrawn after everything he witnesses. After Lee gets killed by Secret Service agents, he coldly lets the WF soldiers execute the president out of anger over his friend's death.

tropes.name: Heroic Bystander
tropes.html: After Jessie gets hurt during the riot, a woman can be seen asking if she's alright and trying to shield her before Lee goes to make sure she's okay.

tropes.name: Heroic Sacrifice
tropes.html:
• Sammy drives in to save the other three journalists from the unnamed soldier about to kill them, and they manage to escape - but he gets a bullet for his trouble and dies.
  • At the climax of the film, Lee sacrifices her life to save Jessie's during the invasion of the White House.

tropes.name: Hide Your Children
tropes.html: Although the group journeys across multiple states, they see hardly any children outside of a few in the scenes in New York City and the refugee camp in West Virginia (not including children that appear in flashbacks of Lee photographing other warzones).

tropes.name: Highly Conspicuous Uniform
tropes.html:
• A group of gunmen (credited only as "commercial soldiers") the group observe fighting Loyalist troops are seen wearing colorful Hawaiian shirts with their camo and grey body armor.
  • Downplayed: If you look closely during the Sniper Duel, the sniper team the journalists wind up with have dyed hair and painted fingernails, which would be a huge no in any military.

tropes.name: Hollywood Tactics
tropes.html: The United States military is generally considered to have some of the best-trained soldiers and officers in the world, with plenty of recent battlefield experience. So it's very jarring to see tactical blunders like a helicopter gunship dropping down to near ground level (where even small arms fire can reliably hit it) to take out a couple of soldiers in a building, or leading an attack with a Fragile Speedster Humvee instead of a armored Abrams tank.

tropes.name: Humans Are Bastards
tropes.html:
Much like any movie that shows humanity would be happy to destroy itself for whatever reason, only here it's worse when a single country of humans is happy to destroy itself for whatever reason. All of the factions, especially the WF, have absolutely no qualms killing anybody who don't think or act like they do, which goes to show how far America has fallen, and that even goes for the civilians:
  • Jesse's first brush with the cruelty of war are gas station owners gleefully torturing two looters (who may not even have been looters); one of the owners chortles that they have been hanging them for days, nonchalantly states he personally knew one of the looters, and ignores the fact the looter was doing it to feed his kids. The owner then asks Jessie, who is visibly frightened and a rookie reporter, to decide if they should shoot the men now or leaving them hanging and maybe free them if they're lucky enough to not die of their injuries.
  • It's implied the sniper the journalists encounter has just been shooting everyone in sight, and it took attracting a sniper team to kill them in the middle of a war.
  • Later, the team runs into a band of racist soldiers who casually execute two foreign and non-white journalists after psychologically torturing them, and nearly shoot a Hispanic man with a seemingly non-US accent before the survivors are rescued by Sammy; what's more, Sammy is certain they wiped out a town and are burying its victims.
  • The Western Forces are given orders to kill everyone in the White House, down to innocent staffers and Secret Service agents trying to negotiate.

tropes.name: Hypocrite
tropes.html: The film posits that anyone who claims they're "staying out of the war" are simply either putting their heads in the sand or lying about their involvement in it; both Lee and Jessie's parents act like nothing in America is out of the ordinary, despite their daughters risking their lives on the frontline, and a small town that is secure and stable claim to "stay out of politics", but as Lee and Sammy observe militia watching them closely, it's left unsaid that even enforced neutrality isn't "staying out of politics".

tropes.name: Ignorance Is Bliss
tropes.html: The small town in West Virginia that Lee and her group pass through, who are just "trying to stay out" of being involved in the ongoing conflict. Lee and Jessie also mention that their parents (who live in Colorado and Missouri, respectively) are also "pretending like none of this is happening".

tropes.name: Intergenerational Friendship
tropes.html: The four journalists at the film's center are a multigenerational bunch—Sammy being the oldest of them by several decades, Lee and Joel being around the same age and presumably around their forties, while Jessie is twenty-three. Lee and Joel are already close friends and colleagues, with Sammy being their old mentor, and the three of them include Jessie into the group very quickly.

tropes.name: Intrepid Reporter
tropes.html: Deconstructed. It doesn't get more intrepid than risking life and limb to document the horrors of war, but the four journalists at the film's center are shown to be hardened, broken people who struggle with unimaginable trauma - all for news outlets that may or may not even function anymore. (Sammy is said to work for "what remains of the New York Times".) Their treatment by the various soldiers and militiamen they follow varies from gladly allowing them to follow along in combat and film everything, to being highly irritated that they're in the way of an active warzone.

tropes.name: Jerkass Has a Point
tropes.html: Sammy acknowledges that Lee is not wrong for telling Jessie she needs to accept the realities of war journalism, but points out berating her while she's crying is pretty terrible regardless.

tropes.name: Judge, Jury, and Executioner
tropes.html: It seems the capacity of local law enforcement is either stretched incredibly thin, or is non-existent due to the ongoing conflict, especially in rural areas. This leads to people taking the law into their own hands. The best example is Eddie and Pete, the gas station owners who act like a Vigilante Militia and savagely beat up two men and hang them up by their wrists for two days outside without food or water, before executing them. All because they got caught trying to loot their local store.

tropes.name: Karmic Death
tropes.html: The sociopathic soldier played by Jesse Plemons, who likes killing foreigners, gets plowed by a truck and falls into the very same hole he dumped all bodies of his victims.

tropes.name: Know When to Fold 'Em
tropes.html: Two counts toward the end of the film. With inevitable defeat looming for the remaining Loyalist forces, their generals and the vast majority of their number surrender when the Western Forces advance on Washington, D.C. Joel invokes this when he tells the group that they'll never make it to the President before he flees or is killed, but Lee defies this and insists they press on anyways. Sure enough, they ultimately make it to the White House.

tropes.name: Lame Last Words
tropes.html: The President himself, when asked for a quote comes out with a stuttering "Don't let them kill me.", to which Joel coldly replies "That'll do." and lets the soldiers kill him.

tropes.name: Lampshade Hanging
tropes.html: During a pep talk with newcomer Jesse, Joel promises her they'll finally see some action tomorrow. What follows is the first real action sequence of the movie after fleshing out the journalists for about half an hour.

tropes.name: Last Stand
tropes.html: At the end of the film the majority of the federal Loyalist soldiers and command have surrendered, leaving only a small holdout of devoted troops and Secret Service agents. They hole up in the fortified White House to try and protect the defiant President from the advancing Western Forces.

tropes.name: Late to the Tragedy
tropes.html: The journalists en route from New York to Washington DC pass by several former battlegrounds, such as the freeway leading out of New York being littered with civilian vehicles (which eerily resembles to the Highway of Death in Kuwait) and smoldering buildings with remnants of military vehicles being strewn about.

tropes.name: Leave No Survivors
tropes.html: The chosen rules of engagement for the Western Forces once they gain access to the White House. Another journalist, Dave, mentions the WF have specific orders to kill, not capture. This applies to the President and all other occupants, armed or otherwise.

tropes.name: Leeroy Jenkins
tropes.html: In a mix of inexperience and youthful stupidity, Jessie becomes extremely reckless while she and the journalists are being escorted by a WF convoy during the invasion of Washington D.C.. She tries to get closer to the battlefield, refuses to seek cover unlike the rest of the group, and has to be physically held back by soldiers several times. Her recklessness leads to her nearly getting killed and for Lee to die taking a bullet meant for her.

tropes.name: Man on Fire
tropes.html:
• In a flashback to one of Lee's assignments in an African country, she witnesses (and photographs) a man being burned alive whilst trapped in a car tyre, commonly referred to as necklacing.
  • A Western Forces soldier also gets set on fire when his Humvee is blown up by federal Loyalist forces defending the White House. Jessie takes several pictures of him as he flails in agony.

tropes.name: Married to the Job
tropes.html: Neither Lee nor Joel seem to have families even though they're in their forties, and even Sammy never brings up a spouse or children, with their closest relationships seemingly being with each other. Lee herself is almost single-mindedly on her career at the expense of even her own friends, and it's implied that the lack of anyone tying them down contributes to the group's general attitude towards the atrocities they document.

tropes.name: Mauve Shirt
tropes.html: During the assault on DC, Lee, Jessie, and Joel spend the duration of the assault in the company of a single military squad, particularly once they enter the White House. We don't exactly get to know them but they at least make themselves more distinct than the other soldiers in the assault. Indeed, the final photo that the credits play over is of the squad standing over the dead president and posing for the camera.

tropes.name: Mentor Occupational Hazard
tropes.html: Sammy is Lee's mentor, and Lee herself becomes Jessie's mentor. Both end up killed.

tropes.name: Modern Stasis
tropes.html: It's ambiguous exactly how distant this future is, but forty-one-year-old Kirsten Dunst plays Lee, who is mentioned as having taken pictures of the Antifa Massacre in college. Assuming that Lee is around Dunst's age, that was around twenty years ago or more. It likely couldn't have taken place earlier than 2016, since that was when "Antifa" became a particular buzzword for left-wing causes. Combined with the fact that the president's in his third term, that would place the story in around 2036, but there's no new slang, technology, or even clothing showcased in the movie. Another possibility is that the film takes place close to the present in an alternate timeline.

tropes.name: Monumental Damage
tropes.html: Inevitable with a film involving an armed conflict on American soil whose climax takes place in DC. When fighting federal Loyalist soldiers, Western Forces troops destroy part of the Lincoln Memorial with a Javelin missile.

tropes.name: Most Writers Are Writers
tropes.html: A film about journalists, where according to Garland, are explicitly the heroes capturing the horrors and events of the civil war to inform the public.

tropes.name: My God, What Have I Done?
tropes.html: Implied. After Jessie photographs Lee's death, she puts down the camera with a look of heartbreak and horror. It’s implied she did so instinctively and without thinking, only realizing afterwards she just photographed the gruesome death of her mentor and friend.

tropes.name: Never Trust a Trailer
tropes.html:
• Marketing ahead of the film's release heavily emphasized the specific scenario, identifying the loyalist and rebellious states, showing battles and troops in various cities around the country, and stirring up speculation as to the cause and course of the war. It also heavily featured the President. However, in the movie itself, the worldbuilding is mostly left up to Cryptic Background References and the President only appears at the very beginning and very end — far more important are the characters and their road trip from New York to Washington, D.C.
  • The film is about an American civil war, and every trailer and commercial prominently featured Jesse Plemmons' character grilling the protagonists about "what kind of American" they are, implying that he's asking which side of the conflict they're on. In the film, however, the line he says immediately afterward clarifies that he's asking if they're immigrants, since he's just a racist.

tropes.name: Nice, Mean, and In-Between
tropes.html: The three other photojournalists with their attitude towards Jessie. The warm and jocular Sammy is nice. The bitter and cold Lee is mean (though she becomes a Defrosting Ice Queen), and Joel is in-between (more welcoming to Jessie, but more downbeat and pessimistic than Sammy).

tropes.name: No Bikes in the Apocalypse
tropes.html: Averted in New York City, where there are few civilian road vehicles and commuters are seen travelling by bicycle; likely because of the scarcity of gasoline or it being commandeered for military purposes. Played straight otherwise, as no bicycles are seen in the more rural areas the protagonists travel through.

tropes.name: Noodle Incident
tropes.html:
• What started the war in the first place is never examined beyond the implication that it was caused by the president, which makes the whole thing even worse.
  • When Tony and Bohai catch up to the group, Tony tells Lee that they knew where the group was going because Joel got very drunk back in New York and told them the entire plan, and that he was also so wasted that he tried to hit on Jessie. This incident is never elaborated upon.

tropes.name: No Party Given
tropes.html: The exact political situation that caused the war to happen is not explained, only that there is the main Loyalist government in DC and the opposing faction that is most prominent in the film is called the Western Forces. Any given group the main characters come across are not specified as to which side they are fighting for, excepting the very end as they accompany the Western Forces on their invasion of DC. The Western Forces are said to be primarily backed by California and Texas; those states could hardly be more diametrically opposed to each other politically at the time of the film's release, but it's possible this world's politics are different or even that one or both states' governments have been deposed by the rebel forces. The current President is said to have disbanded the FBI, used drone and aircraft strikes against US citizens and on a third term, none being party specific hot points (though may be inspired by claims of specific individuals). There's also the possibility that both the Democratic and Republican parties might not even exist anymore in such an atmosphere.

tropes.name: No Such Thing as Bad Publicity
tropes.html: Implied to be the reason why most of the various rebels and militias let the journalists take pictures of them executing prisoners and unarmed combatants.

tropes.name: Pet the Dog
tropes.html:
• The Western Forces soldiers at least are compassionate enough to tell the photojournalists to stay close with them in order to prevent being shot and even telling them to get back from being in the line of fire. They even managed to hold back from executing the President just so Joel can get a quote from the former, to which in return they even get a photo of themselves standing over the President's body post-execution (implied to be taken by Jessie). Earlier, they get Sammy's body into a coffin after his death at the hands of a white nationalist militia.
  • It's more of a coincidence, but the sniper and spotter team of unknown allegiance that the protagonists come across let them take cover from the sniper who set up a death trap and is shooting everyone on sight, and are, for two soldiers who are under heavy fire and have been locked in a Sniper Duel for days, very patient with Joel asking them dumb questions while they're fighting for their lives. They're also nice enough to let them know when they've killed the enemy sniper.

tropes.name: Punch-Clock Hero
tropes.html: Lee asserts that as a journalist, her job isn't to think about what's going on but to take photographs and let others think about it. Though haunted by the events she sees, she maintains her focus simply on doing her job by getting good shots. Her colleagues Anya and Dave also seem quite unconcerned by the storming of the White House, with Dave smiling in excitement as he relates the latest developments, apparently because it will make more lurid reporting.

tropes.name: Race Against the Clock
tropes.html: The Western Forces aim to reach Washington by the Fourth of July. The journalists have to beat them to the punch so they can interview the President.

tropes.name: Reactive Continuous Scream
tropes.html: A very rare example of this trope not being Played for Laughs; after the encounter with the white nationalists, Joel and Jessie are so shaken by their shared traumatic experience that their reaction to it is to scream at each other in terror once they get in the car, clearly trying to process what they've just been through.

tropes.name: Red Oni, Blue Oni
tropes.html:
• The Hot-Blooded, extroverted, and relatively easygoing adrenaline junkie Joel is the Red to the more icy, stoic, and trauma-stricken Lee's Blue.
  • Dave is absolutely giddy about capturing battles on camera in contrast to the stoic Anya.

tropes.name: Retro Universe
tropes.html: Played with; while the film is explicitly set sometime in the near future, things like the almost complete lack of modern technology such as the Internet or social media and the presence of a character like Jessie, who's so set in the Good Old Ways that she uses a black-and-white film camera, give it an unquestionably old-fashioned feel despite its 20 Minutes in the Future setting. This might also be justified, as much of society has broken down due to the war.

tropes.name: The Revolution Will Not Be Civilized
tropes.html: The Western Forces successfully overthrow the tyrannical President of the United States in a chaotic battle between them and the Secret Service, then execute him at point-blank range inside the ruins of the Oval Office.

tropes.name: Riddle for the Ages
tropes.html: It's unclear what side the Winter Wonderland snipers are fighting on, or even if they're officially on a side. It's also unclear who is in the house and why they're seemingly shooting everyone they see. Our protagonists seem to leave before we get any answers.

tropes.name: Ridiculous Exchange Rates
tropes.html: The Second American Civil War was devastating enough that it managed to tank one of the most valuable currencies on the planet. At one point when Lee is negotiating with one of the gas station attendants, she says that she'll offer $300 dollars for gas but they mention that $300 is barely enough for a sandwich — ham or cheese. Lee then bluntly says that she's talking about Canadian dollars, leading to them closing the deal.

tropes.name: Right-Wing Militia Fanatic
tropes.html:
• It's implied the suicide bombing in the intro is carried out by some kind of ultranationalist faction — the bombings are apparently common enough that everyone knows exactly what anyone waving an American flag running full-tilt at a crowd means.
  • The first real action scene follows what are strongly implied to be "Boogaloo boys", who annihilate a Loyalist holdout and execute the survivors.
  • The President's rhetoric dismisses every secessionist state as one, but out of the opposing forces, the Florida Alliance are dismissed by everyone as barely-competent militia yahoos.
  • The soldiers who capture Bohai and Jessie and later kill Bohai and Tony are noted not to be government forces, but it's not clear who they are fighting for. They wear no unit or rank insignia and they espouse virulent anti-immigrant, white nationalist beliefs while interrogating the protagonists. They might just be a couple of racists who got their hands on some guns and camo, or even looted the uniforms off of soldiers they killed.

tropes.name: Road Trip Plot
tropes.html: Elements of this, combined with Deadly Road Trip. The majority of the film is the protagonists driving from New York City to Charlottesville and then Washington, D.C. and documenting the conflict on the way. Their drive time is extended considerably given that the interstate highways have been "incinerated" by bombings, meaning they have to take the back roads for the bulk of the trip.

tropes.name: Scenery Dissonance
tropes.html:
• Much of the film takes place during absolutely beautiful and sunny summer days, providing a contrast to the battles and wartime atrocities that the group documents.
    • Jessie photographs a crashed and burned out military helicopter, which wouldn't look out of place in various foreign warzones. However, it is in the parking lot of a JCPenney in a suburban commercial shopping district. Bullet ridden Humvees and feral dogs are also seen running around the same area.
    • An overpass that the crew pass underneath where someone had spray-painted "Go Steelers" has several bodies hanging under it.
    • The Sniper Duel that the group ends up getting caught in the middle of is set at an abandoned Christmas fair, with the requisite bright, cheery decorations still being up and Christmas music playing in the background.
  • The grand interior corridors and state rooms of the White House, which are filled with dead staffers who committed suicide rather than be captured than the approaching Western Forces, and are later the setting of a violent indoor shootout between WF soldiers and the Secret Service.

tropes.name: Screw This, I'm Outta Here
tropes.html: A day before the Western Forces begin their siege on Washington, the Loyalist forces officially surrender to them. Most of the Loyalist generals and their soldiers wisely decide to desert the capital, leaving behind only a handful of troops and Secret Service agents still loyal to the president.

tropes.name: Second American Civil War
tropes.html: The film is about this very concept, with the US vs several breakaway factions, mainly the Western Forces and Florida Alliance.

tropes.name: Senseless Sacrifice
tropes.html: Defied. Sammie saving the remainder of the original group from the white supremacists costs him his own life, but it seems like that the entire trip (and Sammie's sacrifice) was for nothing when D.C.'s forces surrender and all but guarantee that the journalists will never make it to the White House before it falls. Lee ensures that it wasn't in vain, and has everyone proceed onwards regardless, and they ultimately make it to the White House.

tropes.name: Series Continuity Error
tropes.html: The official map released ahead of the film plus a TV broadcast in the beginning lists Alaska as a Loyalist state, but in the film itself, Alaska is noted as being "neutral territory" — indicating it is either not participating in the war or has outright declared independence. It’s possible that the government might not even actually control all the Loyalist states and has censored any information about them in the media, or that Alaska had cut ties with the United States as the government fell.

tropes.name: She Cleans Up Nicely
tropes.html: In the clothing store the protagonists come across Lee gets to try on a pretty dress, and Jessie compliments her as she wears it.

tropes.name: Shell-Shock Silence
tropes.html: After a suicide bomber detonates in the middle of a crowd in New York City, the scene is silent as the protagonists survey the carnage. The only sound is the clicking of camera shutters when they take pictures.

tropes.name: Shoot the Messenger
tropes.html: When the Western Forces take the White House, an unarmed Secret Service agent attempts to negotiate the safe surrender and extraction of the President. She is quickly gunned down by the soldiers, who have orders to kill the President and clearly view her negotiation attempts as no more than a delaying tactic.

tropes.name: Signature Team Transport
tropes.html: The group has their trusty Ford SUV, which they spend most of their time in. It remains remarkably intact despite getting shot at several times and later being used to run over and kill a pair of militiamen, and is such an important part of the plot that it's practically its own character.

tropes.name: Sociopathic Soldier
tropes.html:
• Earlier, the militia in West Virginia, heavily implied to be "boogaloo boys", shoot and kill a heavily wounded Loyalist who isn't armed and is in no state to fight back.
  • Whoever set up the creepy trap at a farmhouse consisting of a dead and bloodied soldier to bait anyone who sees it into stopping long enough to be shot; it's not known if they are from any military, but they've been shooting everything in sight, to the point they've got a sniper team pinned down.

tropes.name: Soundtrack Dissonance
tropes.html:
• The second trailer is set to a slowed-down whistled rendition of "America the Beautiful", set to scenes showing a not-so-beautiful America and quite a bit of violence.
  • In the film itself, a scene where a militia captures Loyalists and summarily execute them is soundtracked by De La Soul's peppy "Say No Go".
  • Later, the protagonists come across a rotting soldier posed next to a theme park's Christmas display as cheerful Christmas music. It's a trap for a sniper.
  • The end credits is set to "Dream Baby Dream" by Suicide.

tropes.name: Spreading Disaster Map Graphic
tropes.html: A map of the current divisions between states is briefly shown as a graphic during a news broadcast watched by Lee in her hotel room in New York City at the start of the film.

tropes.name: Stepford Suburbia
tropes.html: Along the way to D.C., the journalists stop over by a town in which people seem to act like the civil war isn't happening around them, in which Joel remarks if they went back in time while Jessie comments like they're in The Twilight Zone. A shop owner even nonchalantly states that they 'stay out of it' (i.e. avoid watching the news) before telling Joel to let her know if he and his colleagues need anything. This doesn't stop the town from having some kind of defense however, as Sammy notes to Lee to be subtle in seeing couple of snipers in a building looking at them.

tropes.name: Stress Vomit
tropes.html: Jessie has a particularly gnarly one after the encounter with the racist soldiers that Sammy saves the crew from. She's so shaken up by the deaths she's witnessed that she doesn't even try to roll the window down and puke out the car window; she's such an absolute mess that she just vomits in her lap on the spot in the back seat of the van, in a way that's less of an explosive clenching of muscles and more a complete slackening of them as the adrenaline wears off.

tropes.name: Suicide Attack
tropes.html: One of the first major setpieces of the film is a suicide bombing in New York City.

tropes.name: Suicide Mission
tropes.html: The trip to Washington, D.C. amounts to one. Although death is not necessarily guaranteed, the active war zone and the administration's policy of shooting journalists on sight means that it is extremely dangerous.

tropes.name: Symbolism
tropes.html: In a form of symbolic irony, the Lincoln Memorial, a monument to the President who led the U.S. through the first civil war, is destroyed in the second by secessionists.

tropes.name: Three Successful Generations
tropes.html: Although they're not related, this is the setup of the Power Trio. Jessie is the youth, looking to make her own way; Lee and Joel are the adults, who are trying to rediscover their hope for journalism, and Sammy is the elder - he was Lee's mentor, he looks after Jessie, and he ultimately sacrifices his life for them.

tropes.name: The Three Faces of Adam
tropes.html: Sammy is the prophet. He's looking back on his life and highly respected by the other characters. The President is the lord; he only appears briefly but is implied to have committed vast Offstage Villainy at the moment that he's being deposed. Joel is the hunter, as a Hot-Blooded war photographer who undergoes a Heroic BSoD after witnessing violence and bloodshed.

tropes.name: Too Dumb to Live
tropes.html:
• It's unclear whether it's due to delusions of victory or just sheer hubris, but the President doesn't bother fleeing the White House or Washington, D.C. even as separatist military forces are bearing down on it and the bulk of the defending Loyalist forces have surrendered, and all he achieves is getting himself and his remaining Secret Service agents trapped and then swiftly killed.
  • There's also the group of White House staffers who attempt to speed through the Western Forces troops attacking the White House in order to save themselves and accomplish nothing other than getting themselves killed. However, considering the soldiers had orders to kill everyone in the White House it was likely done out of sheer desperation. It's also likely they were decoys intended to keep the president inside.

tropes.name: A Tragedy of Impulsiveness
tropes.html: Ultimately, this is what leads to Lee's death during the Washington D.C. battle; the rush of combat causes Jessie to become incredibly reckless for the sake of getting some good shots. Lee and Joel, her de facto caretakers, can barely pay much attention to her due to Lee having a PTSD attack and Joel being preoccupied with taking care of her while on the battlefield. This only emboldens Jessie to get even more reckless, enough that she ends up directly within the line of fire during the White House invasion, necessitating Lee to sacrifice her life to save her.

tropes.name: The Un-Reveal
tropes.html: The agenda of Western Forces and Florida Alliance when it comes to ideology and policy isn't specified. The most we know is that they seceded from the USA for reasons that probably included objecting to the actions of the President, and now one their war goals is to depose him. Furthermore, the New People's Army isn't mentioned in the film other than being present in the official map posted on social media and an aside reference to "Portland Maoists".note The fact that they share the name with the Filipino Maoist rebel group that has been fighting the Philippine government since 1969 could be a factor.

tropes.name: Unwitting Instigator of Doom
tropes.html: Jessie impulsively deciding to switch cars after seeing Tony do the same ends up leading to a series of events that nearly dooms the entire group.

tropes.name: Villain Ball
tropes.html: Once the majority of his forces desert him, the President's most logical course of action would have been to try to flee D.C., either to attempt to lead a resistance in exile or to just save his own skin. However, he instead orders the last of his loyal troops and guards to put up a pointless Last Stand, guaranteeing his death and resulting in even greater loss of life for both sides, purely to spend a few more hours in the Oval Office—he doesn't even attempt to hole up in the White House's command bunker—and to make the ending of the movie more exciting. Even sending the presidential limo with the First Lady and a few aides straight into the fray to be mown down by the WF serves no purpose other than make him seem more evil, as he seemingly doesn't even attempt to flee the White House during the few seconds the troops might have thought they'd killed their target.

tropes.name: Vitriolic Best Buds
tropes.html: Lee and Joel have diametrically opposed personalities and most of their interactions usually end up devolving into petty bickering, but they've known each other for a long time and are clearly good friends. Joel is completely devastated by Lee's death at the hands of Secret Service agents and lets the president get executed by the Western Forces as a result.

tropes.name: Vomit Indiscretion Shot
tropes.html: Jessie's Stress Vomit after watching two journalists get executed in front of her is not hidden from the camera in any way.

tropes.name: War Crime Subverts Heroism
tropes.html: The Western Forces are able to take Washington, D.C. and overthrow the dictatorial fascist President, as well as his government and military forces. They also murder numerous unarmed civilians and surrendering combatants whilst doing so, and execute the President in the Oval Office instead of capturing him to stand trial for his crimes. Soldiers even pose for a photo with his corpse afterwards.

tropes.name: War Is Hell
tropes.html: The four protagonists pass by several former battlegrounds highlighting the damage and scale of the Second American Civil War, even getting roped up in a couple of skirmishes.

tropes.name: War Refugees
tropes.html: Displaced people appear throughout the film. The group of journalists pass people walking on foot with suitcases along a damaged highway, and cars overloaded with possessions driving the opposite direction to them fleeing from the violence. They even spend the night at a refugee camp in West Virginia located in a disused sports stadium.

tropes.name: The War Room
tropes.html: Played with. Inside the White House, several state rooms and the cabinet room are filled with a mess of desks, communications equipment and abandoned food, indicating extensive use for tactical planning in the lead up to the invasion of Washington, D.C. Interestingly, the Presidential Emergency Operations Centre (PEOC), the building's actual war room located under the East Wing in a bunker, is not shown.

tropes.name: When She Smiles
tropes.html: In the clothing store Lee smiles warmly and sincerely after being told by Jessie she'd look pretty doing so. Jessie eventually photographs Lee doing just that.

tropes.name: The White House
tropes.html: When the Western Forces arrive in D.C., they find the White House has been heavily fortified, with large concrete walls erected around the entire estate (as well as the Eisenhower Executive Office Building and the Treasury Building). However, with their superior firepower they are able to breach the walls, fight off the remaining loyalist Secret Service agents and ultimately capture and kill the President in the Oval Office.

tropes.name: With a Friend and a Stranger
tropes.html: Lee is accompanied by her colleague Joel, her old mentor Sammy, and Jessie, a plucky aspiring photojournalist that she meets in New York.

tropes.name: World Limited to the Plot
tropes.html: While the civil war is raging in America, almost nothing is said about what the state of the rest of the world is in with the world's largest superpower essentially collapsing overnight. Besides a scene showing how Canadian dollars are now worth more than American ones and several foreign journalists covering the war, most prominently a British journalist covering the battle in D.C., absolutely nothing is known about what is happening outside of America's borders.

tropes.name: Yank the Dog's Chain
tropes.html: When the Western Forces soldiers drag the President out from under the Resolute Desk, Joel yells at them to stop and not shoot - because he needs one quote from the man before the soldiers kill him.

tropes.name: Action Girl
tropes.html: Emma is the best shooter in Rose Creek, being almost on par with the Seven.

tropes.name: Actor Allusion
tropes.html: This isn't the first time Byung-hun Lee has played a Blade Enthusiast assassin, having done the same as Chang-yi in The Good, The Bad, The Weird.

tropes.name: Actually Pretty Funny
tropes.html: When Emma defends her decision to recruit the seven, she defiantly tells some of the townspeople "Well maybe I was the only one with balls enough to do so." In the background you can see a few of the seven break into chuckles.

tropes.name: Adaptational Diversity
tropes.html: The Magnificent Seven in the original film were mostly white aside from the half-Irish/half-Mexican Bernard O'Reilly and there were no major female characters aside from Chico's love interest Petra. The remake has a much more diverse cast with a black Union officer as the leader as well as a Native American, an Asian, and a (mestizo) Mexican as part of the team in addition to having three white teammates of different backgrounds. Not to mention that the movie has a major female character (Emma) who forms the Magnificent Seven to get revenge on the men who killed her husband.

tropes.name: Aerith and Bob
tropes.html: Men named Joshua and Vasquez share the movie with someone named Goodnight.

tropes.name: Affectionate Nickname
tropes.html: Billy and Chisolm refer to Goodnight as "Goody" when talking to him.

tropes.name: Affirmative Action Girl
tropes.html: The original film was almost entirely male-centered, with Chico's love interest Petra as the only woman with a proper speaking part. This remake has the character that assembles the Seven be female and includes a few minor female supporting characters. Emma is also the one that kills Bogue.

tropes.name: Agony of the Feet
tropes.html:
One of the gunmen in Amador City is shot in the foot by Chisolm.
"He shot my damn foot!"

tropes.name: The Alcoholic
tropes.html: Being the Old West, everyone drinks. However, Faraday's day drinking is more than a little heavy.

tropes.name: Alliterative Name
tropes.html: Bartholomew Bogue, the film's Big Bad.

tropes.name: Ammunition Conservation
tropes.html: When Farraday, suspicious of Goodnight's shooting abilities, challenges the latter to shoot a target, Goodnight declines, citing a desire to save his bullets as the reason.

tropes.name: Anachronism Stew
tropes.html:
• Josh Faraday refers to the American Civil War as "The War of Northern Aggression," a term that wouldn't come into use until the 1950snote To elaborate, Faraday, a Southerner, is speaking to a group of townspeople asking if any of them have combat experience. Given their geographic location and the film's time period, many of them would likely be Confederate veterans, and as such would've likely aligned with the "Lost Cause of the South". A more era-appropriate pro-Southern term for the Civil War would've been "The War of Southern Independence."
  • As the crew tries to score some dynamite, a 45-starred American flag is flying on a wooden pole. The flag wouldn't have 45 stars until 1896; in 1879 the flag would have had only 38 stars.
  • Bogue uses the word "capitalism," a term coined by Karl Marx and known in 1879 only to economic philosophers who could read German.

tropes.name: Annoying Arrows
tropes.html: Averted. Red Harvest takes down multiple enemies with a single arrow apiece, and whilst it does take three to kill Jack Horne, each one clearly hurts.

tropes.name: Anti-Hero
tropes.html: All the Seven are pretty ruthless people (and some of them are somewhat racist), but they're on the track to do some good.

tropes.name: Anyone Can Die
tropes.html: By the end of the movie, only three of the Seven are still alive, just as it was in the original film and the original Seven Samurai movie as well. Most of the townsfolk and all of Bogue’s men are also dead.

tropes.name: Arc Words
tropes.html: "So far, so good.", which references a joke Faraday tells about a man who falls down a building and every floor he passes by hears him scream "So far, so good!". Which ends up quite analogous to the Seven heading to their quite possible death in the battle against Bogue. This joke originates from the original film as one of Vin's quips.

tropes.name: Arrows on Fire
tropes.html: Red Harvest uses burning arrows to light some wagons strewn with straw in order to frighten horses during the Final Battle.

tropes.name: Artistic License – Engineering
tropes.html:
• Faraday asks Teddy Q if he was in the army because he carried a .45 Colt Open Top. Open Tops were .44 caliber, not .45.
  • The Gatling gun is shown loaded with a single 20-round magazine and is never reloaded (reloading requires stopping the gun, even if briefly, and the fire shown and heard is continuous), yet the gun fires for an extended period, shooting several hundred rounds during the entire engagement.

tropes.name: Artistic License – History
tropes.html:
• In the 1870s American West, no "respectable" woman like Emma would expose her upper torso, arms, or legs in public; this was seen as a trademark of prostitutes. Emma also isn't wearing a hat or bonnet, something women didn't leave the house without back then.
  • When Faraday tells the townspeople about Goodnight's history, he says that he had "23 confirmed kills at Antietam." Both men were Confederates, so they would've called it Sharpsburg, not Antietam.

tropes.name: Artistic License – Linguistics
tropes.html: Red Harvest is supposed to be Comanche, but he sometimes speaks in Tlingit (Martin Sensmeier is a Native Alaskan member of this tribe).

tropes.name: Back-to-Back Badasses
tropes.html: Faraday and Vasquez briefly do this during the first shootout.

tropes.name: Badass Crew
tropes.html:
The posse that Chisolm assembles to help Emma is composed by people who individually qualify for One-Man Army status. Each of them is responsible for at least a dozen deaths during the film, just see this video:
  • Chisolm: 38
  • Faraday: 43
  • Goodnight: 16
  • Horne: 36
  • Billy Rocks: 47
  • Vasquez: 13
  • Red Harvest: 13

tropes.name: Bad Boss
tropes.html: Bogue doesn't give a single damn about the well-being of his employees. He treats the workers at his mine little better than slaves and opens fire on the town with the Gatling gun while his goons are still in it. He also guns down a loyal man for delivering a message he doesn't like.

tropes.name: Bait-and-Switch Gunshot
tropes.html: As Chisolm is strangling Bogue, the latter pulls out a small revolver and appears to fire it, but in fact was shot by Emma.

tropes.name: Bandito
tropes.html: Vasquez is a Mexican criminal on the run.

tropes.name: Bar Brawl
tropes.html: Goodnight mentions that he met Billy when the latter took on a whole barful of people who didn't serve his kind.

tropes.name: Bash Brothers
tropes.html:
• Rocks and Robicheaux are such close friends, it's practically a bromance.
  • Faraday and Vasquez evolve into this over the course of the film.

tropes.name: Batman Gambit
tropes.html: Chisolm's own tactics count primarily on Bogue's hubris, and he says this to everyone explicitly. While setting up the defenses for the town, the Seven anticipate what the attackers will do and design their plan accordingly, assuming they won't do anything but charge in guns blazing. It works perfectly. Only Bogue's Gatling gun gives his force a chance of victory, and even then he'd have been down to less than a dozen survivors.

tropes.name: Beard of Evil
tropes.html: All of the bad guys are unshaven, except for Denali.

tropes.name: Berserk Button
tropes.html:
Faraday is usually one of the most easygoing people you will ever meet. Unless you touch his guns. Then he will end you.
  • Goodnight showed shades of this when Faraday pushes him too far by forcing him to show off his sharpshooting skills. Not only did Goodnight blast the dummy's head clean off, he becomes an absolutely terrifying drill sergeant in the process - and it cuts to Faraday giving an Oh, Crap! expression.

tropes.name: Beware the Silly Ones
tropes.html: Faraday is a jokester, often quite silly, and generally comes across as an easygoing sort of fellow... but when he's driven to kill, he can get downright cruel. He's very merciless and very fast on the trigger, and frequently uses card tricks and misdirection to throw people off guard.

tropes.name: Big Bad
tropes.html: Bartholomew Bogue is not only the main antagonist but spends every single second he is on screen kicking puppies.

tropes.name: Big Badass Battle Sequence
tropes.html: The entire final act is dedicated to the final showdown with Bogue's forces.

tropes.name: Big Guy Fatality Syndrome
tropes.html: Jack Horne is the first of the Seven to die, shot with several arrows by Denali.

tropes.name: Bilingual Bonus
tropes.html: A large portion of what Vasquez says is in Spanish, with very little of it subtitled. Most of it's swearing. In addition, it's a sign of how their Odd Friendship has progressed when Vasquez upgrades Faraday's Affectionate Nickname from "guero" to "guerito."

tropes.name: Bilingual Dialogue
tropes.html: Red Harvest and Chisolm's first conversation is entirely (and accurately) in Comanche, along with a few other lines from Red that are either in Comanche or Martin Sensmeier's native Tlinglit. And, of course, Vasquez's Spanish.

tropes.name: Bittersweet Ending
tropes.html: The town is saved and Bogue and all his men are dead. But four of the Seven are dead, along with a significant portion of the townsfolk. And the town is in ruins. Hopefully, they'll help themselves to Bogue's gold in order to rebuild it.

tropes.name: Black-and-Gray Morality
tropes.html: To quote Emma, "I seek righteousness as all people should, but I'll take revenge." The Seven are all unsavoury characters with fairly ruthless natures, but despite that, this Lovable Rogue crew is much more heroic than the murderous and tyrannical Bartholomew Bogue.

tropes.name: Black Dude Dies First
tropes.html: Averted. In fact, the three survivors are an African-American, a Native American, and a Mexican, whilst all three of the white dudes end up dead.

tropes.name: Blasting It Out of Their Hands
tropes.html: Chisolm does this to a bad guy in the climax. Unlike most examples, it is explicitly framed as a sadistic gesture to savour his fear rather than a heroic "no kill" one. In a more realistic outcome, Bogues' hand is mutilated from it.

tropes.name: Bling-Bling-BANG!
tropes.html: Chisolm uses a nickel-plated Colt Single Action Army revolver with a 5.5 inch barrel, known as the "Artillery" model. Vasquez wields two.

tropes.name: Bloodier and Gorier
tropes.html: The original film had maybe 70 deaths and a squib or two. Here, more than 200 people are killed onscreen throughout the film, several rather messily thanks to the Gatling gun.

tropes.name: Blood-Stained Glass Windows
tropes.html: Part of the final showdown between Chisolm and Bogue takes place in the burnt down church.

tropes.name: Boisterous Bruiser
tropes.html: Subverted with Jack Horne. He's a bear of a man with a few screws loose and a propensity for violence to match. So you might expect him to be a thunderous, cackling madman. Instead, he's actually very soft spoken.

tropes.name: Bookends
tropes.html: Bogue's first and last scenes in the film are in Rose Creek's church. In fact, he dies on very nearly the same spot where he made his Blasphemous Boast in the beginning.

tropes.name: Boom, Headshot!
tropes.html: Goodnight, being a sharpshooter/sniper. Faraday started to think he was a fraud, due to his panicking and not firing his gun; after Faraday insisted he show the townsfolk how to shoot, Goodnight blasts the dummy's head clean off. Considering that the dummy's neck was a fairly sturdy chunk of wood, that's even more impressive, because it took half a dozen shots to do it.

tropes.name: Boom Town
tropes.html: The central conflict is Bogue wanting to wipe out Rose Creek from the map for its gold.

tropes.name: Bounty Hunter
tropes.html: Horne is a former bounty hunter of Indian rewards and Chisolm is a working one.

tropes.name: Brick Joke
tropes.html:
Several scenes after Faraday jokes about having a Mexican Standoff with no Mexicans, he meets Vasquez, and remarks thus:
"Oh, we found a Mexican."

tropes.name: But for Me, It Was Tuesday
tropes.html: Even after being told his name and the place where he wronged him, Bogue still can't recall why Chisolm might have a personal vendetta against him.

tropes.name: Butt-Monkey
tropes.html: The owner of Rose Creek's sole saloon gets no respect from absolutely nobody... on both sides.

tropes.name: Card Sharp
tropes.html: Faraday is remarkably skilled at handling cards, a skill that also translates into magic tricks.

tropes.name: Category Traitor
tropes.html: Red Harvest takes an instant and virulent loathing towards Mr. Denali because he considers him a traitor to his own people. The fact that on top of being Bogue's right hand man, he also wears a US Cavalry uniform might account for this.

tropes.name: The Centerpiece Spectacular
tropes.html: The gunfight between the Seven and the Blackstone Detectives, retaking the town away from Bogue's men.

tropes.name: Changed My Mind, Kid
tropes.html: Goodnight, unable to bring himself to partake in the fight due to his shell shock, leaves the night before. However, he comes charging back in, guns blazing, during the big shootout, and warning them of the Gatling gun.

tropes.name: Chekhov's Gag
tropes.html: When the badly inexperienced townsfolk first arrive to be trained by the Seven, Faraday snarks, "Oh good, they've got their pitchforks. We may actually stand a chance." In the final battle, some of the townsfolk actually are seen using farm implements effectively — one man in particular uses a shovel to brutally clothesline Bogue's men off their horses.

tropes.name: Chekhov's Gun
tropes.html:
• Faraday offers to teach one of the settlers about gunfighting, starting with having him grab the playing card from Faraday's hand. After several failed attempts, Faraday draws his gun on the settler, telling him the point of the lesson: It was never about the cards. Many of their tactics in the final battle involve misdirection and luring their enemies into traps, and Faraday tricks the bad guys at the Gatling gun into letting him light a stick of dynamite by making a show of trying to light his last cigar, his deck of cards prominently shown immediately beforehand.
  • Halfway through the film, Bogue pulls a gun out of a drawer and uses it to kill Sheriff Harp. At the end of the film, he tries to draw the same gun to kill Chisolm, but is shot by Emma before he can fire it.

tropes.name: Christianity Is Catholic
tropes.html:
There are more Catholic overtones to the movie than one might expect given the setting.
  • Bogue prays in Latin (badly) when crawling into the church to try and get away from Chisolm.
  • Vasquez crosses himself upon entering the church earlier, but he is Mexican, and Mexico by 1879 would have been predominantly Catholic.
  • On the other hand, Faraday describes himself as a Baptist.
  • The denomination of the town is never brought up, but while the church appears to be generic Protestant, the clergyman is noticeably Irish. However, there were Irish Protestants in the United States in 1879.

tropes.name: Cigar-Fuse Lighting
tropes.html: Faraday does this with a stick of dynamite just before he blows up the Gatling gun, and himself.

tropes.name: Cloudcuckoolander
tropes.html: Jack Horne is a powerfully-built bear of a man who speaks mostly in Bible verses and turns down the group's offer to join up, only to trail them afterwards. It's implied he has a few screws loose due to having lost his family in the past.

tropes.name: Co-Dragons
tropes.html: Bartholomew Bogue has McCann and Denali as his main enforcers. Both are killed early in the Final Battle.

tropes.name: Commonality Connection
tropes.html: While Sam and Emma are extremely different people, It's Personal for both of them to go after Bogue.

tropes.name: Composite Character
tropes.html:
• Vasquez is a Composite Character Expy of O'Reilly and Harry Luck. He has Harry's boisterous personality and shady exterior, and a Deleted Scene shows him giving to a kid Bernardo's lecture about how a father is braver than a gunfighter.
  • Robicheaux is mostly based on Lee, but he has elements of Harry Luck, too, in that he's Only in It for the Money.

tropes.name: Conveniently Timed Attack from Behind
tropes.html: Combined with a Bait-and-Switch Gunshot. While Chisolm is monologuing and prolonging Bogue's strangulation, Bogue is busily fishing a derringer out of his boot with which to shoot Chisolm. Emma shows up just in time to shoot Bogue before Bogue can shoot Chisolm. Played with in that Emma comes up behind Chisolm and not Bogue in order to deliver the fatal shot.

tropes.name: Contrasting Sequel Antagonist
tropes.html: Well, remake antagonist - Calvera from the original was an Affably Evil bandito who's friendly towards the Seven when he isn't kicking their asses. Bogue, on the other hand, is a sinister robber baron who doesn't even pretend to be friendly at all. There's also the added contrast that Calvera was a regular (if rather sharp) bandito, while Bogue is a tyrannical tycoon, putting them at opposite ends of the social scale.

tropes.name: Corrupt Corporate Executive
tropes.html: Bartholomew Bogue is the 'Robber Baron' version. Faraday even refers to him as 'Robber Baron' Bogue.

tropes.name: Curb-Stomp Battle
tropes.html:
• Any fight involving the Seven (individually or as a group) where they're not massively outnumbered will end with their opposition utterly destroyed with very little effort.
  • Red Harvest vs. Denali. Denali is set up as Bogue's dragon and Red Harvest's Evil Counterpart, Red Harvest intervenes with Denali coming after Emma, and you think you're going to get a long battle of the two Badass Native warriors going at it. Nope. Denali gets all of two good moves in before Red Harvest pokes him full of holes, snaps off a Pre-Mortem One-Liner, and kicks him down a balcony to his doom. The entire thing lasts maybe sixty seconds, if that.
  • The final battle threatens to turn into one once Bogue's men open up with a Gatling gun. The gun is eventually destroyed... at a cost.

tropes.name: Dark and Troubled Past
tropes.html:
The Seven might all behave with unflinching heroism during the events of the movie, but most of them have some dark stuff in their past.
  • Chisolm was a USCT in the Civil War and became a bounty hunter after witnessing his mother and sisters get raped and murdered by ex-Rebel mercenaries working for Bogue.
  • Jack Horne used to hunt and kill Indians for the government bounty. He also had a wife and children. It's hinted but never stated that he lost the latter in a way that motivated him to take up the former.
  • Vasquez is wanted for the murder of a Texas Ranger. No details are given, other than Vasquez suggesting that maybe he had it coming.
  • Goodnight is a former Confederate sharpshooter suffering from Survivor's Guilt and Post-Traumatic Stress. He mostly tries to use his reputation to avoid conflict, believing that he will die if he pulls a trigger in violence again.
  • Billy Rocks is a Chinese immigrant who is highly skilled at every form of violence known to man. He's such a badass because there's simply no other way he could have survived this long. He also has an Ambiguous Criminal History, being the subject of an arrest warrant, but for what is never stated.

tropes.name: Dark Is Not Evil
tropes.html: Chisolm wears all black and is The Leader of the Seven.

tropes.name: Dawn Attack
tropes.html: The Final Battle starts when Bogue's men arrive at Rose Creek as dawn breaks.

tropes.name: Decoy Protagonist
tropes.html: You could easily assume that Matt Bomer's character was going to be a major one since he is the most courageous and handsome of the men focused on in the meeting in the opening. Then he gets gunned down by Bogue before the opening credits even start. It's his wife who is a major character.

tropes.name: Determinator
tropes.html: Faraday and Horne in their dying moments of awesome.

tropes.name: Determined Homesteader
tropes.html: Most of the people in Rose Creek valley are willing to do anything to protect their land and homes. They just lack the training and skill.

tropes.name: Dirty Cop
tropes.html: Rose Creek's sheriff is completely in Bogue's pocket, though it's implied he's not exactly happy with the situation. The villain's main goons are also corrupt private detectives.

tropes.name: Dirty Coward
tropes.html:
• Bartholomew Bogue is ultimately a sniveling coward who'd do anything to survive.
  • Rose Creek's corrupt sheriff hides under a porch while all the rest of Bogue's men are getting killed, and scurries away to break the news to Bogue afterward. He gets shot dead by Bogue for his trouble.
  • Bogue's right-hand man McCann counts too. During the first shootout, he is seen running for cover while his men are slaughtered by the Seven.
  • Chisolm criticizes Bogue's Blackstone mooks as cowards only good at busting unions and backshooting women, but fold when faced with opposition who can fight back.

tropes.name: Distaff Counterpart
tropes.html: Emma is one of Rikichi from Seven Samurai. Both actively seek out the heroes needed to protect their towns, and both Took a Level in Badass over the course of the film after the deaths of their respective spouses.

tropes.name: The Dreaded
tropes.html:
• Bogue's reputation is widespread. Chisolm himself, if not exactly dreaded by most, is looked upon with fear by several townsfolk who know that violence won't be long in coming.
  • Robicheaux is a textbook example. Billy wins both of them a bet and one of the losers refuses to pay, somebody points out that this is Goodnight Robicheaux, he becomes terrified, apologizes, and when Robicheaux tells him to pay double, he does so with no reluctance.

tropes.name: The Drifter
tropes.html: Faraday and Chisolm are the wandering gunmen, one because he's a trickster, the other's a bounty hunter.

tropes.name: Ear Ache
tropes.html: Faraday shoots off Earl's ear to teach him a lesson.

tropes.name: Epic Fail
tropes.html: Billy's attempt to teach melee combat (via stabbing the dummies several times) results in everyone walking out.

tropes.name: Establishing Character Moment
tropes.html:
All of the Seven get one.
  • Chisolm approaches a target in a friendly, calm manner, slowly reveals his real agenda, non-lethally disarms his bouncers, and then kills him.
  • Faraday is introduced gambling and then uses a card trick to distract and kill two disgruntled players he scammed.
  • Vasquez is found hiding out in an abandoned cabin, lassos Emma, and claims the man he murdered deserved it.
  • Billy is introduced killing a man armed with a gun using a thrown hairpin.
  • Goodnight frightens a man who insulted Billy into apologizing with nothing but his reputation. He later freezes during the first battle.
  • Horne is introduced killing two wannabe bounty hunters, one with an axe and the other with his bare hands. Keep in mind this was after he had his head smashed by a boulder and got pushed off a cliff.
  • Red Harvest claims he is on a sacred quest from his elders. He then joins the party and seals the deal by sharing a raw deer liver with Chisolm.

tropes.name: Even Evil Has Standards
tropes.html: One of Bogue's men is hesitant about using the Gatling gun because Bogue's men are still in the town. Bogue barely responds with a shrug.

tropes.name: Every Man Has His Price
tropes.html: Bogue is a firm believer in this, as he bought the loyalty of Rose Creek's Sheriff. This also ties into his approach to taking Rose Creek for the Final Battle: hiring hundreds of mercenaries (who are stated to be private detectives) and purchasing a Gatling gun as an artillery piece.

tropes.name: Expy
tropes.html:
• Billy Rocks is based on Britt from the original film (who himself is an Expy of Kyuzo).
  • Faraday is one of Vin from the original film, with his tendency to wisecrack and eye for prettiness. He even tells Vin's "So far, so good" parable.
  • Red Harvest has some similarities to Chico, in that he's a loner who feels isolated from his past home and pursues the Seven before being allowed to join them. He's also apparently the youngest of the team.
  • Chisolm, whose counterparts are Chris and Kambei, is likely based on real-life lawman Bass Reeves, right down to the mustache.
  • Horne, a pious Mountain Man, is likely based on Josiah Sanchez, the eccentric preacher from the short-lived Magnificent Seven TV series.. He also seems to be based on the real life Liver Eating Johnson, who was also known as "Crow Killer", as well as Orrin Porter Rockwell

tropes.name: Face Death with Dignity
tropes.html:
All of the Seven who fall in battle face their ends with dignity. Horne dies in a Obi-Wan Moment of tranquility, Faraday grins triumphant with dynamite in hand as he saves his friends via a Heroic Sacrifice, Billy and Goodnight help Faraday even under Gatling gun fire, sharing one last back-and-forth. Guess who doesn't face the prospect of his possible death with dignity?
  • Even before their actual deaths, the Seven all make it clear that they acknowledge the prospect that they may die in battle and accept that; Horne himself states outright that he couldn't ask for a better fate than to give his life in the service of others alongside men he respects.

tropes.name: Fiery Redhead
tropes.html: Emma has a mane of bright red hair and spends the bulk of the movie barely being able to contain her anger at the death of her husband.

tropes.name: Final Battle
tropes.html: The Seven and the citizens of Rose Creek vs. Bogue and his men.

tropes.name: Finishing Stomp
tropes.html: Horne ends his Curb-Stomp Battle against the Pigeon brothers by stomping on Ken Pigeon's head.

tropes.name: Five-Token Band
tropes.html: In addition to three Caucasian members (one of whom claims to be Irish, which was transitioning from being considered a separate race at the time), the Seven includes an Asian, a Hispanic, an African-American, and a Native-American.

tropes.name: For Doom the Bell Tolls
tropes.html:
• A deep bell tone is heard as the camera focuses on each of the Seven as dawn breaks for the Final Battle.
  • A deep chime rings out when Goodnight and Billy are mowed down by the Gatling gun, followed by a low One-Woman Wail as Billy lies mortally wounded in the belfry.

tropes.name: Foreshadowing
tropes.html:
• There are several clues early in the film that suggest a personal connection between Chisolm and Bogue. Chisolm initially is not interested in Rose Creek's plight until he hears Bogue is involved. In addition, Robicheaux notes that Cullen apparently reminds Chisolm of his sister and warns him about getting hung up on his past, suggesting something had happened to Chisolm's family.
  • Faraday's use of sleight of hand to distract the two outlaw brothers so they won't notice him going for his holdout revolver is echoed by him using a similar trick to smuggle in a stick of dynamite to blow up Bogue's Gatling gun after being fatally wounded himself near the end.
  • Two nights before the final battle,Goodnight Robicheaux tells Billy Rocks that he had heard "the voice" and that if "I pull that trigger in violence again, I'm gonna die a ghastly death". The following day, after shooting his weapon in the battle, Goodnight is shot down from the church steeple and falls to his death.
  • A townswoman who fixes Horne's jacket boasts "That stitching will outlast you." It's true, since he dies.
  • The fact that Bogue's miners run out to help put out the fire at the church in the opening before being chased away by Bogue's men. Later on, Chisolm recruits the miners to help the townsfolk out for a chance of driving Bogue out.

tropes.name: Frothy Mugs of Water
tropes.html: According to the actors, the cigarettes Goodnight and Billy are frequently shown sharing are laced with opium, although this is never explicitly mentioned in the film.

tropes.name: Gatling Good
tropes.html: The bad guys get a Gatling gun for the climax. In a very unusual move, it is actually utilized as its designer intended (and how the Union Army did it) as an emplaced long-range weapon traversing only a few degrees to sweep a wide area several hundred yards away with sustained fire, and the effect is devastating.

tropes.name: Genre Throwback
tropes.html: It is a remake of a western after all. But reviews have observed how it makes a point to be as unabashedly "old school western" as possible: The Gun Twirling, the lonesome rider introduced enigmatically walking into town, the several, drawn-out Mexican standoffs, the larger than life villains and heroes, etc.

tropes.name: A Good Way to Die
tropes.html: When Chisolm tells them, the night before the big showdown, that they likely ride to their deaths and thus are free to leave if they so desire, Horne takes a moment to say how there's no other place that he'd like to die than facing such fearful odds alongside men he respects so deeply. The others silently nod and agree with his words. This later is proven when during his death, Horne becomes very calm and tranquil, almost happy that he could die in such a heroic manner.

tropes.name: The Gunfighter Wannabe
tropes.html: Earl, a.k.a. 'the Two Gun Kid', is a gunfighter wannabe who challenges Faraday to a gunfight early in the film. Faraday shoots off his ear to teach him a lesson.

tropes.name: Guns Akimbo
tropes.html: Vasquez wields twin revolvers in every shoot-out. Faraday also carries two revolvers, but doesn't usually use them both at once, instead more likely carrying two so that he can pull off a quick-draw with either hand at any time. He also has a backup revolver he stores in the back of his pants. Billy also wields two revolvers, though like Faraday not at once.

tropes.name: Gun Twirling
tropes.html: Everyone twirls their guns. The most memorable case might be Vasquez, who at one point twirls both of his revolvers for several seconds before putting them back in their holsters.

tropes.name: The Gunslinger
tropes.html:
Six of the Seven are shown to be incredibly skilled gunmen:
  • The Quick Draw — Chisolm who can outdraw four men at once, Faraday who is skilled at the surprise draw, and Billy who can pull this off with knives as well as his revolver. Billy takes it up to eleven in his introductory scene when he wins a Quick Draw contest to the death with a hairpin tangled in his hair.
  • Friendly Sniper — Goodnight, a legendary sharpshooter. While it takes a while for him to break through his PTSD, once he does — he doesn't miss.
  • Cold Sniper (of the Archer variety) — Red Harvest, though he does carry a gun on him, his bow is his primary weapon.
  • The Woo: Chisolm is shown employing some Gun Fu during the Final Battle, at one point killing several Mooks by hitting them in the face with the stock of his rifle then shooting them.
  • On the other hand, while Jack Horne has a gun, most of his kills are racked up with a tomahawk, which he usually goes in close for — though he can throw it with lethal accuracy if he chooses to.

tropes.name: Hard-Work Montage
tropes.html: When the Seven and the townsfolk are shown preparing Rose Creek for the arrival of Bogue's army. It comprises most of the second act.

tropes.name: Hearing Voices
tropes.html: It's implied that this happens to Goodnight due to his PTSD.

tropes.name: Heroic Sacrifice
tropes.html: Faraday gives up his life in a suicide ride to blow up the Gatling gun with a stick of dynamite. Horne also dies trying to reach The Brute, likely in a (successful) attempt to steer his attention from the wounded soldier behind him. Billy and Goodnight die providing cover fire so Faraday can destroy the Gatling gun.

tropes.name: Heterosexual Life-Partners
tropes.html: Billy and Goodnight are extremely close friends. Billy Is also very sympathetic to Goodnight, (who due to his PTSD is often unable to function) by lying that Goodnight's rifle was jammed rather than him just being too shell shocked to shoot it, offering him his cigarette when he's clearly on edge, reassuring him that his hallucinations are "just dreams" and that nothing had followed him.

tropes.name: Hidden Weapons
tropes.html: Faraday uses a concealed Webley Bulldog revolver to defeat two attackers who ambush him early in the movie. Near the end, Bogue nearly kills Chisolm with a Smith & Wesson Model 1 1/2 revolver hidden in his boot.

tropes.name: Hoist by His Own Petard
tropes.html: In one of the most literal examples of this trope, the stockpiles of dynamite from Bogue's own mine are used to great effect to decimate his forces.

tropes.name: Hollywood Tactics
tropes.html:
The final battle is a perfect example of just how effective these tactics would be against an opponent who uses actual tactics:
  • On the attackers' side, Bogue's goons ride straight towards the town in a mad charge without bothering to check what possible countermeasures might be in place, all the while Bogue makes no attempt to use the Gatling gun he brought along until after most of his men had gotten either slaughtered... or pinned down in the line of fire.
  • The defenders on the other hand employ every single force multiplier available to them: using skirmishers, a variety of traps and obstacles, fighting trenches, sharpshooters in elevated positions, and exploiting the terrain (and the poorly-thought-out tactics of Bogue's hired guns) to lure his men into a series of ambushes.
  • That said, Goodnight and Billy meet their end because they made the critical error of sniping from a very obvious location with limited cover, despite the fact that the film made a show of them discussing the pros and cons of various locations ahead of time.

tropes.name: Horseback Heroism
tropes.html: Chisolm and Faraday are fond of showing off their Improbable Aiming Skills while riding (such as accurately fanning a revolver from horseback), and make heroic charges at different points in the film.

tropes.name: Hypocrite
tropes.html: Bogue. At the start of the film, he makes a Blasphemous Boast before setting fire to the church. At the film's climax, he has the audacity to seek refuge in the burnt out hulk of that same church, praying for mercy and appealing to Chisolm's religious side. All this earns him is a moment's respite as Chisolm removes his hat in respect before marching into the church after him.

tropes.name: I Call Her "Vera"
tropes.html: Faraday's revolvers are named Ethel (his wife) and Maria; Ethel doesn't know about her. Do NOT touch his ladies (and do not tell Ethel about Maria).

tropes.name: I Owe You My Life
tropes.html:
• When confronted by Blackstones, Chisolm pretends Billy Rocks is his manservant, whose life he saved in Shanghai.
  • Goodnight to Chisolm. Goodnight was being beaten up by Union Civil War veterans after the war and Chisolm saved him.

tropes.name: Impaled Palm
tropes.html:
• Chisolm shoots one of his assailants in the Amador City bar by shooting through his hand.
  • When Denali shoots Jack Horne, the last arrow goes through his hand.

tropes.name: Impaled with Extreme Prejudice
tropes.html: During the first shootout, Billy kills one of Bogue's men by stabbing through him and into the post behind him.

tropes.name: Imperial Stormtrooper Marksmanship Academy
tropes.html:
Unfortunately for the Seven, this applies to the civilians they're attempting to train to defend the town, with every single one of a long line of men failing to hit a single target.
Faraday: Statistically speaking, they should've hit something.

tropes.name: Implacable Man
tropes.html: Horne is unstoppable. Even off-screen he survives being smashed with a rock and thrown off a cliff. It takes about seven arrows, three of them directly to the chest, to put him down.

tropes.name: Improbable Aiming Skills
tropes.html: If one of the Seven shoots at something (with guns, arrows, knives, or tomahawks) they will hit it, no matter how improbable the odds.

tropes.name: Informed Attribute
tropes.html: Vasquez is introduced as a dangerous wanted criminal with a large US$ 500 bounty on his headnote Approx. $12,834 in 2015 money. Yet during the whole course of the movie he always behaves as unflinchingly heroically as the rest of the Seven. He does claim that his victim had it coming, so maybe the deck was just stacked against him, but still.

tropes.name: Insistent Terminology
tropes.html: Sam Chisolm would have you know that he is a duly sworn warrant officer, not a bounty hunter — primarily meaning that he is sent to track specific men for specific crimes, not merely gunning down criminals for cash.

tropes.name: Instant Marksman: Just Squeeze Trigger!
tropes.html: Goodnight's lecture when training the villagers riffs on similar advice given in the 1960 film (with similarly effective results).

tropes.name: Invulnerable Horses
tropes.html: Chisolm rides his horse through the glass door of a restaurant with it seemingly suffering no ill effects.

tropes.name: It's Personal
tropes.html: The reason why Chisolm accepts Emma's suicidal job offer. Bart Bogue is the man responsible for the brutal murders of Chisolm's mother and sisters.

tropes.name: Karmic Death
tropes.html:
• The film begins with Bogue burning down the town church. At the end of the final battle, Bogue is killed in the ruins of the very same church.
  • Jack Horne made his living killing Indians for profit. He is the only one of the seven to be killed by Denali.

tropes.name: Last-Name Basis
tropes.html: We never learn Vasquez' first name.

tropes.name: Let's Split Up, Gang!
tropes.html: Used early in the film. When Chisolm and Faraday start recruiting with Emma and Teddy, they decide to split up to cover more ground; Chisolm and Emma go to find Vasquez while Faraday and Teddy recruit Goodnight and Billy.

tropes.name: Living Emotional Crutch
tropes.html: Billy is this for Goodnight. The latter saying the former "keeps him on the level." Subverted as once Goodnight skips town, Billy hits the drink hard.

tropes.name: Living Legend
tropes.html: Horne and Goodnight, who are both actually described as "living legends". Horne is legendary as a tough-as-nails badass who survived all manner of bizarre stuff in the wilderness and hunted down several Indians, and Goodnight is a legend as the most feared Confederate sharpshooter during the war (thus, his Red Baron of "The Angel of Death").

tropes.name: The Lost Lenore
tropes.html: Rare male example. Emma's husband Matthew is killed in the opening after he tries to stand up to Bogue, and she assembles the Seven partially out of a desire to avenge his death.

tropes.name: Made of Iron
tropes.html: Horne gets shot with four arrows, two to the chest, before he goes down, and before that is not severely impaired by having a rock smashed into his head. Faraday also gets shot an impressive amount of times before going down (and even then, it takes being blown up to kill him).

tropes.name: Man on Fire
tropes.html: Happens to one of Bogue's Mooks during the Final Battle when he gets thrown off his horse onto a fire.

tropes.name: The Man They Couldn't Hang
tropes.html: At the very end of the movie, it is revealed that Chisolm has a scar around the base of his neck from where a group of Confederate renegades tried to hang him on Bogue's orders, back in Kansas.

tropes.name: Mexican Standoff
tropes.html: Mentioned by name and joked with. Faraday observes it is a weird Mexican Standoff when the participants are an Irishman and a Baptist, so he's not sure what to call it. There are also several standoffs of this kind during the movie.

tropes.name: Mickey Mousing
tropes.html: When the Seven raid Bogue's mine, whoever kills the Mooks there times their shots with explosions.

tropes.name: Mistreatment-Induced Betrayal
tropes.html: Bogue treats his miners so badly that they gladly join the townsfolk in fighting him.

tropes.name: More Deadly Than the Male
tropes.html: Emma Cullen is the single biggest badass in Rose Creek, and by far more deadly than any of the male townsfolk.

tropes.name: Mountain Man
tropes.html:
Jack Horne is a quintessential example, dressed all in furs and living in the wild.
Joshua Faraday: [as Horne walks back into the mountains] I believe that bear is wearing people clothes.

tropes.name: Murder Is the Best Solution
tropes.html: Bogue's go to tactic when someone has something he wants, be it land or anything else, is to send a whole bunch of hired goons and kill everyone in sight. Not only does he do it on Rose Creek, but he did the exact same thing shortly after the war in Lincoln, Kansas to a group of homesteaders that included Chisolm and his family.

tropes.name: Mythology Gag
tropes.html:
• Red Harvest tracks the Six the same way Chico and Kikuchiyo do, although unlike the other two he never had a formal introduction beforehand.
  • Billy Rocks' Establishing Character Moment is almost identical to Kyuzo's introduction, and subsequently Britt's.
