tropes.html: When Longlegs is finally arrested, a huge problem is that, despite all of his Satanic journals and Lee's childhood memories of him threatening her mother, there's zero hard evidence he's killed anyone. As Browning points out, while Longlegs may be an avowed Satan worshipper, that's not a crime under US law. The FBI worries if they don't crack him in interrogation and identify his accomplice, he won't ever be convicted.

tropes.name: Affably Evil
tropes.html: Even after being revealed to be Longlegs' accomplice, Ruth's politeness isn't an act, and she admits her heinous crimes with the same gentle tone as seen previously in the movie.

tropes.name: All According to Plan
tropes.html: The final scenes imply that everything from his capture to suicide was all part of Kobble's plan to make Lee suffer. When she has to shoot her own mother, we see a shot of Kobble laughing hysterically before he ends the film singing happy birthday to her and then blowing the camera a triumphant kiss.

tropes.name: All There in the Manual
tropes.html: The Birthday Murders website gives more background information on each of Longlegs's prior victims, who are otherwise glossed over in the movie due to Conservation of Detail.

tropes.name: Alternate Reality Game
tropes.html: Most of the movie's viral marketing, including a website, revolved around solving Longlegs's codes, which were often featured in the trailers or on the aforementioned website. Downloadable files on the website also required passwords for access.

tropes.name: Ambiguous Ending
tropes.html: Lee is forced to kill her mother to stop her from killing Ruby, but runs out of bullets before she is able to destroy the Carter family doll. Lee tells Ruby that they have to leave, but then remains frozen in place, staring at the doll. The movie then cuts back to Longlegs in the interrogation room, hailing Satan and blowing a kiss before a cut to black.

tropes.name: Ambiguous Situation
tropes.html:
Quite a few.
  • Does Lee genuinely have psychic powers, and if so, does the FBI believe in that (unlike Satanic magic)? On the one hand, Lee does correctly identify the killer's house in the beginning with no evidence other than just a gut feeling and attains a high score on the FBI's strange test of object association and number prediction by getting the latter right 8 times, which impresses Carter. On the other hand, Lee never displays the same intuition for the rest of the movie when dealing with Kobble (though she still effectively pieces together hidden details about the case by simply poring over the files in exhaustive detail for hours on end) as she needs a new letter from Kobble with a free cipher for his coded writing to actually translate his other letters and gets caught off guard by her mother's involvement with Kobble; additionally, she brushes off her test results because she also got the number prediction wrong 8 times, implying that either she was lucky with her correct predictions or that the psychic examination itself is mere pseudoscience. Furthermore, if she really is psychic, does the Deal with the Devil that Ruth made with Kobble have something to do with it (hence why she's "cut off" from using it on the Longlegs case) or is it preexisting?
  • Why did Longlegs come to Ruth and Lee's house in the first place? The scene apparently predates Longlegs' killing spree, but, his consistent MO is to only go after nuclear families, whereas Ruth is a single mom. He also mentions a birthday gift, indicating he already made the doll of Lee; did Longlegs used to have another accomplice prior to Ruth? Further, his tying up Ruth with the apparent intention of killing her also violates his usual MO of being hands-off with his victims and killing them through supernatural means; this may have been because Ruth was the only parent (that we know of) to reject his gift of the doll, as indicated by his line about her refusing to "play nice" with him, angering him enough to try and kill her himself.
  • It is unclear what exactly happened when Ruth shoots Lee's doll at the end of the movie, destroying the metal ball inside. When she does, black smoke both pours out of the doll and also drifts out of the back of Lee's head before she passes out. Does destroying the doll free Lee from Satan's grasp or did something else happen (such as her regaining her memory of the deal Ruth made with Kobble)? Lee at least seems to retain her sense of self throughout the rest of the movie.
  • It's also unclear what precisely happens after Lee kills her mother and Carter. She's run out of bullets, so she can't shoot the Ruby doll, but when she tells Ruby they need to leave, she just stands there and stares. Has Lee come under Satan's influence now that her mother is dead? Is Ruby possessed or in some sort of trance state? Or is she just coming to the realization that even if she does come back and destroy the doll with some other weapon, nothing's stopping this from occurring all over again with another fervent worshipper of the devil?

tropes.name: AM/FM Characterization
tropes.html: Longlegs shows an obsession for 70s glam rock. Contrasted with Lee who apparently has a taste for new wave music.

tropes.name: Anyone Can Die
tropes.html: By the end, the only remaining living named characters are Lee and Ruby, and Ruby's mental state is a big question mark.

tropes.name: Arbitrary Skepticism
tropes.html: Carter seems to believe pretty firmly in Lee's apparent psychic powers, trusting the vast majority of her inputs on the case even with very little to otherwise back them. Satanic magic, on the other hand? Nope.

tropes.name: Arc Words
tropes.html: "The Man Downstairs." Longlegs claims to serve and attributes his mission to "The Man Downstairs." We later learn that, following his deal with Ruth, he's been living and operating out of her basement, literally making Longlegs himself "The Man Downstairs." Though the "Man Downstairs" that Longlegs himself serves is Satan.

tropes.name: Aspect Ratio Switch
tropes.html: Scenes alternate between widescreen in the present day and square for flashbacks.

tropes.name: Attention Whore
tropes.html: Word of God is that Kobble is a failed glam rocker who later turned to devil worship. One interpretation for Kobble's sheer glee in the ending is that he achieved fame and notoriety and put on a performance nobody will ever forget.

tropes.name: The Bad Guy Wins
tropes.html: While Kobble dies, he goes out on his own terms and has killed countless innocents over the years. While his soul presumably goes to Hell, he wanted that anyway. Even if the final doll doesn't result in a total family massacre, the final shots imply Kobble's fully satisfied with how everything turned out with a triumphant "Hail Satan!"

tropes.name: Bathos
tropes.html: The movie opens with an ominous epigraph... attributed to Marc Bolan's band T. Rex, since, in context, it's the lyrics to their song "Bang a Gong (Get it On)". The song also plays over the credits immediately following Carter's Demonic Possession-induced Pater Familicide.

tropes.name: Be as Unhelpful as Possible
tropes.html: It's pretty clear Kobble is delighting in playing with law enforcement, answering in riddles, and giving them absolutely zero useful answers.

tropes.name: Beauty Inversion
tropes.html: The normally unconventionally attractive Nicolas Cage is absolutely unrecognizable under Longlegs' chalk-white skin and hair and horrible facial deformities. Word of God says Longlegs' design was meant to evoke numerous botched plastic surgeries in an effort to "make himself look beautiful for Satan."

tropes.name: Being Evil Sucks
tropes.html: Longlegs is an unabashed Satanist who revels in murder For the Evulz, and he has no problem with going to hell in service to his master. However, there is a moment that shows his inability to gain acceptance from other people gets to him at times. He creeps out the young girl at the drugstore, who tells her father that the "gross old guy" is back. Afterwards, we see him driving away in his car, throwing a screaming fit behind the wheel. It might suggest that there's a part of him, however tiny, that wishes he could be a part of normal society but has extremely low self-esteem because he knows that's an impossibility. Notably, he screams a song lyric that includes "save me from the hell of living," the closest thing he ever expresses to either a motive or regret.

tropes.name: Benevolent Boss
tropes.html: Carter is very warm to Lee and it's implied he tries to fill the void of a father figure in her life. He respects her judgement and intuition and doesn't want her to go too deeply into Longlegs' murders for her own well-being. He only gets mad when Kobble commits suicide and when he's under the influence of Satan himself.

tropes.name: Berserk Button
tropes.html: Refusing Kobble's "gifts" apparently infuriates him. Ruth trying to make him get lost results in him singing a warning at her of what he'll do if she continues to refuse, and it's notably the one thing that ever makes him decide to kill someone with his own hands.

tropes.name: A Birthday, Not a Break
tropes.html: Lee's birthday was when Kobble found and tried to kill her, with the horror culminating right near the anniversary. Kobble and his accomplice likewise target little Ruby Carter and their other victims on or near their birthdays.

tropes.name: Bittersweet Ending
tropes.html: Kobble and his accomplice are dead and their killing spree is stopped. However, the nicest interpretation is that Lee is traumatized and will have to live with the fact she had to kill her own mother. She didn't save her boss's family and only his young daughter Ruby survived, but the girl's mental state is unclear. Even if she recovers her sense of self, her family was horribly murdered and there's no telling if the Devil is done with Lee yet. The worst interpretation is that Lee's hesitance to leave the house with Ruby indicates she has now come under the sway of the same demonic forces that drove Kobble, and will use her position as an FBI agent to follow in his footsteps. No matter what happens from here, Kobble hints that he's just fine and dandy with how it all turned out, blowing the audience a triumphant kiss.

tropes.name: Black Comedy
tropes.html: Under interrogation by the FBI, Kobble sings "Happy Birthday" to Lee in a decidedly creepy manner (and the importance of birthdays to his killing spree makes this particularly pointed). Browning stops the tape and wryly notes, "It goes on like that for a while." When Lee asks exactly how long, Browning matter-of-factly says, "24 minutes."

tropes.name: Bolivian Army Ending
tropes.html: In a way. After Lee witnesses Carter murdering his wife and offs both him and her mother, she tries to shoot at the cursed doll, only to find out that her gun is already dry. She tries to save Ruby and says "Let's get out of here", but instead of actually walking out with her, she remains frozen in place, staring at the doll; this is the last we see of her before the movie ends. It is uncertain if Lee was merely traumatized by her experiences or fell under Satan's influence — and, if the latter is the case, whether she is going to shake off said influence or succumb to possession.

tropes.name: Boom, Headshot!
tropes.html:
• Lee's partner is abruptly killed in one of the early scenes this way, right after knocking on the door of the house that Lee suspected their killer was in. Turns out she was right.
  • Ruth takes out Browning by blowing her head off with a shotgun — once from the driver's side of the car, then again from the other side for god knows what reason.
  • Finally, Lee kills Ruth herself this way when the latter comes at Ruby with a ritual dagger; notably, it's the only one of the three instances portrayed as relatively neat.

tropes.name: Bunny-Ears Lawyer
tropes.html: A truly dark example, but Longlegs, AKA Dale Ferdinand Kobble, is an absolute weirdo who screams to himself, acts strange to everyone he meets and bursts into song and dance at random intervals. He is also a terrifyingly clever and effective serial killer who's evaded justice for decades. Also, his doll-making skills are beyond reproach, as the doctor who assesses the Carrie doll Lee brings him says only a master toymaker would be capable of such work.

tropes.name: Casting Gag
tropes.html: Blair Underwood's career heyday was in the 90s, and this film is set...in the 90s. His big break was playing a civil and defense attorney in LA Law, and now he's on the other side of the aisle.

tropes.name: Chekhov's Gun
tropes.html: There is a literal gun in the form of the break-action shotgun Ruth owns.

tropes.name: Chekhov's Gunman
tropes.html: The young girl in the prologue is Lee.

tropes.name: Chekhov's Party
tropes.html: In her first appearance, Ruby tells Lee that her birthday is coming up in a few days and invites Lee to the party. This becomes important halfway through and is ultimately the setting for the ending.

tropes.name: Cloudcuckoolander
tropes.html: Longlegs isn't just creepy, he's weird, too. He goes off on bizarre tangents at random, acts strange to people he meets (including, fittingly, an imitation of a cuckoo clock at one point), and bursts into song and dance at various points with no provocation. What any of this means- if anything- is known only to him. He also apparently spends most of his downtime in between murders sitting in a red-lit basement, staring off into space while listening to old records for what seems to be hours, if not days, on end.

tropes.name: Connect the Deaths
tropes.html: When researching the Longlegs murders, Lee begins to notice patterns that correlate to specific dates in tracking him down.

tropes.name: The Corrupter
tropes.html: Longlegs' dolls corrupt fathers into murdering their families, if not outright opening them to Demonic Possession. He also steadily corrupted Lee's mother Ruth into being his accomplice and a horrific killer herself.

tropes.name: Creative Closing Credits
tropes.html: Downplayed. The credits are a normal centered list of names and roles, but they're played in reverse, descending the screen instead of ascending.

tropes.name: Creator Thumbprint
tropes.html:
• Oz Perkins really loves young, introspective women with oddly psychic abilities and connections to supernatural villains. The Blackcoat's Daughter and Gretel and Hansel have both featured similar motifs before Longlegs.
  • Longlegs' algorithm centers around young women born on the 14th of each month. Oz Perkins' mother, Berry Berenson, was born on April 14.

tropes.name: Creepy Basement
tropes.html: Longlegs lives in a surreal basement that doubles as a workshop for creating his dolls. It's shot to be as unnerving as possible: it's lit almost entirely with red lights, his bed is a dirty mattress on the floor with old, ratty sheets; the bathroom is cramped, dimly lit, and cluttered with junk; and the only decor are some record albums and photos of rock stars mounted to the walls. The only vaguely comforting aspect is the sound of his favorite music — 70s glam rock — on an old record player. Turns out this is Lee's childhood home's basement, and she later awakens there after her doll is destroyed.

tropes.name: Creepy Child
tropes.html: Carrie Anne, the sole survivor of Longlegs' killings by virtue of having been at school the day her family was killed, has spent the years since in a borderline catatonic state at a psychiatric hospital. When speaking to Lee, she casually recounts her parents' deaths and mentions that she'd happily commit suicide or kill Lee with her bare hands if she was commanded to by the Devil.

tropes.name: Creepy Doll
tropes.html: Longlegs sends dolls that induce trances in families. The one survivor says she can still hear her doll speak to her. And Lee's unused doll gave her her Psychic Powers - probably.

tropes.name: Creepy High-Pitched Voice
tropes.html: Longlegs speaks in an unnerving falsetto that only highlights how inhuman he appears.

tropes.name: Cursed Item
tropes.html: The dolls are imbued with powerful dark magic that allows Satan to influence his victims through them.

tropes.name: The Dark Side Will Make You Forget
tropes.html:
• In all her flashbacks, Ruth is portrayed as a loving and caring mother, while also well-groomed and obviously taking good care of their house. In the present, after helping Longlegs with so many of his murders, she looks like a classic case of Diogenes syndrome, and is incredibly emotionally distant. On top of that, Longlegs is literally capable of making people forget.
  • After a whole film worth of portraying him as a kind family man, in the finale, when under the influence of the Creepy Doll, Carter acts in a really aggressive and abusive way, while being not just foul-mouthed, but outright insulting toward his wife.

tropes.name: Deadly Euphemism
tropes.html: When the mind-controlled Agent Carter talks about needing a knife to "cut the cake," it sounds downright sinister. When he takes his wife to the kitchen, he remarks he'll be back, but she'll still be in the kitchen...

tropes.name: Deal with the Devil
tropes.html: In exchange for sparing Lee's life, Longlegs forces her mother to become his accomplice by having her deliver the dolls which induce the murderous trance and stand there and watch the murders.

tropes.name: Demonic Possession
tropes.html: Longlegs commits his murders using magical dolls that allow Satan to possess anyone nearby. The father is possessed and made to kill his family and himself, while other members of the family can also be controlled to ensure that they die.

tropes.name: Diagonal Billing
tropes.html: Not quite diagonal, but Nicolas Cage and Maika Monroe both get equal "and" billing.

tropes.name: Dragon Their Feet
tropes.html: After Longlegs kills himself, Lee’s mother Ruth, who was his accomplice all along, is left to target Carter and his family with one of Longlegs’s dolls.

tropes.name: Driven to Suicide
tropes.html: Carrie Anne, a survivor of Longlegs' killing spree who spent the 8 years since essentially in a coma, mentions during a conversation with Lee that if the Man Downstairs asked her to jump off a building to her death, she'd happily do so. She does so offscreen right at the same time that Longlegs kills himself while incarcerated.

tropes.name: Enemy Rising Behind
tropes.html: Ruth sneaks up with a shotgun on unsuspecting Browning. By the time the agent realises what's up, she doesn't even have enough time to turn her head in that direction.

tropes.name: Even Evil Has Loved Ones
tropes.html: Ruth has become a child-killing, Satan-worshiping monster by film's end, but she's driven by love for her daughter.

tropes.name: Evil Cannot Stand Cuteness
tropes.html: Or cannot stand Christian devoutness in this instance. Longleg's primary targets are certainly young girls who have a birthday on the 14th day of the month. But he also seems to target girls who have that birthday and are part of devoted Christian families. Agent Carter mentions that the wife in one of the murdered families regularly participated in a church sale. The family we see getting butchered in a Flashback had a Christian minister in the house at the time, and he shares the same gruesome fate as the rest of the family (save Carrie Anne).

tropes.name: Evil Counterpart
tropes.html: Longlegs and Lee parallel one another in many ways. Both are extremely good at their roles, albeit on opposite sides of the board. Kobble is a Serial Killer and Lee is an FBI agent. Both are loners who cannot fit in well with other people. Lee originally wanted to be an actress while Word of God implies that Kobble is a failed glam rocker.

tropes.name: Evil Is Hammy
tropes.html: Longlegs takes big, gaping bites of the scenery and chews it with relish. Being so bizarre and over the top only contributes to how menacing and inhuman he appears.

tropes.name: Evil Phone
tropes.html: Multiple times during the movie, Lee hears creepy static over the phone. At the end of the movie when she wakes up in Longlegs' shop in her mom's basement, the phone upstairs rings for an unnaturally long time as she slowly gets her bearings and makes her way upstairs. When she answers, a creepy voice covered in static reminds her that it is Ruby's birthday today, with all the implications that has. Whether it was Longlegs from beyond the grave or perhaps Satan himself is unknown.

tropes.name: Extremely Short Timespan
tropes.html: Downplayed. The main story takes place within a week or so, but the whole thing is filmed and edited in such a way it gives an impression of going on for months until the actual flow of time is mentioned.

tropes.name: Facial Horror
tropes.html: Longlegs leaves his face gruesomely bloodied and without a nose after smashing it against the table in the interrogation room.

tropes.name: Family Extermination
tropes.html: Longlegs’ MO. Every Longlegs killing is a massacre of an entire family, always including at least one young daughter. They appear to be murder-suicides committed by the father, and are only connected by the letters Longlegs leaves at the crime scene.

tropes.name: Faux Affably Evil
tropes.html: Longlegs is, in his own bizarre and unsettling way, friendly. While it's very difficult to parse what's going on inside his head and how much is deliberately false or a sincere but very bizarre attempt at relating to others, he's very dangerous to be around and takes pleasure in tormenting people.

tropes.name: Fighting from the Inside
tropes.html: Carter's wife, despite being controlled by the evil within Kobble's final doll, is able to give a wrenching sob at Ruby's party with the implication she's trying to fight the influence but can't manage it.

tropes.name: Forced into Evil
tropes.html: Lee's mother Ruth is Kobble's partner and accomplice, delivering the dolls to families so the devil can twist the fathers' minds into killing the entire family. She made this bargain to spare a young Lee from being murdered by Kobble.

tropes.name: Foreshadowing
tropes.html:
• When Lee calls her mom early on and hesitates to give her details about the Longlegs investigation, Ruth reminds Lee that she used to be a nurse and has seen her share of gruesome deaths. Of course, since it turns out she was Longlegs's accomplice, she's caused many gruesome deaths too.
  • Carter takes Lee to meet his family early in the film (specifically after she drives him home due to him having a few too many drinks). In the process, Lee meets his daughter Ruby, who mentions that her birthday is coming up and asks if Lee can come. She is the final intended victim of Longlegs' modern murder spree, and the climax has Lee forced to kill Carter to stop him from killing Ruby under the doll's influence that Ruth gives Ruby.
  • The note Longlegs leaves Lee states that deciphering it will lead to her mother's murder. Which it does since it's revealed that Ruth is Longlegs' accomplice and Lee will have to shoot her to protect herself and Ruby.
  • After Longlegs kills himself in his interrogation room, Carter is unusually agitated and announces that the case is shut. This is likely due to the fact that his daughter's birthday happens to be on the day that the missing murder will happen on and he is highly uncomfortable about that, or perhaps already under the beginnings of the final doll's influence. And indeed, Longlegs' accomplice does show up at Ruby's party to gift her the doll, which makes Carter murder his wife and attempt to kill Ruby.
  • Additionally, Ruth openly admitting her faithlessness to Lee, ruminating on how many little things don't get to "grow up" because of the brutality of the world, and bluntly stating that prayers to God don't do anything make her the character most likely to be involved with Kobble, a servant of Satan, as well as hint toward the Deal with the Devil she made with him.
  • One of the flashbacks Lee has, shows her imagining her mother spotting an intruder and going for a shotgun, carrying and loading the thing in a very specific way. When the accomplice is revealed, it is obvious it's Ruth before her face is in the frame, as she carries and loads the same gun in the exact same way two decades later.
  • The coroner that Lee and Carter have investigated the doll they found in the abandoned farm stables mentions that when he held the metal orb that was inside the doll's head, it made him think of his ex-wife for the first time in years. He says this with an odd look on his face. The orbs inside the dolls that Longlegs distributes causes the husbands of families to turn violent against their wives and children. Even though he wasn't even married anymore, the orb was affecting the coroner with the presumably last major woman in his life.
  • Kobble knowing Lee's name and several personal details about her, along with his machinations in guiding her along a certain path once she gets involved in the investigation, seems like an indication of a savant intellect, akin to The Riddler in The Batman, but him not doing this with any other officer in the case or even any other character in the story hints that he can do so because he has not only a personal history with Lee but a direct connection to her and a source of information about her in the form of her mother, Ruth.
  • The opening flashback of Kobble claiming he's delivering a birthday present to a young Lee is an early indication of how he's making fathers kill their families and themselves, an answer that eludes the FBI since they won't consider supernatural elements.
  • When Kobble threatens Ruth during a flashback he mentions coming back "as many times as I like!" In the present day it's revealed that he's living and operating out of Ruth's basement, coming and going as he pleases.
  • The FBI mentions that when they have Kobble, despite all his clear satanism there exists no physical evidence linking him to any murder. This is because Kobble has never gotten his own hands dirty. He creates dolls that channel Satan to possess and corrupt fathers into murdering their families behind closed doors without Kobble ever having to personally shed a drop of blood.

tropes.name: For the Evulz
tropes.html: Ultimately, Kobble's goals are spreading murder and evil for the sheer wicked glee of serving Satan as an end unto itself.

tropes.name: The Fourth Wall Will Not Protect You
tropes.html: Oddly enough, an in-universe example. When Harker and the other agents are watching the tape of Longlegs' interrogation after his capture, he talks about the ending of the story between him and Harker, before turning his head in different directions saying that "you, and you, and you will be there." Due to the angle of the TV, he appears to be addressing Harker, Carter, and Browning- all three of whom are present at the climax.

tropes.name: Freeze-Frame Bonus
tropes.html:
• According to "Look Closer", there are fifteen appearances from Satan's silhouette, all scattered throughout various points in the film.
  • When Lee is searching through her old polaroids and discovers one of Longlegs, a sudden jarring flashback to the photo being taken also flashes some distorted negatives of an unclear figure for a split second. Late in the film the real image is shown, Lee's mother Ruth bloodstained and exulting Satan after aiding Longlegs in another family's murder.

tropes.name: The Fundamentalist
tropes.html: Ruth is deeply religious and constantly cautions Lee to remember her prayers. It takes a dark turn that she's become a devout satanist to keep her daughter from being taken by Satan and Longlegs.

tropes.name: Gory Discretion Shot
tropes.html: If the audience is witness to a family slaying, the blow will noticeably land where the camera isn't looking.

tropes.name: Greater-Scope Villain
tropes.html: Satan/The Devil is Kobble/Longlegs' master, driving him to murder innocents. Though Lee never confronts him directly, the influence of "The Man Downstairs" hangs heavy over the movie, and a demonic presence can be spotted hiding in the background of various scenes, sometimes explicitly, sometimes as a subliminal "easter egg."

tropes.name: Gunman with Three Names
tropes.html: Longlegs' real name is Dale Ferdinand Kobble.

tropes.name: Hammy Villain, Serious Hero
tropes.html: The titular Longlegs is a hammy weirdo fond of randomly singing and dancing and laughing maniacally. Our protagonist Lee, on the other hand, is a rather reserved Perpetual Frowner.

tropes.name: Hollywood Satanism
tropes.html: Longlegs is revealed to be a devil-worshiping killer who commits his crimes to appease Lucifer himself. "Hail Satan!" and all.

tropes.name: Human Sacrifice
tropes.html: The true purpose of Kobble's murders are to offer the families as sacrifices to the Devil.

tropes.name: Hyper-Competent Sidekick
tropes.html: A very dark version, but Ruth is extremely good at being Kobble's accomplice. She's a very mild-mannered and gentle-seeming woman who utterly sells the kind gift-giver persona required to trick so many families as opposed to Kobble's utter lack of social skills and subtlety. Without Ruth, it's very doubtful Kobble could have lasted as long as he did.

tropes.name: I Gave My Word
tropes.html: Kobble promises not to harm Lee in exchange for Ruth helping him and surprisingly keeps it. Despite living with them for decades, he never lays a finger on Lee. However, it's implied he has no compunction in arranging events to hurt Lee so bad that she might wish for death.

tropes.name: I Shall Taunt You
tropes.html: Longlegs leaves behind taunting notes to police, leaves a note for Lee at her house to mock her, and spends much of his interrogation with the FBI and Lee specifically mocking them all the while.

tropes.name: Implied Death Threat
tropes.html: Ruth telling Kobble to get lost and leave her daughter be results in his dancing and singing with the lyrics "Let me in now!" and promise if they don't "make nice," he'll be back "as many times as I like!" Sure enough, this was a death threat and he later tried to make good on it that night.

tropes.name: Intelligence Equals Isolation
tropes.html: Lee is a very good agent and very good at her job. Despite her bursts of insight and good analysis, she has no real friends and has seemingly no idea how to act around other people.

tropes.name: It Gets Easier
tropes.html: Ruth's assistance to Kobble to protect Lee seems to be this - when she starts out delivering his dolls to families and witnessing the ensuing massacres, she's horrified beyond belief and has several freakouts in and around her car in the aftermath, but by the present day, she's a stone-cold killer carrying out Kobble's will even after his death whose only soft spot lies in Lee herself. Corruption by the Devil may have played a part in this.

tropes.name: It's Personal
tropes.html:
Ruth refusing the gift of Kobble's doll means that Kobble fixated on her and Lee for the "insult" and he has maintained an obsession with Lee for years after.
"You could've made nice with me... but you didn't. And now that has led to all of this."

tropes.name: Improbable Infant Survival
tropes.html: Played with, as Longlegs is a Serial Killer of young children. However, the man himself never kills anyone, he just compels fathers to kill their children, their wives, and themselves with Satanic magic. Additionally, three girls do survive the massacres he arranges via outside circumstances: Lee, because her mother made a Deal with the Devil; Carrie, who happened to be at school when the massacre took place; and Ruby, whom Lee saves by killing Carter and Ruth before they can finish the job.

tropes.name: Killed Mid-Sentence
tropes.html: Lee's partner in the opening is shot mid-word when unknowingly talking to the suspect they are after.

tropes.name: Knight Templar Parent
tropes.html: Ruth's entire motivation is to protect her daughter. She worships Satan under the belief that if the sacrificial rituals are incomplete, Lee is cursed to "twist and burn" in hell forever.

tropes.name: Kooky Cascadia
tropes.html: The crimes of the eponymous Hollywood Satanist Serial Killer, and the subsequent investigation into them, happen in Oregon in The '90s, but while the film was shot in Vancouver and fully exploits the perpetually overcast northwestern atmosphere (including allusions to Twin Peaks) to build its mood, it doesn't go out of its way to highlight the setting.

tropes.name: Lack of Empathy
tropes.html: Kobble possesses no care for other people and barely seems to comprehend humans exist aside from him.

tropes.name: Large Ham
tropes.html:
Did you think Nicolas Cage as a satanic serial killer wouldn't be totally over the top? If so, you thought wrong. After Ruth turns Longlegs away from Lee as a child, he sings a warning to Ruth.
"LET ME IN NOOOOOOW, AND IT CAN BEEEE NIIIIIIICE!
MAKE ME GOOO NOOOOOOW, AND I'LL HAVE TO COME BAAAAACK!
NOT OOOOONCE, NOT TWIIIIIICE, BUT AS MANY TIIIIMES AS I LIIIIIIIIIIKE!"

tropes.name: Laughably Evil
tropes.html: Longlegs is incredibly creepy, but his behavior is just so bizarre that it becomes funny at times. His penchant for randomly breaking into song and dance in particular is incredibly funny; he does so at one point while shopping and then stands there awkwardly when the clerk bluntly asks what he's even doing.

tropes.name: Light Is Not Good
tropes.html: Longlegs dresses all in white and has pale skin and white hair. Despite the brightness, he's a twisted serial killer.

tropes.name: Literal Metaphor
tropes.html: The Man Downstairs isn't just a flowery way to talk about Satan. That's literally where Longlegs has been living for the past twenty or so years.

tropes.name: Loners Are Freaks
tropes.html:
• Dale Ferdinand Kobble lives a nomadic lifestyle and tends to avoid most people. Setting aside the Satanic Serial Killer thing, he's just a total weirdo who doesn't seem to know how to function in modern society.
  • Lee is a Good Counterpart. Though she is a hero, she has no friends and takes no pleasure in even talking to people except perhaps her mother Ruth.

tropes.name: Magical Realism
tropes.html: Name-dropped by James A. Janisse when discussing Lee Harker's potentially psychic powers, showing that the setting has a margin of supernaturalism to it, or at least greater belief in it. The killer himself is motivated to kill in the name of Satan, with it even being implied that Harper's powers are the result of his presence in her formative years.

tropes.name: The Main Characters Do Everything
tropes.html: Carter has an entire task force on the case, but still personally heads into the field with Lee to investigate leads. He really should be staying behind his desk. The one time he's not available (because Longlegs killed himself on Carter's watch), the random agent who drives Lee to Lee's mum ends up dead instead. Good thing, because if Carter had been there, Longlegs' plot would've failed.

tropes.name: Mentor Occupational Hazard
tropes.html: Poor Carter winds up dead at Lee's own hand in order to prevent him from slaughtering his own daughter under Satan's control. It's implied that he was specifically targeted by Longlegs in order to hurt her as much as possible, punishing her for beginning to forge a friendship with the man and his family; so if he hadn't taken Lee under his wing, none of this would have happened to him.

tropes.name: Mind Rape
tropes.html: Kobble's dolls channel his own dark magic and Satan's influence to mentally crush a father into family annihilation. It's implied the victims know what's happening and are in utter mental anguish from pain and fear.

tropes.name: Moral Myopia
tropes.html: Kobble may be a satanic serial killer, but he's legitimately furious at anyone denying his "gifts" to them. Not letting him murder someone via satanic magic is the one thing that makes him go to kill them with his bare hands, implying that this is bizarrely personal for him.

tropes.name: My God, What Have I Done?
tropes.html: Ruth breaks down crying with horror and remorse when she realizes her hands are stained with blood as a result of helping Kobble. She loses this trait as time goes on and is nearly as monstrous as Kobble by the end.

tropes.name: Mysterious Past
tropes.html: When caught by the FBI, Kobble seems to be a ghost. He has no traceable past or connections and how he gained his black magic and turned to worshiping Satan are never explained.

tropes.name: Never Trust a Trailer
tropes.html: An interesting tonal case. The numerous, cryptic teasers sell Longlegs as a deathly serious killer thriller in the vein of The Silence of the Lambs. While the film itself is a sincere work of horror and undeniably dread-inducing, it's also surreal and even goofy in the vein of David Lynch and the short films broadcast on [adult swim]'s Infomercials.

tropes.name: Nobody Suspects the Woman
tropes.html: When the police figure out that Longlegs has an accomplice, Lee floats that it would need to be someone the families felt they could trust, and felt comfortable letting into their homes. She suggests a child. Lee doesn't mention a woman, but the killer turns out to be a woman - her own mother, Ruth, who dons a nurse's habit and poses as bringing a gift, and is accordingly let into all the murdered family's homes and watches them die.

tropes.name: No Good Deed Goes Unpunished
tropes.html:
• Agent Browning drives Lee over to her mother's house so that she can confront her after Longlegs' death, since Lee has just witnessed a traumatic event and isn't in a good state to drive alone. She's rewarded for this act of kindness with two gunshots to the head courtesy of Ruth.
  • Agent Carter looks after Lee and seems a genuinely fatherly figure to her, pushing her to come to meet his family and not to get too wrapped up in the case for her own mental health. His closeness to her is presumably why Longlegs targets his family and why he and his wife die in such horrific circumstances.

tropes.name: No Social Skills
tropes.html:
• Lee is a reserved workaholic who is awkward at best in social situations. When Carter invites her to meet his family, she asks bluntly, "Do I have to?" When given a tour of the daughter's bedroom, she looks like she's adrift in a lifeboat.
  • The one time Kobble interacts with someone who isn't a potential victim or law enforcement, he squeals about how close it must be to her birthday and shrieks "cuckoo" at her, with her noting this isn't the first time he's done this. He doesn't seem to be aware of how to behave like an ordinary human being.

tropes.name: Not-So-Harmless Villain
tropes.html: Played With. The audience learns of Longlegs' horrendous crimes very early on and his first appearance to Lee is genuinely unnerving. However, the first time we really see Kobble in the present day, his bizarre appearance and behavior utterly repel the counter girl at the hardware store, but he seems more childish and antisocial than a genuine menace. Indeed, he eventually is apprehended without any resistance by the police, harming no one before killing himself and quickly being overshadowed by Ruth, who actually does kill some people directly and plays an equal role in the Satanic plot. However, Longlegs is ultimately responsible for the ruination of Lee's life and numerous murders, and he gets the literal last laugh in the film.

tropes.name: Obvious Villain, Secret Villain
tropes.html: Longlegs/Kobble is extremely weird in addition to his very obvious evil, so there's no doubt from anyone that he's the killer. His dragon, Ruth, is Lee's mother and her involvement in the plot is a complete surprise.

tropes.name: Off the Grid
tropes.html: Kobble seems to be a drifter with no fixed home save for the years he spends in the Harkers' basement, which makes it easier for him to scout and find victims, as well as evade law enforcement.

tropes.name: Once More, with Clarity
tropes.html: The young girl in the prologue who encounters Longlegs turns out to be a young Lee.

tropes.name: Only the Leads Get a Downer Ending
tropes.html: Regardless of whether he's happy in hell or not, Longlegs is dead and gone and can hurt nobody else ever again, along with Ruth. Lee is at best traumatized, potentially still influenced by Satan, her boss dead, and had to kill her own mother.

tropes.name: OOC Is Serious Business
tropes.html: The one time Longlegs stops being weird and flighty is when Lee interrogates him. He still talks in riddles but also speaks to Lee with utter malice and clues her into "Go ask your mommy!" with a sudden shift in personality that's simply jarring.

tropes.name: Pater Familicide
tropes.html: Longlegs' crimes all take the appearance of a man who "snaps" and murders his wife and daughter(s), then kills himself, with Longlegs' presence only being indicated by the coded notes he leaves at the scene of the crime.

tropes.name: Perpetual Frowner
tropes.html: Lee barely smiles throughout the entire film, mostly due to the distressing nature of her job.

tropes.name: Perp Sweating
tropes.html: When Kobble is arrested, the FBI keeps him in an interrogation room to try to uncover his accomplice. Lee herself enters the room for a chat with him and figure out why he's so fixated on her.

tropes.name: Police Are Useless
tropes.html: Surprising subversion. The FBI can't catch Kobble, but it's not really their fault they don't know he's killing via black magic. When Lee provides a photo of Kobble, he's located and captured in very short order.

tropes.name: Pragmatic Villainy
tropes.html: Kobble is enraged that he couldn't deliver a doll to Lee and sacrifice her to Satan. However, he never harms Lee decades after, keeping his word to Ruth. That said, it's implied he's only doing so because Ruth turns out to be an excellent accomplice who facilitates more bloodshed than Kobble probably could manage on his own.

tropes.name: Psychic-Assisted Suicide
tropes.html: The fathers who kill their families during Longlegs’ crimes are in fact forced to do so by the fragment of Satan inside the doll Longlegs planted in their home. Longlegs also does this personally to Carrie Ann Camera, visiting her at the mental hospital and ordering her to jump off the roof in two days’ time.

tropes.name: Psychopathic Manchild
tropes.html: Longlegs is childish and immature, acting more like an overgrown little boy than a grown man even twenty years ago. He is still a very vicious serial killer who revels in murder.

tropes.name: Real After All
tropes.html: The method by which Longlegs has his victims murdered seems utterly impossible without the assistance of some supernatural, demonic force, but Lee and Carter remain dedicated to uncovering how exactly he does it and speculate he has an accomplice. There are also accompanying hints at the supernatural throughout the movie, and Lee herself has some psychic medium capabilities, but she's also able to deduce things like Longlegs' algorithm suggesting there might be a rational explanation behind everything. While Longlegs does have an accomplice in Ruth, Lee's mother, the supernatural turns out to be real after all. Longlegs is an agent of Satan who corrupts fathers into doing murder-suicides to complete a devil's triangle of killings, and Satan wants Lee herself for what is implied to be her capacity as a psychic.

tropes.name: Red Is Violent
tropes.html: All of the film's marketing features bright red writing or backgrounds to invoke this association, as well as drawing attention to red costuming. Longlegs also lives and operates out of an almost entirely red-lit basement, and Lee's psychic flashes are mostly seen through a red filter.

tropes.name: Religious Horror
tropes.html: The film has heavy religious overtones and ultimately comes to Devil forcing a devout woman to cause countless murders in exchange for sparing her daughter.

tropes.name: The Reveal
tropes.html: Lee's mother Ruth is Kobble's accomplice and Kobble had been living in their basement for years after Ruth struck a horrible bargain to spare her daughter.

tropes.name: Rewatch Bonus
tropes.html: Perkins hides multiple shots of the Devil throughout the film to show Mr. Downstairs is never far from Lee and watching everything unfold.

tropes.name: Rule of Drama
tropes.html: The film treats Longlegs' cipher as extremely difficult to crack, until he essentially gives Lee an answer key. It's actually a Vigenère cipher, which isn't impossible if you guess the length of the ciphertext. Which is his codename. The name he keeps signing his notes with.

tropes.name: Rule of Symbolism
tropes.html: Longlegs is an exceedingly pale man who dresses to match, and drives a white car with a stallion-shaped bottle-opener hanging from the rearview mirror; he's a pale rider upon a pale horse, and accordingly acts as Death.

tropes.name: Sanity Has Advantages
tropes.html: Ruth is very good at delivering Kobble's dolls to target families, probably because she knows how to at least pretend to be a functioning human as opposed to screaming "cuckoo" and bursting into song at them.

tropes.name: Sanity Slippage
tropes.html: Ruth's final scene with the Carters shows that guilt and pressure have utterly eroded her mind into a broken madwoman who serves Satan wholeheartedly.

tropes.name: Secret Squatter
tropes.html: It's revealed that Longlegs lived in the Harkers' basement for years after Ruth struck a bargain with him. Ruth, however, was always aware of him; Lee was not.

tropes.name: Self-Disposing Villain
tropes.html: After he is arrested and Lee attempts to interrogate him, Longlegs violently smashes his own face against the table in the interrogation room until he is dead.

tropes.name: Self-Made Orphan
tropes.html: Lee is forced to shoot her own mother in the head to save Ruby.

tropes.name: Serial Killer
tropes.html: "Longlegs" is a killer who's operated for decades, specifically specializing in family annihilation.

tropes.name: Serial Killings, Specific Target
tropes.html: While Kobble targets entire families, his primary targets are the little girls who are intended as human sacrifices to Satan. The family slayings obscure this detail and how Kobble always targets them on specific dates.

tropes.name: Shout-Out
tropes.html:
• Longlegs is evidently a big fan of Marc Bolan - aside from the quote from "Bang a Gong (Get It On)" that appears before the opening credits, he's repeatedly seen listening to T-Rex while driving and keeps a photo of Marc in a room that otherwise is full of various occult symbols.
  • Longlegs also owns a copy of Lou Reed's 1972 album Transformer, prominently displayed above his mirror.
  • Meanwhile, Lee Harker was evidently a fan of Duran Duran in her youth - the cover of Rio (Album) can be seen on display in her childhood room.

tropes.name: Sir Not-Appearing-in-This-Trailer
tropes.html: The trailers go out of their way to avoid showing Nicolas Cage as Longlegs, going so far to censor or otherwise distort the rare scenes of him they do show.

tropes.name: Sliding Scale of Gameplay and Story Integration
tropes.html: The film's alternate reality game had the players translating Longlegs's messages with a cipher provided by the teasers spelling out the movie's title in Longlegs's code. In the film itself, Lee uses Longlegs's threat letter as a cipher to decode the killer's other messages. Said threat letter also reuses an image from the Birthday Murders website and the Bible verse "Stood upon the sand of the sea", which was a secret message in one trailer.

tropes.name: Snow Means Death
tropes.html: The opening flashback scene to Lee's first meeting with Longlegs as a child takes place in midwinter.

tropes.name: The Sociopath
tropes.html: Kobble conveys nothing resembling empathy, remorse, or kindness, carrying out the brutal murders of men, women, and children for the purpose of serving the devil with sadistic glee. He can barely comprehend other human beings exist except as things to manipulate and hurt.

tropes.name: Sole Survivor
tropes.html: Carrie Ann is the only survivor of the Longlegs murders, though her sanity has not endured.

tropes.name: The Soulsaver
tropes.html: A very dark example, but Ruth states if she doesn't keep murdering innocent people, Satan will claim Lee's soul and her own, condemning them to "burn and twist" in hell forever.

tropes.name: The Spook
tropes.html: When the FBI finally captures Kobble, they're unable to turn up anything about his past or any paperwork on his life, not even a birth certificate - they only know his name because he gave it to them, and he certainly doesn't give them anything else.

tropes.name: Swiss-Cheese Security
tropes.html: It turns out Longlegs had visited Carrie Ann in the mental hospital using Lee's name, given "Lee Harker" is rather gender ambiguous. When asked if they bother to check identification, the director pauses and admits that would probably be good protocol from thereon.

tropes.name: Teeth-Clenched Teamwork
tropes.html: While an excellent working pair, it's implied Kobble and Ruth don't care for one another very much. The latter is only involved to spare her daughter from Satan after being threatened by Kobble and when Kobble obliquely refers to his accomplice, he is uncharacteristically venomous in tone.

tropes.name: Theme Serial Killer
tropes.html: Longlegs patterns his kills around specific dates, utilizes dolls in the murders, and ensures a satanic bent to the murders.

tropes.name: Title Confusion
tropes.html: At one point in explaining her investigations to her boss, Agent Carter, she quotes from the Bible. His partner, Browning, recognizes the quote and attributes it to "Revelations", but Lee quickly corrects her that the book is just "Revelation" singular. This is a common mistake, and it makes sense that Lee, raised by a devout single mother, would be quick to correct it.

tropes.name: Title Drop
tropes.html: In the opening scene, Longlegs meets a little girl (a young Lee) and cheerfully brings up that he's wearing his "longlegs."

tropes.name: Tom the Dark Lord
tropes.html: The monstrously evil and dangerous Satanist serial killer Longlegs's real name is the very quotidian Dale.

tropes.name: Too Dumb to Live
tropes.html: Carter knows the killer goes after girls whose birthdays are on the 14th. This includes his daughter. He also knows Longlegs is obsessed with Lee, the agent he's been mentoring. Somehow, he doesn't seem to realize he might be a target.

tropes.name: Too Good for This Sinful Earth
tropes.html: A rare example of this happening to an older male character; Agent Carter is shown to be a kind and good-natured Family Man who takes on a paternal role towards Lee after noticing her talent. His family is the last target of Longlegs' killing spree and the corrupting influence of the Devil leads him to kill his wife before Lee is forced to kill him in order to save Ruby.

tropes.name: Tragic Villain
tropes.html: Ruth is revealed to be an accomplice to Longlegs, helping him to carrying his brutal killings. However, it's also revealed she was forced into it by Longlegs to spare Lee's life from him and Satan.

tropes.name: Trash of the Titans
tropes.html: Ruth is a compulsive hoarder and her house is covered to the brim with items that she's accumulated over the years and never threw away. Some of her dialogue implies that this is due to not wanting to let go of the past, as her future in the service to Satan offers her little to look forward to.

tropes.name: Uncanny Valley
tropes.html: The dolls are so humanlike that it highlights how inhuman they are at the same time.

tropes.name: Uncertain Doom
tropes.html: Ruth tells Lee that they will "burn and twist and burn and twist, in hell. Forever and ever" if she fails to kill the Carter family. Seeing as Lee prevents Ruby from being killed by a possessed Det. Carter, it's unknown what fate awaits her in the afterlife. It's also possible that Ruth could be burning in hell now since she was killed by Lee before she could annihilate the Carter family.

tropes.name: Unfazed Everyman
tropes.html: The teenage cashier at the store that Longlegs stops by isn't fazed in the slightest by any of his antics, reacting to it with bored indifference and telling her father that the "gross old guy" is back again, implying that this isn't the first time that he's done this.

tropes.name: Unknown Relative
tropes.html: There is no indication of who Lee's father is. Ruth never mentions him, even in her stories, or gives any indication of who he is and what happened between them.

tropes.name: Unknown Rival
tropes.html: As Lee dedicates herself to hunting Longlegs, Kobble steadily reveals he has obsessed over Lee her entire life. It is implied that her being the only victim to ever escape his killing spree has led to him setting events for the sole purpose of hurting her as much as possible.

tropes.name: Unseen Evil
tropes.html: Satan himself is lurking around, only seen in dark shadow, and implied to be a monstrously eldritch beast right out of the Book of Revelation. All we ever see is a shadowy silhouette or gleaming eyes.

tropes.name: Vague Age
tropes.html: Tying in with Longlegs' Mysterious Past, it's hard to tell how old he is. Noticeably, he doesn't seem to age at all in two entire decades and his facial deformities further obscure the matter.

tropes.name: Villainous Breakdown
tropes.html: A rather darkly comic example. After going shopping and having the teenage clerk call him a "gross guy" to his face because of his bizarre behavior, Longlegs has a screaming breakdown in his car as he drives away.

tropes.name: Villainous Parental Instinct
tropes.html: Ruth would even kill innocent people for Lee's sake.

tropes.name: Vomit Indiscretion Shot
tropes.html: After one of the familicides she helps orchestrate, implied to be one of the early ones, Ruth pulls over to the side of the road and throws up in horror and shame.

tropes.name: Wham Line
tropes.html: "You're late... For Miss Ruby's birthday party." Said by a demonic voice on the phone when Lee picks it up during the climax. It may very well be Satan's.

tropes.name: Wham Shot
tropes.html: Ruth lifting a shotgun to the car where Agent Browning is waiting for Lee, revealing herself as the film's other villain.

tropes.name: Wicked Toymaker
tropes.html: Longlegs, AKA Dale Ferdinand Kobble, is a dollmaker who utilizes dark magic with each doll he creates in the image of a child. This allows the devil to twist the victims' minds until they kill their families.

tropes.name: Would Hurt a Child
tropes.html: Every single family annihilation Longlegs commits includes children. In fact, the young girls of the family are apparently the primary targets of the attack.

tropes.name: You Will Be Spared
tropes.html: Kobble promised Ruth she and her daughter would be spared in exchange for Ruth's help. Ruth strongly implies that Satan himself promised that her soul would be spared eternal torture should she complete his rituals.

tropes.name: Abuse Escalation
tropes.html: John starts out charming and friendly, courting a lonely Elton and keeping his promise to meet him in London. He then nudges him into a heavily hedonistic lifestyle, which resulted in Elton's many addictions, though he's still portrayed positively at this point. A moment during "Honky Cat" shows him beginning to cheat, which he'd eventually start doing very blatantly. After becoming Elton's manager, he loses his facade scene by scene. First he fires Elton's old team and dismisses Elton's sadness about losing Ray, before pressuring him to come out to his parents. He mocks him when he's scared to talk to his mom and even admits he doesn't care about Elton's feelings on the matter. When Elton does leave to tell her but jeopardizes a concert by doing so, John's mask drops completely as he storms over, grabs him, shouts at him, and then hits him. He's completely unfazed when caught cheating in a later scene, proceeds to mock him more when Elton's justifiably furious, and even insults him while he's being rescued from his attempted suicide. By the end, John has become so toxic that Elton fully believes John hates him and isn't capable of love, as he spends his last two scenes ridiculing him, dismissing his problems, and prioritizing money above Elton's safety.

tropes.name: Abusive Parents
tropes.html:
Both of Elton's parents are portrayed as different shades of neglectful and emotionally toxic to him.
  • His mother Sheila is portrayed as callous and narcissistic, doing very little to encourage her son's interest in music until her mother convinces her to do it. She openly cheats on her husband with the man she eventually remarries with. When Elton confesses to her that he's gay, she tells him he'll never find love because of it. At the height of his success (and his various addictions), all she can talk about is how she is affected by his antics, dismissing his success as though his feelings mattered less than hers.
  • His father Stanley is portrayed as emotionally muted, doing everything to avoid any emotional bond with his son. Whenever Elton tries to get any affection out of him (like asking for a hug after his father promised to give him one the other night) or is exposed to anything slightly feminine (like Sheila leaving a fashion magazine out), Stanley denies him these things under the assumption that they will turn him into a "fairy". When Elton tries reconnecting years later after he becomes a star, Stanley acts as though he is a complete stranger, insisting that he autograph a record not for himself, but for a coworker. It is especially painful for Elton when he sees that not only does he have two new sons in his new life, but that he is way more affectionate with them than he ever was with him.
  • His stepfather, though, is portrayed as more of a Ditz than as abusive. He's always nice and friendly to Reggie/Elton (if not a little snarky) and even helps him get started on a path to Rock n' Roll.

tropes.name: Abusive Personality Shift
tropes.html: When Elton meets John for the first time, he starts out sweet and supportive; he's the only one interested in talking to Elton at the party and praises his potential. They sleep together and Elton is smitten. John makes good on his promise to return, they get into a relationship, and dive into the rockstar life together as depicted in "Honky Cat". However, when John is sighed on as Elton's new manager, things take a turn; John begins to engage in pretty blatant emotional abuse, Callously Casual Cheating, and is transparently fixated on money. They break up, but as manager, John can't be fired and sticks around, his actions only worsening. He implies heavily that he knew exactly what he was doing from the start and never really cared for Elton, while Elton comes to the conclusion that John both hates him and isn't even capable of love.

tropes.name: Addiction Realization
tropes.html:
• Implied with Bernie. While his addiction is never outright addressed, he's shown heavily drinking in several scenes and seemed interested in the idea of a traditional Sex, Drugs, and Rock & Roll lifestyle. We see him respond to Elton's rudeness in one scene by suggesting he and the women he's with go drink, despite already acting drunk. Then Elton tries to drown himself after, and Bernie is horrified, silent and shaking. The next time we see him, he's on the jet with Elton after a concert and is acting much differently, quietly suggesting they both take a break from the industry to go home and just write music like old times, hinting at a deeper life decision caused by Elton's suicide attempt. For the rest of the movie, he's not shown drinking, and he tries to encourage Elton to get the help he needs.
  • Elton is knee-deep in his many addictions by the end of the movie, and is going through a severe emotional downspiral after Bernie walks out on him at dinner. After he nearly overdoses that same night and is then expected to have a concert immediately after, he shakily goes for his cocaine to try and calm himself down... only to find himself with a nosebleed. After staring himself down in the mirror and contemplating his situation through the lyrics of "Goodbye Yellow Brick Road"... he marches out of the venue, still in costume, and takes a cab directly to rehab — circling back to the start of the movie where he first arrives in rehab in said costume.

tropes.name: Affair Partner Denial
tropes.html: Played with; Young Reggie encounters his mother having Auto Erotica with a man who isn't his father. When they're caught, it's the man, Fred, who very hastily tries to cover it up by introducing himself as "a friend of your mum's", with an awkward smile. Reggie obviously knows what's actually happening and just stares at him in shock and despair. It doesn't even last long enough for anyone to lie to his father, because the next scene is his parents having a loud and messy divorce over Sheila's cheating.

tropes.name: The Alcoholic
tropes.html: One of the many addictions he develops after becoming famous. At one point, Elton pours half a bottle of vodka in a tall glass before mixing it with orange juice, as part of his morning breakfast. He quits drinking when he goes into rehab and has remained sober ever since.

tropes.name: Alliance of the Alienated
tropes.html: Implied with Elton and Bernie. Elton has severe self-esteem issues, very troubled relationships, and was ignored or mistreated off-stage; even his own parties saw him alone. Bernie didn't seem to think highly of his own lyrics and was startled by Elton's glowing praise, suggesting a history of rejection. They bond over a love for country music, which they're equally embarrassed by. It's also lightly deconstructed; Their friendship is strong enough to overcome an initial struggle to be respected as artists, but their lack of other healthy relationships results in occasional distress — Bernie is uncomfortable when the production grows beyond them, while Elton can't handle Bernie "leaving" him. However, this friendship is also what saves Elton's life, with Bernie as his lone supporter and the only one who genuinely loves the authentic Reggie Dwight beneath it all.

tropes.name: Amicable Exes
tropes.html: Elton and Renate's marriage quietly falls apart for obvious reasons. However, their final exchange on-screen implies both separated on good and understanding terms, even if Elton felt remorseful for hurting her.

tropes.name: Amoral Talent Agent
tropes.html:
• Downplayed with Dick, Elton's first manager. He's rude and hard to impress, and his business-oriented focus means that he's not immediately into Elton and Bernie. He's uninterested when he first meets them, doesn't find their first few songs good enough, and later suggests that they make Bernie the singer because "he's the good looking one" — something he says right in front of Elton, and which is swiftly shut down by Bernie. But Dick ultimately ends up firmly on Elton's side and believes in him enough to get him a gig at the Troubadour, which is a huge gamble at that point. His argument with John makes it clear that he likes working with Elton and is offended by being replaced, even if he's still got a bad attitude.
  • After he and Elton date for a while, John is signed on as his new manager. This turns out to be a huge mistake. John proceeds to remove people who like and care about Elton and justifies it as a business move. He becomes openly motivated by money; he calls "rock and roll" a business, and is dismissive of Elton's work and problems, only caring to the extent that it impacts his ability to profit. By the end of the movie, he's not only failing to do the bare minimum and sell the music, but he's willingly putting Elton's life at risk with nonstop shows just after a bad overdose. This was all calculated; his contracts were written to allow him to profit even if Elton dies, and he'd convinced Elton to sign them while they were still a couple, before dropping his mask; John smugly explains this to him, and exploits it gleefully.

tropes.name: Anguished Declaration of Love
tropes.html: During their last conversation before Elton decides to go into rehab, he angrily confesses he always needed Bernie, and his best friend was never around. He doesn't outright say it, but brings up how Bernie left him for Heather with a decent amount of distress. Bernie doesn't really know how to respond to this, but does seem a bit shaken and tries instead to get through to him one last time before leaving.

tropes.name: Arson, Murder, and Jaywalking
tropes.html: In a group therapy session, Elton shares that his addictions include booze, drugs, sex and shopping. He manages to kick all of them but the last.

tropes.name: Autobiography
tropes.html: The film is a musical retelling of Elton John's rise, fall, and rehab, and while John didn't write the movie, he was an executive producernote with his husband David Furnish being a regular producer and called most of the shots.

tropes.name: Auto Erotica
tropes.html: Young Reggie comes across his mother and a man who is not his father making out in a car.

tropes.name: Babies Ever After
tropes.html: The ending reveals that he and his husband David have two children at the time the film ended.

tropes.name: Bait the Dog
tropes.html: John Reid makes his entrance by bringing a drink to a despairing Elton as he watches Bernie walk off with a woman named Heather. They talk, hook up, and promise to catch up. John then does find him in England, and they get together. The minute John becomes his manager, however? John becomes abusive, emotionally and physically, and pretty much tells Elton he's only interested in the man's money.

tropes.name: Beauty Inversion
tropes.html: Bryce Dallas Howard plays Elton's mother, and is made up to look heavier and be more frumpy than she normally is. Becomes more apparent when she wears old age make-up to portray the character decades later.

tropes.name: Be Yourself
tropes.html: As Elton's personal life begins spiraling out of control thanks to emotional and substance abuse, Bernie notices and pleads with him to for once drop the flamboyant paraphernalia and try playing as Reggie Dwight. Elton is furious at the notion and proclaims That Man Is Dead. It's only when he goes to rehab that he reconnects with his Reggie persona and takes a long-needed break from being Elton John, eventually finding his funk again and managing to find a path to happiness finally.

tropes.name: Big Entrance
tropes.html: Subverted. The opening of the film shows Elton John walking into the camera in slow-motion, framed by blinding lights behind him that heavily shadow him, wearing one of his famous flamboyant costumes featuring goggles, sequins, devil horns, and huge red wings... only to walk into a rehab group, sit down, and begin talking about his many addictions, eventually admitting that he needs help.

tropes.name: Blunt "No"
tropes.html: Someone at the AA meeting asks Elton if marriage made him happy and responds, bluntly and with a bit of annoyance, "Not really, I'm gay."

tropes.name: Bungled Suicide
tropes.html: At one point Elton tries to commit suicide, though he is revived by emergency medical technicians. His survival was a Foregone Conclusion even to those who don't know that he's still alive in real life, because he's describing this at rehab after the fact.

tropes.name: Burden Rant
tropes.html:
Happens twice in the span of two back-to-back scenes, where Elton ends up ranting to both his mother and Bernie at dinner after finally snapping from the compounding stress and loneliness he's been suffering from.
  • Played With. When he goes to see his mother and Fred following his divorce with Renate, he's immediately hit with how his mother wants him to buy her a new house far away from him. When she furiously admits that he's driving her away and then goes onto twist the knife, blaming him for her divorce with his Abusive Dad (which took place when he was a child and because she was caught having an affair), he responds with a rant of his own. He admits that he's sick of hiding who he is, sounding on the verge of tears before deciding that he won't be apologizing for anything, bragging about trying every drug and claiming he's "had sex with everything that moves", crossing from complaining about his problems to misguidedly trying to boast about his life in the same speech.
  • When he's at dinner with Bernie not long later, he's already awkward and bitter, dodging a question about John and focusing on his drink. It's Bernie making a snarky comment about his alcoholism that makes him snap, calling out his best friend for being gone so often and abandoning him after the Troubadour in favor of Heather, who he'd only just met. While Bernie tries to encourage him to get help, Elton continues the rant, furiously pointing out that they started their career together but now he's the one who can't live a normal life, while claiming Bernie just "sits with [his] feet on a desk, chewing on the end of a fucking pencil". This is what makes Bernie point out that he was told not to help, which Elton furiously claims was a test, causing Bernie to leave in frustration.

tropes.name: Callously Casual Cheating
tropes.html: As a continuation of his generally abusive nature, John Reid had the tendency to cheat on Elton — and did so in plain sight, adding to the nastiness of it. The tension around it grows each time it happens. First, he was shown flirting with someone in the middle of "Honky Cat", but Elton didn't catch it. Later, Elton and Bernie spotted him leaning over someone in the hall before a concert, implied to be more flirting. Though Bernie tried to encourage him to stand up for himself, Elton was not in the position to address it yet. His last straw comes when he catches him getting a blowjob, outside his house, from his secretary, in broad daylight. He immediately calls him out and dumps him, but John has no remorse, dismissing it as "rock and roll" and mocking Elton for being upset about it by saying he's "predictable".

tropes.name: Camp Gay
tropes.html: Played with. Naturally, as Elton John is one of the biggest poster boys for glam and stage camp in rock music, the movie reflects that by putting him in many of the iconic flamboyant costumes he's known for (as well as some original costumes inspired by them, such as a massive orange winged number embellished with Swarovski crystals and a Queen Elizabeth gown), and he certainly hams it up when on-stage. He is also shown to have a lot of stereotypically "gay" interests in things like fashion, clubbing, shopping, etc. However, the movie also suggests that a lot of this is just part of his stage persona; off-stage, he's not especially camp and in fact generally comes across as rather Straight Gay. This is both intentional (Egerton, as a straight actor, commented in several interviews that he felt a responsibility to the LGBTQ+ community to not depict Elton John as an overly campy caricature) and apparently reflects Truth in Television, as various invokedWord of God statements note that Elton himself is actually quite traditionally masculine or "blokey" when not performing to an audience.

tropes.name: Child Prodigy
tropes.html: Little Reggie is shown playing music by ear after only hearing it once, including part of Mozart's Rondo alla turca.

tropes.name: Commonality Connection
tropes.html: Elton and Bernie's first meeting starts out awkward, though amicable. It's not until Elton reveals his real name that they actually become friends, as Bernie immediately calls Reg Dwight a "cowboy name" and opens up about liking country western music. Elton admits he likes it too, though quietly. Bernie starts singing "Streets of Laredo", and Elton joining in is what cements their bond, as they then turn up the volume and launch into the song without shame.

tropes.name: Conservative Dad, Liberal Mom
tropes.html: Downplayed with Elton's parents, in that their views aren't terribly different. Stanley is transparently homophobic and concerned with a view of masculinity so strict, he insults his son for simply wanting a hug. He also seems to have no respect for his wife, and remains unable to tolerate Elton's lifestyle even when he's a famous and wealthy rockstar. Sheila is a bit better, as she's more tolerant of her son's path and even allows him some unique expression, like getting an Elvis haircut. When he comes out to her over the phone, however, her claim that she already knows and doesn't care that he's gay is quickly ruined by how she goes onto tell him he'll be alone and unloved forever, as well as that he's "too open" about it (despite that he's closeted). Ultimately, while she's not as outright traditional as her husband, she's not much better when it comes to actually accepting Elton's sexuality and lifestyle. Stanley and Sheila got divorced after a few years, and Elton's stepfather Fred turned out to be the most accepting of these things, never expressing conservative viewpoints and encouraging his stepson's passions right away.

tropes.name: Contrasting New Love Interest
tropes.html: Elton had three on-screen relationships, each wildly different from the last. His first girlfriend was Arabella, the aggressive and loud landlady of the flat he and Bernie move into. The relationship is short lived, both because of her temper and because he's encouraged to come out to her — which results in a comically destructive screaming fit. He next dates John Reid, who initially seems very charming and sweet, seeking him out when he's miserable and alone to gush about his talent and flirt, leading to Elton's first ever sexual encounter. John's Toxic Lover Influence pushes Elton into a hedonistic, expensive, addictive lifestyle, before he starts to engage in Domestic Abuse, both emotional and physical, and reveals his truly explosive, selfish, and empathy-lacking nature. Elton leaves John and, in a few years, meets Renate — a sweet, supportive, gentle woman who gives Elton sympathy when he's at his worst. Elton, desperate for love, marries her, but it doesn't work out — not because of any flaw on Renate's part, but because he couldn't handle having to hide anymore. She's the only one of his exes that he splits with on a mutual note, as he acknowledges that she hadn't done anything wrong, and she doesn't blame him for what happened. In addition, the credits end by talking about how Elton would eventually meet and marry David Furnish, who is someone that finally "loves him properly"; he also has a crush on his sweet, supportive, and creative best friend best friend Bernie throughout the film, though Bernie was quick to clarify that he doesn't love Elton romantically.

tropes.name: Cool Shades
tropes.html: All through the movie, including a scene of Elton with a suitcase containing nothing but his fancy glasses.

tropes.name: Creative Closing Credits
tropes.html: The end credits feature scenes of the movie interspersed with photographs of the actual real life events.

tropes.name: Darker and Edgier
tropes.html: Compared to Bohemian Rhapsody, Rocketman isn't afraid to show a warts-and-all depiction of Elton John. Its R rating means that we see Elton going on coke binges; orgies are more openly depicted; the dialogue swings into Cluster F-Bomb territory (with occasional heavier language); and a much darker side of show business is seen. John Reid's character is also more sinister and manipulative than he was in Bohemian Rhapsody. Despite that, however, the film ends on a hopeful and upbeat note.

tropes.name: Dashing Pompadour
tropes.html: Pre-teen Reggie eventually gets a pompadour, suggested by Fred in an effort to encourage his rockstar dreams. Fittingly, Reggie is shown to be rebellious and brave during "Saturday Night's Alright", talking back to a rude adult with a Badass Boast before launching into the song and smashing his way through a bar window. The pompadour is also used for comedy, as the first time we see it, his rebellious new style is contrasted by the fact that he's playing classical music at a piano recital.

tropes.name: Descent into Addiction
tropes.html: A central theme. Elton becomes addicted to drugs, materialism, and sex. At one point during an orgy, there's a shot of Elton looking distraught while on the floor, surrounded by dozens of writhing bodies; he's aware that he won't be satisfied after relying on these things for happiness, but it'll take a while until he can break this pattern of self-destructive behavior. (And meet his great love, David Furnish, an event that isn't in the movie but is a Foregone Conclusion.)

tropes.name: Destructive Romance
tropes.html: Elton's relationship with John is portrayed in this way, because John more or less introduces Elton to all the vices that'll plague him in his career.

tropes.name: Disappeared Dad
tropes.html: Elton's father was physically there but absent emotionally from him as a child. Cold and distant, he showed no interest in him, before leaving entirely when Elton's mother had an affair. Later when Elton tries to reconnect with him, he's only marginally better, and he's very hurt at seeing his father lavish far more affection on his half-brothers than he'd ever received.

tropes.name: Divorce? Blame the Offspring!
tropes.html: When Elton is a pre-teen, his parents split thanks to a vicious argument caused by Sheila being caught cheating. This is unambiguous, as is the fact that Stanley was the one leaving. However, decades later, Sheila brings up the divorce in a narcissism-fueled rant. She tells Elton she "left his father" for him, framing the entire situation as somehow being his fault while painting herself as a good mother selflessly splitting from his Abusive Parent. This is a clear attempt to hurt him and deny her own guilt, and it cuts Elton deeply; he calls her heartless.

tropes.name: Does Not Know Their Own Potential
tropes.html: Elton knows that he's a talented pianist and dreams of becoming a star, but his insecurities keep him from realizing just how far he could take it. He is surprised that Ray is so fascinated by his on-the-spot composing, seeming to think it's normal. Even as Bernie gushes about his talent and tells him that people like his demos, he still thinks he's not what people are looking for. At the Troubadour, he hides himself away before his concert, terrified that he'll mess up in front of his American heroes. Even though that concert went amazingly, he's still flattered when John praises his talent and tells him he could be the biggest star in America, sheepishly asking if it means he liked the song. Naturally, everyone else is proven right as he becomes a very popular rockstar, and the conflict evolves into focusing on his other issues.

tropes.name: Domestic Abuse
tropes.html: A rare male-on-male example. John Reid is portrayed as a predator who uses Elton for sex and his earning potential. He starts out nice, buying Elton a drink when the latter is pining after Bernie and comforting him about his great performance. When they start dating, he's the one who gets Elton to engage in what would become his many addictions, even labeling his humble life as "embarrassing" and egging him on to want more. Things get much more overtly toxic when he's signed on as Elton's manager. He starts by removing Ray, someone Elton genuinely liked. From there, he turns up the emotional abuse and bullies him into coming out to his mother, only to hit him when he's having a breakdown over her nasty reaction.
