  • The actual Mortal Kombat Tournament doesn't start in this film, probably so that the movie focuses on developing the lore and the characters.
  • The Lin-Kuei aren't implied to be active, unlike in the games, to avoid answering why a bunch of Chinese assassins are running around in the modern day. Instead, Sub-Zero is depicted as being aligned with Outworld while he was with the Lin-Kuei in the 1600s, way before the plot of the movie begins.

tropes.name: Pre-Mortem One-Liner
tropes.html: Natch for Shang Tsung, "Your Soul Is Mine!" shortly before sucking that of Kung Lao.

tropes.name: Punctuated!  For!  Emphasis!
tropes.html: Sonya owes Kano "THREE! MILLION! DOLLARS!"

tropes.name: Race Lift
tropes.html: Of a sort. Mortal Kombat's Raiden was based on a god from Japanese Mythology, but Latino and Caucasian men have played him for the franchise's entire existence. This is the first time an actual Asian has portrayed him, specifically the Japanese Tadanobu Asano.

tropes.name: Ragnarök-Proofing
tropes.html: Hanzo's first spear - a completely normal, human gardening trowel - was last used by Bi-Han to mortally stab Hanzo in the shoulder, and then found by Raiden after Hanzo's death. By the time Raiden gives it to Cole in the climax of the movie, it's been four hundred years and the blade is still covered in blood, but is sharp enough to make Cole's hand bleed when the blood would've rusted it and taken away all of its sharpness.

tropes.name: Really Seven Hundred Years Old
tropes.html: Sub-Zero is a little over 400 years old, but still looks like a young man (minus being pale with bright eyes).

tropes.name: Sacrificial Lion
tropes.html: Kung Lao fights to buy Cole and Liu Kang time to escape, only for Shang Tsung to steal his soul.

tropes.name: Saved for the Sequel
tropes.html: The final shot of the film firmly teases that Johnny Cage will make his anticipated reboot debut in the next film.

tropes.name: Screw the Rules, They Broke Them First!
tropes.html: To ensure Earthrealm will have no Champions come the next tournament, the bulk of the film involves Earthrealm's Champions being hunted down by Sub-Zero and the rest of Shang Tsung's assassins. The final act sees the Champions, with assistance from Raiden, tracking down and assassinating the assassins, so Outworld will have no Champions themselves come to the tournament. Then again, Mortal Kombat has always been about fighting dirty, and this is not technically illegal by the established rules of the tournament.

tropes.name: Screw This, I'm Outta Here
tropes.html:
• After Cole's fight with Goro, Allison and Emily both wisely choose to leave the place where they're staying to avoid anyone else showing up. They don't get away in time before Sub-Zero finds and captures them.
  • Said by Kano when he uses Reptile's acid/saliva to get out of his handcuffs.
  • Not too long after Kano kills Reptile, he tells this much to Sonya and Cole after drinking some of Sonya's beer and talking about Raiden's temple.

tropes.name: See the Invisible
tropes.html: Kano uses the flare on Reptile to make Reptile visible during his bout with Sonya, Cole, and Kano.

tropes.name: Self-Fulfilling Prophecy
tropes.html: The prophecy that foretells Hanzo's blood descendants being the key to preventing Outworld's invasion comes true, despite Shang Tsung's machinations to eliminate the possibility and, indeed, even because of what he does. Every assault on the heroes only drives Cole that much closer to becoming a true Champion and after Shang Tsung steals Kung Lao's soul, it's Cole who rallies the Earthrealm fighters, making the plan that wins them the day.

tropes.name: Sequel Hook
tropes.html: Before being banished back to Outworld by Raiden, Shang Tsung vows to return with more than just fighters, but armies. He also makes comments that imply Bi-Han's eventual resurrection as Noob Saibot. Cole also goes off in search of more fighters on his own, starting with Johnny Cage. Oh, and the actual tournament hasn't happened yet...

tropes.name: Shout-Out
tropes.html: Kano gives other characters a few snarky pop-culture nicknames; he calls Liu Kang "David Copperfield" and "Magic Mike", and calls Raiden "Gandalf".

tropes.name: Shown Their Work
tropes.html: A pre-Scorpion Hanzo creates a prototype of his infamous rope-kunai spear with a rope lying around and a kunai stuck in a garden bed; kunai are believed to have been used as masonry trowels before being modified as tools or weapons by ninjas.

tropes.name: Shut Up, Hannibal!
tropes.html: As Shang Tsung vows to return with armies, Raiden banishes him and says, "He talks too much."

tropes.name: Small Role, Big Impact
tropes.html: By saving her daughter, and hiding her within the hidden compartments of her house, Hanzo's wife effectively ensured her daughter survives so that the Shirai-Ryu can live on, and is taken to be raised by monks thanks to Raiden saving her. She is who Cole and his daughter are descended from, and helps Scorpion defeat Sub-Zero.

tropes.name: Sole Survivor
tropes.html: Hanzo's unnamed daughter is the only survivor of the Shirai Ryu massacre.

tropes.name: Sorting Algorithm of Evil
tropes.html: Invoked. At the end of the movie, the heroes elect to take on all of Shang Tsung's champions 1-on-1, leaving Sub-Zero for last so they can fight him 4-on-1 because he is the most dangerous of them all.

tropes.name: Spoiler Cover
tropes.html: The film's poster shows Cole's Arcana.

tropes.name: Summon Bigger Fish
tropes.html: Unintentionally. Cole's blood reacts with Hanzo Hasashi's kunai to summon him from Netherrealm when Cole is hopelessly outmatched by Sub-Zero. Raiden may or may not have had something to do with that.

tropes.name: Super-Strength
tropes.html:
• What Jax's Arcana appears to be, which extends to his mechanical arms when it finally manifests. This is indicated by him having the Required Secondary Power to brace himself well enough to lift a boulder off Sonya and block blows from Reiko's hammer without being pushed back.
  • Downplayed with Sub-Zero. While he's not strong enough to lift a boulder, he is seen effortlessly tossing fighters larger than him, like Hanzo and Jax, several feet into the air.

tropes.name: Surprisingly Realistic Outcome
tropes.html:
Several, as part of the film's goal to set itself apart from its predecessors and play more by "real world" logic. For example...
  • In the opening, a mortally wounded Hanzo hears his daughter crying and starts to crawl toward her. He makes it a few feet before keeling over dead. Despite his determination and fatherly instincts, he is simply too badly injured to get very far.
  • Sonya introduces Cole to her research, ending with the reveal that the markings and fighters are building towards Mortal Kombat. Cole wastes no time in pointing out how silly it sounds, including the fact they spelled it wrong.
  • When Kung Lao is first introduced, Kano asks who he is, and Kung Lao delivers a Badass Boast worthy of a klassic martial arts movie, complete with rousing music and dramatically speaking of his ancestor, the Great Kung Lao. Kano is unimpressed, and clearly has no idea who the Great Kung Lao is, as the Mortal Kombat tournaments have been hidden from the outside world for thousands of years.
  • Kano may have the mark and be a fairly skilled brawler, but he's still an uncouth thug going up against people who've been training for the majority of their lives in formal martial arts. Even when he gets his laser eye, he's still hopelessly outmatched against even the Badass Normal Sonya Blade, and becomes the only fighter with an Arcana to be killed by someone without one on screen.
  • In a similar vein, Cole wins only one fight (against Goro), but struggles with battling Mileena and Sub-Zero, requiring outside help in both cases, because despite being an MMA fighter, he isn't trained to fight in order to kill or defend against people actively trying to murder him. His victory with Goro was only because he unlocked his Arcana in time, as well as some timely intervention by his wife. Very much truth in television as trained martial artists and MMA fighters have said that being good at fighting in a controlled environment is completely different from fighting in a life-or-death brawl or a street fight.
  • In a broader sense with the series' klassic Fatalities. Because the main series are video games, characters can inflict horrific damage on each other before simply moving into the next match. Here, Fatalities are depicted with exactly the kind of outcome one would expect.

tropes.name: Teeth-Clenched Teamwork
tropes.html: Sonya and Kano do not like each other, do not get along, and can barely tolerate having to work together to save the world. Thus it should be no surprise that Kano promptly turns traitor once Kabal gives him a better offer on behalf of Shang Tsung. Or that Sonya kills him to get his dragon mark without a qualm.

tropes.name: This Is Gonna Suck
tropes.html: A minor example occurs when Kano is training with Liu Kang. After already leg sweeping him twice, when Liu Kang fakes Kano in jumping to dodge his leg sweep, Kano mutters "Ah, fuck" as he lands, since he knows he's going to be eating a third one.

tropes.name: Throwing Your Sword Always Works
tropes.html: Hanzo kills a Lin-Kuei assassin by throwing his wakizashi into his back. This forces him to create his signature spear with a rope dart since his sword is now stuck inside the house.

tropes.name: Token Evil Teammate
tropes.html: Kano, for the Earthrealm Champions. He ultimately betrays them and sides with Shang Tsung's forces.

tropes.name: Took a Level in Badass
tropes.html: An extremely fast example. When Bi-Han is introduced attacking Hanzo Hasashi's farm in the 1600s, he can "merely" make a room cold with his presence and freeze his hands, and even has trouble using his ice powers against Hanzo himself, relying more on physical kombat. When he is re-introduced as Sub-Zero, with over 400 more years of kombat experience, he can freeze entire rooms in seconds, blanket streets in ice shards with a wave of his hands, and stop shotgun pellets at point-blank range.

tropes.name: Torso with a View
tropes.html: Sonya uses the powers from the mark she inherited after killing Kano, to punch a hole through Mileena.

tropes.name: Tragic Keepsake
tropes.html:
• Scorpion's first rope spear used a kunai that his wife used as a garden trowel.
  • After being killed, Kung Lao's hat flies towards the heroes when Raiden teleports them away from the infiltrated temple and is held briefly by Liu Kang. The red scarf ornamenting it is taken to be used as Liu Kang's trademark headband in his fight with Kabal.

tropes.name: The Unchosen One
tropes.html: Part of the reason Sonya gets ostracized by those who have the mark, and Mileena considers her Not Worth Killing, is because of this. She eventually gains a mark after killing Kano.

tropes.name: Undignified Death
tropes.html: In a movie where fights tend to end with the loser being killed in a spectacular fashion, we also get Kano's death by getting stabbed through the eye with a lawn gnome's pointy hat.

tropes.name: Video Credits
tropes.html: As part of the Creative Closing Credits, each actor's name appears next to a red and black silhouette of his or her character.

tropes.name: Villainous Valour
tropes.html: In the final fight against Cole Young and Scorpion, Sub-Zero realizes he is no match for the combined power of his foes. He still rises to his feet, calmly states his Battle Cry, and engages both of them in kombat.

tropes.name: The Voiceless
tropes.html: Nitara has no lines of dialogue. Not that she's alive long enough to really say anything.

tropes.name: Void Between the Worlds
tropes.html: At a certain point, Raiden takes Earthrealm's champions to the indicatively titled "Void," a featureless plane between realms.

tropes.name: We Hardly Knew Ye
tropes.html: Nitara virtually only exists to be very quickly cut in half by Kung Lao's sawblade fatality.

tropes.name: Worthy Opponent
tropes.html: The MMA fighter Ramirez (who defeats Cole at the beginning) thanks him for a good fight.

tropes.name: Xtreme Kool Letterz
tropes.html: Cole initially scoffs at the concept of Mortal Kombat by pointing out that it isn't even spelled correctly.

tropes.name: You Kill It, You Bought It
tropes.html: There are two ways of becoming chosen: either the mark is passed on to you by one of your parents, or you kill the person who currently has it.

tropes.name: Your Soul Is Mine!
tropes.html: Shang Tsung (naturally) steals the soul of Kung Lao. He even says the trope name as he does so!

tropes.name: Arc Words
tropes.html: "Exit" during Emily's part of the story and "poisonous fog" during Dr. Banks'. They're both red herrings.

tropes.name: Bait the Dog
tropes.html: Banks and the viewing audience are made to feel sad for Emily and her becoming a victim of prescription medicine after she killed her husband. Then you find out the truth that Emily is a Devil in Plain Sight.

tropes.name: Batman Gambit
tropes.html: Played straight and then subverted. Emily and Siebert's plan involved a lot of things they could hope would happen, but not guarantee. To wit, they had to get Banks to both prescribe Ablixa to Emily (despite the fact it was a drug he wasn't very familiar with) and not take her off it when she seemingly started sleepwalking (not necessarily the best medical course of action). They also assumed that they would be successful in being able to get Emily a plea deal from the prosecutor, but this is incredibly risky and betting that A) the lawyer that Martin's mother chose and hired would be up to the task, and B) that Banks, who was only Emily's psychiatrist through bad luck, would be a good enough expert witness to potentially sway the jury. This all goes exactly as planned without hiccups. However, it's then subverted and comes crashing down when something they couldn't plan for occurs: that Banks, the randomly chosen psychiatrist, is actually a devious Magnificent Bastard who could beat them at their own game.

tropes.name: Beware the Nice Ones
tropes.html: Dr. Banks is a kind and sincere man who genuinely cares about his patients and wants to help them through their struggles as well as a loving husband and father. But when pushed too far, he can be terrifyingly ruthless as Emily finds out the hard way.

tropes.name: Big Bad Duumvirate
tropes.html: Emily and Siebert. Each of them think that the other's The Dragon to them. Emily is the one who backstabs first.

tropes.name: Bitch in Sheep's Clothing
tropes.html: Emily, who appears to be an innocent, fragile young woman who is struggling with her husband's return from prison. It turns out she's actually a vicious, sociopathic Gold Digger.

tropes.name: Bland-Name Product
tropes.html: Averted with the medication discussed during the film, except for Ablixa.

tropes.name: Bond Villain Stupidity
tropes.html: Averted. Emily's two biggest mistakes (not knowing the truth serum was fake, and not knowing about the Loophole Abuse that Banks uses to lock her up again) are things she could not have anticipated, given her specific background of learning insider trading from Martin and acting from Siebert.

tropes.name: Bookends
tropes.html: The film begins with a helicopter shot zooming in to the window of Emily's apartment, and ends with a helicopter shot zooming out of the window of Emily's new residence.

tropes.name: Bungled Suicide
tropes.html: Emily attempts suicide early on by driving straight into a wall, but survives with only minor injuries. Subverted when it's discovered she staged it simply to take a new antidepressant in a plot for another purpose, and kept her seat belt on specifically to survive.

tropes.name: Clear My Name
tropes.html: Part of Banks's motivation following the incident with Emily.

tropes.name: Color Wash
tropes.html: Many scenes have a warm yellow tint, especially in the first half of the film.

tropes.name: Crying Wolf
tropes.html: At the end of the film, Emily realizes that Banks plans to send her back to the psychiatric ward and keep her doped up on Thorazine and Depakote. She tries to flee, and when she's restrained is frantically protesting that she's not sick — but due to her previous scheming, while Banks and a select few know the truth, no one else believes her.

tropes.name: Dead Star Walking
tropes.html: The trailer, poster and other promotional materials of the film lead you you believe that Channing Tatum plays a major role in the plot, only for his character to get killed roughly thirty minutes in.

tropes.name: Decon-Recon Switch
tropes.html: Of the Clear My Name storyline. Banks obsesses over the case, following false leads and becoming more disheveled in his quest for Revenge, losing his wife and child in the process. But by the end, he is proven right, the bad guys either go to prison or are recommitted/incarcerated, and he gets his family back.

tropes.name: Decoy Protagonist
tropes.html: The story focuses on Emily's struggle with depression until about a third of the way in, where it switches to Banks' point of view and Emily is revealed to be part of a Big Bad Duumvirate.

tropes.name: Depraved Bisexual
tropes.html: While it's not clear how genuine the attraction is, Emily slept with and married Martin for his money, and had an affair with Siebert in order to make millions.

tropes.name: Distracted by the Sexy
tropes.html: How Emily manages to activate the police tracker on Siebert.

tropes.name: Electric Torture
tropes.html: Threatened. After Dr Banks's suspicions about Emily start to harden, he takes her to see an electro-convulsive therapy session in the secure hospital. He tells her that it's a very effective treatment for depression, "but who knows what it could do if there's nothing wrong with you?"

tropes.name: Establishing Character Moment
tropes.html: Banks is introduced having a conversation in French with a new patient and identifying that the man's delusion of seeing his dead father is a fairly normal part of mourning for Haitians. This establishes him as a very intelligent man and a skilled psychiatrist who is not quick to simply dismiss a patient's problems as them being crazy.

tropes.name: "Eureka!" Moment
tropes.html: Early in the film, Banks gets hired by a pharmaceutical company to help conduct a drug trial. After the murder trial, Banks meets with the pharma rep who explains that she has to let him go because of the negative publicity surrounding the case. Offhand, the rep mentions that her company has made an unexpected windfall after the stock of the pharma company which manufactures Ablixa took a nosedive. It occurs to Banks that someone may have financially profited from the murder.

tropes.name: Hidden Depths
tropes.html: Emily, big time. She plans an elaborate scheme involving murder, feigning a suicide attempt and market manipulation with Dr. Siebert, her former psychiatrist and apparent lover, using what she learned about insider trading from Martin and combining it with acting lessons from Siebert. Up until The Reveal, it's very likely that viewers are fully convinced of Emily's innocence and Banks being dangerously unhinged.

tropes.name: Insanity Defense
tropes.html: Suicidal Emily takes various antidepressants before taking a new experimental drug called Ablixa, which appears to be working until she murders her husband while sleepwalking. At the trial, her current psychiatrist Dr. Banks argues that the drug is to blame, and the defense ends up offering an insanity plea. The trope is subverted in that it's specifically mentioned how low the percentage of success for this type of defense is. Emily is only acquitted by reason of insanity in a plea deal, since the prosecutor realizes that he can't win here, and she must remain in a hospital over a set period. Subverted in that she knew precisely what she was doing, and had planned the whole thing with her former psychiatrist Dr. Siebert in order to kill her husband and cash in on the pharmaceutical company's stock plunge. At the end, Dr. Banks figures it out and puts her back into the mental hospital.

tropes.name: Instant Seduction
tropes.html: Emily was able to seduce Dr. Siebert simply by masturbating on her couch in their first session, actively preying on her loneliness.

tropes.name: Laser-Guided Karma
tropes.html: Banks gets Emily readmitted to the psychiatric hospital in almost exactly the same way that Emily back-stabbed Siebert just one scene earlier. He also deliberately prescribes medication for her that genuinely has terrible side-effects unlike the ones she faked previously, and she ends the film drugged into a zombie-like state—plus it's implied that Banks will use his discretion as her doctor to keep her committed for life.

tropes.name: Lipstick Lesbian
tropes.html: Dr. Siebert is a feminine woman who's revealed to have been in a relationship with Emily. The latter might also count, or at least be bisexual, as she's equally feminine.

tropes.name: Magic Feather
tropes.html: The truth serum Banks gives Emily was a placebo, but she acts as though she were given an actual dose.

tropes.name: Morton's Fork
tropes.html: Emily could have taken the medication that left her a zombie, or she could be placed on psychiatric hold for refusing to take her medication that would leave her in Banks' care.

tropes.name: Ms. Fanservice
tropes.html: Rooney Mara as Emily shows explicit nudity in a sex scene, and is also shown masturbating in front of, then kissing, Dr. Siebert.

tropes.name: Never Trust a Trailer
tropes.html: The trailer plays up the medical drama aspect of the movie, emphasizing the idea of Emily dealing with her medicine's side effects and mentioning that it was made by the folks behind Contagion (2011). While the side-effects are relevant, there is a LOT more going on in the movie.

tropes.name: Nice Job Fixing It, Villain!
tropes.html: Emily was able to fix it so everyone got punished for their role in Martin's death. She backstabbed Siebert without a second thought, and then by scamming Banks by pretending to be insane, he was able to turn the tables on her, turn her own con back on itself, and leave her a drugged-up zombie for refusing to take her "medication" that inflicted horrible side effects on her.

tropes.name: Obfuscating Insanity
tropes.html: Emily, it turns out, faked her insanity, with Dr. Siebert advising her on how to do this. It's all part of a plan to kill Emily's husband, blame it on the drug she was taking, and make money by short-selling the manufacturer's stock due to the negative publicity driving down the price.

tropes.name: Pay Evil unto Evil
tropes.html: At the end of the film, Banks double-crosses Emily; he prescribes medication that would render her catatonic, and when she refuses the treatment he gets her sent back to the psychiatric ward, where she's heavily medicated anyway. It's immensely grim, but since double jeopardy meant Emily wouldn't face jailtime for murdering her husband and nearly ruining Banks' life, Banks is likely going to make sure she stays committed for a very long time, if not the rest of her life, to make her pay for what she did.

tropes.name: Predatory Big Pharma
tropes.html: Every which way. At first, this appears to be a more straightforward story about the severely depressed Emily, who is put on Ablixa by Banks, a haughty doctor who has taken money from pharmaceutical companies, only for her to kill her husband while under its effects. It's then revealed that while Banks is taking money from Big Pharma, Emily is conspiring with her former therapist Dr. Siebert to drive down and then inflate the price of Ablixa in order for them to make millions together. She killed her husband and frames multiple people for this scheme. However, at the end, Banks proves he's Not So Above It All by placing Emily in an essential permanent coma of emotional torture for framing him, scheming against him, and killing Martin all for money.

tropes.name: Product Placement
tropes.html: Dr. Banks drinks Red Bull, uses Apple laptops and Blackberry phones, and drives a BMW. Crazy people drive Volkswagen.

tropes.name: Reality Has No Subtitles
tropes.html: Dr. Banks interviews an agitated Haitian in untranslated French, but then summarizes the conversation for the cop who brought him in.

tropes.name: Red Herring
tropes.html:
• The movie knows you're watching a thriller with a massive Chekhov's Armory, and drops as many clues as it can about the makers of Ablixa being behind Martin's murder without following through on any of it.
  • There's also a lot of Subtext suggesting that Banks will be the actual villain, especially given the accusation of sexual impropriety that he kept from his wife. Again, this isn't the case.
  • The exit signs prominent during Emily's first two episodes could be a subversion. On the one hand, they have no relevance to the plot, but they could also be symbolic of Emily's plan to leave ("exit") with the money she got from Siebert.

tropes.name: The Reveal
tropes.html: A big, long one towards the end. Emily and Siebert began sleeping together after Emily saw her for the first time. They taught each other their respective skillsets (with Siebert showing Emily how to act depressed, and Emily explaining what Martin had taught her about financial markets) and orchestrated the whole deal with Ablixa to get rich off the stock market. Banks was just a random casualty of the scheme.

tropes.name: Roaring Rampage of Revenge
tropes.html: Banks goes on this as the film progresses. Ditto for Emily.

tropes.name: Surprisingly Sudden Death
tropes.html: Sleepwalking had already been established as odd but harmless, but in its second appearance there's a rather literal Gut Punch.

tropes.name: Took a Level in Badass
tropes.html: Banks starts off as a polite, well-meaning, and competent psychiatrist. After Emily and Siebert ruin his life, he becomes a ruthless, full-blown Chessmaster in the course of exacting his vengeance.

tropes.name: White-Collar Crime
tropes.html: Why Emily's husband was in jail. Also, it is possible to make money on the stock exchange by betting that a company's shares will go down, rather than up. If you know that a pharmaceutical company's new anti-depressant is going to get some very bad publicity for its side effects, then it's a pretty safe bet.

tropes.name: Wounded Gazelle Gambit
tropes.html: Emily's favorite technique. She pretends to be depressed in order to kill her husband and get away with it; she pretends that Banks seduced her in order to paint herself as a rape victim, and she plays vulnerable throughout it all.

tropes.name: You Have to Believe Me!
tropes.html: Banks spends the second half of the film trying to convince people of his theory, but no one helps him until he has a smoking gun. He then turns the tables on Emily, meaning she's forcibly returned to the psychiatric ward even as she's screaming that she's not sick.
